This is an initial public offering of shares of Class A common stock of Anthropic, PBC. We are selling 801,351,354 shares of Class A common stock and the selling stockholders identified in this prospectus are selling an additional 23,648,646 shares of Class A common stock. We will not receive any proceeds from the sale of shares of our Class A common stock by any of the selling stockholders. We have been approved to list our Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol “ANT.” We have a novel capital and corporate governance structure. We are incorporated as a public benefit corporation under Delaware law, a structure consistent with our commitment to artificial intelligence (“AI”) safety and responsibility. As a public benefit corporation, we are required to balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the specific public benefit purpose identified in our amended and restated certificate of incorporation: the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity. We created our Long-Term Benefit Trust (the “LTBT”) to help ensure that Anthropic, PBC is managed in a manner that responsibly balances its goals as a public benefit corporation. The LTBT is intended to operate as an independent body of financially disinterested trustees with expertise in AI safety, national security, public policy, and social enterprise. Through a special class of common stock, Class T common stock, the LTBT generally has the authority to elect and remove the Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. Our Class T common stock does not otherwise have voting rights with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally and has no economic rights.

text:
The following are abbreviations, acronyms, and definitions of certain terms used in this prospectus:
“accelerators” refer to processors purpose-built or adapted for the large-scale computations required to pre-train, post-train, refine, and run super intelligence models. These processors are significantly more efficient and faster than general-purpose processors for these workloads.
“agent loop” refers to the iterative cycle in which an SI agent receives a task, takes an action, such as planning a project, running code, or calling a tool, observes the result, and decides its next step, with this cycle repeating until the task is complete. The agent loop is the core execution pattern underlying agentic SI behavior.
“agentic AI” or “agentic SI” refers to systems that, with varying degrees of autonomy, can plan, determine, and sequence actions and execute them to accomplish defined objectives, including through interaction with external tools, services, datasets, and environments on behalf of a user.
“API” refers to application programming interface, a standardized interface that allows external software to access a system’s capabilities programmatically. SI model providers may offer APIs that allow software developers to send inputs to a model and receive outputs, enabling integration into the software developers’ products and workflows.
“Applied AI” refers to a discipline and organizational function focused on embedding SI capabilities directly into production business environments to address specific customer requirements. Applied AI teams, which include forward-deployed engineers, work with enterprises to design and deploy custom solutions, specialized workflows, and domain-specific implementations tailored to a customer’s own systems and processes.
“artificial intelligence” or “AI” refers to a machine-based system that learns or is trained from data and, for explicit or implicit objectives and with varying levels of autonomy, processes that data to infer patterns, generate outputs—such as predictions, content, recommendations, and decisions—and act upon physical or virtual environments. For purposes of this prospectus, we use the terms “artificial intelligence,” “AI,” “super intelligence,” and “SI” interchangeably.
“closing the loop” refers to a development cycle in which successive versions of an SI model assist in building the next, with the goal of compounding capability gains over time.
“compute” refers to the computational processing resources used to train and run SI models, including, without limitation, specialized accelerators, memory, networking, storage, and power systems that are deployed in data centers or other physical computing environments.

text:
“compute multipliers” refer to algorithmic and methodological improvements in training and inference that increase the effective output of a given amount of compute.
“computer use” refers to an SI capability that allows a model to observe and interact with a graphical user interface, such as clicking, typing, and navigating applications, similar to how a human operator would.
“Constitutional AI” refers to an approach to training AI models using a set of written principles, which we refer to as Claude’s constitution, currently organized around four priorities: being broadly safe, broadly ethical, compliant with our guidelines, and genuinely helpful. Under Constitutional AI, our models evaluate, critique, and revise their own responses against these principles, enabling us to define and control model behavior through auditable principles, rather than relying solely on fixed rule-based instructions or human reviewers.
“context window” refers to the maximum amount of text, code, or other content, measured in tokens, that an SI model can process in a given request, encompassing instructions, prior conversation history, user input, and the model’s output.
“CSP” refers to a cloud service provider, a technology company that owns and operates large-scale cloud computing infrastructure and provides on-demand compute, storage, and networking. CSPs may also serve as distribution channels through which SI products and services are made available to customers. The largest CSPs, sometimes referred to as hyperscalers, operate at global scale with significant infrastructure and market concentration.
“customer” refers to a prosumer or an organization that uses our models, platform, or applications.

text:
“customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis,” “customers with $1 million or more of revenue on a TTM basis,” and “customers with $10 million or more of revenue on a TTM
basis” each refer to customers contributing revenue equal to or greater than the applicable dollar amount during the trailing twelve-month (“TTM”) period ending on the measurement date. For purposes of this metric, we define a customer as a distinct organization, identified by aggregating the accounts that we determine belong to the same organization based on internal records and available data. We do not separately define or internally track a category of “enterprise” customers, and our customers are not segmented or measured internally by reference to whether a given customer is an “enterprise.” Because spending $100,000 or more on our products is generally characteristic of organizational rather than individual usage, we use the number of and revenue from customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis as our measure of enterprise adoption and engagement with Claude throughout this prospectus, including in references to “enterprise customers” and “enterprise adoption.”
“frontier intelligence” refers to SI systems at the current leading edge of capability and safety, performing at or near the highest levels of any existing system across a broad range of tasks.
“hallucinations” refer to outputs in which an SI model generates factually incorrect or fabricated information with apparent confidence.
“inference” refers to the process by which a trained SI model processes an input and generates an output. Inference occurs each time a user or agent interacts with an SI system.
“interleaved thinking” refers to a capability whereby an SI model interposes discrete reasoning steps between successive tool calls within a single response, rather than confining its reasoning to a single planning phase at the outset.
“interpretability” refers to research into how and why SI models produce specific outputs, with the goal of making model behavior more transparent and verifiable, especially in high-stakes applications.
“knowledge work” refers to complex cognitive work and related professional activities, including obtaining, producing, analyzing, and communicating information through tasks such as coding, drafting analyses, synthesizing research, building financial models, and managing and automating documents and workflows.
“LLMs” refer to large language models, or SI models trained primarily on large datasets to understand and generate natural language and computer code.

text:
“mechanistic interpretability” refers to a subfield of interpretability research focused on reverse-engineering the internal computations of neural networks. Rather than inferring model behavior from inputs and outputs alone, mechanistic interpretability seeks to identify the specific features and circuits within a model that give rise to its behavior with the goal of making model reasoning auditable at the mechanism level and detecting failure modes, including deceptive or unsafe behavior, that may not surface in standard testing.
“model weights” refer to the numerical parameters encoding a trained SI model’s behavior, which are the primary intellectual asset of a frontier intelligence developer, representing the accumulated investment in compute, data, and research.
“multi-agent orchestration” refers to an architecture in which multiple SI agents collaborate on a shared task, with one coordinating while others execute subtasks in parallel, enabling more complex, long-horizon work than a single agent can complete alone.
“Net Revenue Retention” reflects customer expansion, contraction, and churn as of a measurement date. We calculate Net Revenue Retention by dividing the Qualified Customers’ Current Period revenue by their Base Period revenue. A Qualified Customer is a customer with at least $1 of revenue during the Base Period, excluding subscribers to our Claude Pro, Max, and Ultra plans, whose fixed-price subscriptions do not reflect the expansion and contraction behavior this metric is intended to capture. The Base Period is the three months ending a year prior to the measurement date. The Current Period is the three months ending as of the measurement date.
“open-weight” refers to an SI model whose trained model weights are publicly released, allowing third parties to download, run, and modify the model, subject to the terms of the model’s license, without necessarily providing access to the underlying training data or code.
“pay-for-intelligence” or “consumption” refers to our revenue model under which customers pay for their usage of our intelligence service, which is metered in tokens and priced according to the model selected.
“persistent,” in the context of SI applications, refers to denoting data, state, or context that is continuously retained beyond the boundary of a single operation, session, or interaction, remaining accessible for reuse across subsequent steps, sessions, or workflows without requiring reinitialization.

text:
“post-training” refers to the collection of techniques applied to a pre-trained model to refine its behavior, including reinforcement learning, supervised refinement methods, and other alignment methods. Post-training is the stage in which much of the work to make a frontier model helpful, accurate, and safe is performed, including the application of safety and alignment techniques.
“pre-training” refers to the initial stage of training an SI model, in which the model learns general patterns and representations from large-scale datasets of text, code, and other data, typically by predicting the next token in a sequence. The output of pre-training is a base model with broad capabilities that has not yet been adapted for any specific deployment context.
“primitives” refer to the foundational, modular building blocks of a software system from which more complex applications and workflows are constructed.
“prompt injection” refers to an adversarial technique in which malicious instructions are embedded in content an SI model is asked to process, such as websites, documents, or tool outputs, with the aim of overriding or manipulating the model’s intended behavior, typically without the user’s knowledge.
“prosumers” refer to individual users who subscribe to SI tools to perform knowledge work.
“reinforcement learning” refers to a machine learning approach in which a model learns to perform a task by taking actions, receiving feedback signals called rewards, and adjusting its behavior to maximize the rewards it accrues over time. In contemporary SI development, reinforcement learning is widely used to refine model behavior after pre-training, including to improve helpfulness, accuracy, and adherence to safety guidelines.
“RLHF” refers to reinforcement learning from human feedback, a specific form of reinforcement learning in which human evaluators rate the model’s responses, and those ratings are used as the reward signal to guide training.
“Run-Rate Revenue” is an operating metric that refers to the estimated annualized value of our revenue-generating activity as of a measurement date, calculated as the sum of (i) our consumption-based fees during the trailing 28-day period ended on the measurement date, multiplied by 13, and (ii) our aggregate monthly subscription fees as of the measurement date, multiplied by 12. For purposes of calculating Run-Rate Revenue, consumption-based fees and subscription-based fees are derived from customer usage and active subscriptions.

“super intelligence” or “SI” refers to a machine-based system that learns or is trained from data and, for explicit or implicit objectives and with varying levels of autonomy, processes that data to infer patterns, generate outputs—such as predictions, content, recommendations, and decisions—and act upon physical or virtual environments. For purposes of this prospectus, to avoid confusion, we use the terms “super intelligence,” “SI,” “artificial intelligence,” and “AI” interchangeably. On September 29, 2026, the President of the United States issued Executive Order 14434, which directs federal executive departments and agencies to use the terms “Super Intelligence” and “SI” in place of “Artificial Intelligence” and “AI.”
“systems integrators” refer to third-party technology and professional services firms that design, build, and deploy integrated solutions for customers by combining products and services from multiple technology vendors into unified systems tailored to customer needs.
“tokens” refer to numeric units into which an SI model converts the data it processes, including text, images, audio, and video, the number of which varies by the model and tokenizer applied. Tokens are the smallest individual units of data a language model processes and can correspond to words, subwords, characters, or bytes. A tokenizer is the component of a model that converts customer inputs into the sequence of tokens the model processes and then converts the processed tokens into the outputs provided to customers.

location: PROSPECTUS SUMMARY > Overview
text:
For the first time in history, intelligence is something humans can build. The cognitive capability to reason, analyze, synthesize, decide, and create is producible at scale and accessible on demand. We believe this abundance of super intelligence1 will rapidly transform every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet. If this technology truly delivers on its potential—with the risks well managed—it could significantly accelerate global growth and dramatically improve quality of life for people around the world.
Anthropic was founded in 2021 by a team of researchers responsible for many of the breakthroughs that define SI. We are first and foremost a research lab—our mission is the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity. This mission directs our focus—along with our talent and culture, our frontier and safety research, our approach to compute, and our enterprise strategy, it is one of the core advantages that set us apart. These advantages enable us to continuously advance frontier intelligence and shape the standards for its safe and responsible development. Our frontier intelligence, Claude, is delivered to customers through our models, platform, and applications. Claude has experienced the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history, as demonstrated by revenue growing from $0 at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $17.0 billion for the three months ended September 30, 2026. This rapid and growing adoption generates two self-reinforcing dynamics—an improvement loop that advances Claude and an investment loop that helps fund our continued research at the frontier.

location: PROSPECTUS SUMMARY > Overview > Our Core Advantages
text:
Our Core Advantages
Mission & Focus. All of our efforts are guided by a singular focus on our mission. This focus enables us to concentrate talent, research, and compute investment on the highest-value work for humanity and to avoid conflicting priorities. Achieving our mission means the world gains the enormous benefits of frontier intelligence while mitigating the most significant risks, and we believe this requires safety and capability to advance together.
Talent & Culture. Our mission and focus enable us to attract and retain world-class talent, including researchers and engineers who want their work to shape a better future. We also have a culture that promotes a low-ego, truth-seeking environment, where frontier capability and safety are mutually reinforcing. We believe our culture has driven our talent density as we have scaled.
Frontier & Safety Research. We believe that sustained, focused research at the frontier of intelligence is required to build the most capable and safest super intelligence systems. Our frontier capabilities and safety research are deeply integrated and directly shape model design, training, and deployment, helping us produce systems that are more reliable, steerable, and well suited for real-world deployment, particularly in demanding enterprise environments. We translate our research leadership into innovation velocity and have consistently released better models, platform capabilities, and applications. Each version of a Claude model assists in building the next, helping to compress development timelines and produce compounding improvements in the speed at which we innovate. We refer to this recursive dynamic as “closing the loop,” and we believe it is one of the most significant structural advantages in frontier intelligence.

location: PROSPECTUS SUMMARY > Overview > Our Core Advantages
text:
Our Approach to Compute. We manage compute as a single, fungible pool from multiple strategic partners, and we dynamically direct available compute between workloads based on where the marginal unit is expected to be most productive at any given time. We believe that this approach to compute enables us to deliver superior models, serve more customers, and achieve greater productivity from our compute investment. This compute efficiency creates the foundation for us to advance frontier capabilities through research and model development, meet growing demand from customers, and provide for internal usage of Claude. We have achieved this through our research breakthroughs and our multi-chip compute architecture across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs, enabling us to orchestrate workloads to optimize for price and performance. To support our research, model development, customer demand, and internal usage of Claude, we continue to invest at scale. As of and subsequent to September 30, 2026, we have entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements, including short-term commitments, as well as leases not yet commenced, with an aggregate committed spend of approximately $900.9 billion, substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure. These commitments include approximately $451.6 billion expected to be incurred before December 31, 2030, and substantially all of the remainder is expected to be incurred between 2031 and 2045. Approximately $70.7 billion of these commitments are due in the 12 months following September 30, 2026. See the section titled “Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations—Liquidity and Capital Resources—Contractual Obligations” for more information.
Enterprise Strategy. Our enterprise strategy is built on the belief that frontier intelligence is most valuable in real-world settings, as deployment across enterprises is where economic impact is greatest and where the improvement loop from customer feedback is richest. Accordingly, we have organized our research priorities, our product roadmap, and our go-to-market and Applied AI teams around enterprise use cases, which range from routine knowledge work to the most complex problems. The customer feedback we gather directs our research focus and makes Claude more capable over time. This broadens where Claude can be deployed and further expands enterprise adoption, which helps ensure that the benefits of our technology reach people and organizations at scale.

location: PROSPECTUS SUMMARY > Overview > A Near-Term Opportunity to Transform Cognitive Work
text:
A Near-Term Opportunity to Transform Cognitive Work
Frontier intelligence is transforming cognitive work—the application of knowledge, reasoning, and judgment to produce economic value. We believe it will make humans far more capable and expand the world’s overall capacity for that work, including accelerating scientific discovery and helping businesses grow. Knowledge workers are the leading edge of this opportunity. As the frontier advances, more capable models can unlock entirely new use cases while also efficiently serving a wide range of cognitive work at scale across the capability-cost-speed curve. We believe the work that knowledge workers perform represented more than $40 trillion in economic value globally in 2025,2 and with the potential for frontier intelligence to make them meaningfully more productive, our near-term opportunity is to expand this value and accelerate economic growth. While it is still early to forecast the full impact of frontier intelligence across the economy, International Data Corporation (“IDC”) estimates that investment in AI solutions and services will yield a cumulative global economic impact of $22.5 trillion by 2031.3 We believe the impact could be even greater.
title: US-PROSPECTUS (S-1/A, preliminary) | PROSPECTUS SUMMARY > Overview > A Near-Term Opportunity to Transform Cognitive Work

location: PROSPECTUS SUMMARY > Overview > Frontier Intelligence May Reshape Entire Sectors and Accelerate Novel Discoveries
text:
Frontier Intelligence May Reshape Entire Sectors and Accelerate Novel Discoveries
We believe frontier intelligence represents a larger opportunity than any prior technology cycle, and Claude is already demonstrating this potential. Claude can now execute complex projects autonomously and turn open-ended tasks into finished, high-quality deliverables. These capabilities enable it to transform the largest sectors of the economy, driving meaningful gains in productivity and output. Frontier model capabilities may extend beyond current markets to open entirely new ones, reaching domains such as robotics, advanced manufacturing, and logistics, and accelerating progress in scientific research, including drug discovery and materials science. For example, in the life sciences sector, where annual global pharmaceutical spend is expected to exceed $2 trillion in 2026,4 Claude is used in drug discovery and development by our customers, our biotechnology partners, and our own researchers. We are also extending Claude into robotics, where our Model Hardware Standard enables AI agents to operate lab and manufacturing equipment such as microscopes, liquid handlers, and off-the-shelf robotic arms. Ultimately, we believe frontier intelligence will help drive global economic growth. As frontier models make workers and organizations more productive, become embedded in the products and services they deliver, and unlock new business models, they create economic output that did not previously exist. We believe our opportunity is to capture a share not only of today’s economic activity but also of that newly created output as the global economy expands.

text:
The Importance of Safety and Ethical Behavior
See the section titled “Industry, Market, and Other Data” for a description of how we calculate annual economic value attributable
While the potential benefits of super intelligence are extraordinary, its rapid advancement will impact the economy and society in ways that could create significant disruption, particularly if these technologies are not developed and deployed responsibly. For example, bad actors have already conducted high-profile cyberattacks using frontier model capabilities to discover vulnerabilities, generate malware, and evade detection tools; other risks associated with misuse, including in the domain of biology, could result in even greater harm. Frontier models deployed at scale also have the potential to concentrate power and wealth both within and between countries in ways that could erode trust, harm society, and destabilize the geopolitical order. Misaligned models could corrupt institutional decision-making or cause large-scale harm through autonomous actions that are not visible or understandable to their users and operators. We believe that companies at the frontier must invest in safety and alignment to help ensure the responsible diffusion of this technology. We also believe that safety, alignment, and ethical behavior resonate particularly strongly with enterprises, where rigorous safeguards, predictable model behavior, and demonstrable accountability have become decisive criteria in selecting a partner for mission-critical workloads.

location: PROSPECTUS SUMMARY > Overview > Claude as a Virtual Collaborator
text:
Claude as a Virtual Collaborator
We believe we have reached an inflection point where Claude and other super intelligence systems can function as genuine collaborators in professional work. They quickly complete substantive tasks that might otherwise occupy a skilled professional for several hours, a full day, or longer. These systems are also becoming increasingly capable of performing tasks that were previously too difficult or costly to complete or surfacing original insights and analyses. We refer to these systems that work alongside humans to perform complex, multi-step work at professional levels as Virtual Collaborators. Virtual Collaborators carry the access rights, system connections, and context that their organizations grant them, which allows them to function more accurately and reliably. They can navigate and use internal tools and execute workflows that span multiple steps that require sustained reasoning. Virtual Collaborators are AI designed to be embedded where work gets done, and our aim is to continue extending them to knowledge workers globally, a population that is estimated to exceed one billion in 2028.5
Claude Code. The clearest manifestation of Virtual Collaborators today is Claude Code, our coding agent and the product we believe has most concretely defined what autonomous work at the frontier looks like. Claude Code shifted the market’s understanding of what frontier models could do in collaboration with software developers: the model suggests the next line of code and goes further by planning, writing, testing, and debugging—a process that results in production-grade code. Within months of its release, autonomous coding became the reference point for measuring the progress of frontier intelligence. For enterprise use cases, we believe the launch of Claude Code was comparable in its impact to the introduction of the first widely adopted conversational SI assistants. What makes Claude Code a Virtual Collaborator is its sustained reasoning, a harness that translates intent into actions, an execution environment that maintains a persistent state whether on a developer’s machine or in a sandboxed cloud environment, integration with existing tools and systems, and a user-friendly interface. Its uses are highly varied and often surprising: for example, NASA engineers used Claude Code to plan and write navigation commands for the Mars Perseverance rover, resulting in the first SI-planned drive on Mars.

location: PROSPECTUS SUMMARY > Overview > Claude as a Virtual Collaborator
text:
Software developers are powerful advocates for Claude—they understand how systems work, have credibility evaluating technical tools, and often serve as internal champions for adopting new technologies. Winning their trust creates a foundation for broader diffusion of Virtual Collaborators across enterprise workforces. We are already seeing this pattern play out with non-technical teams increasingly adopting Claude Code and Claude Cowork to manage their own workflows.
Claude Cowork. All digital work is ultimately an expression of code, and Claude’s mastery of it powers Virtual Collaborators capable of handling complex work far beyond software development. Claude Cowork extends the agentic architecture of Claude Code to knowledge workers broadly by translating a user’s intent into completed work, autonomously reading files, navigating applications, and executing multi-step workflows on a user’s desktop while the underlying code is abstracted away. By extending beyond Claude Code with applications purpose-built for specific professions and industry verticals, we accelerate Claude’s diffusion into new categories of knowledge work and deepen our presence across the enterprise. As of September 30, 2026, adoption of Claude Cowork, which we made available as a research preview in January 2026, outpaced the adoption Claude Code achieved at the equivalent point following its research preview release in February 2025. In September 2026, we began merging Claude Cowork and Claude.ai, bringing agentic and conversational work into a unified application. Users can now move from a simple question to complex, multi-step tasks in the same conversation.
Extending Virtual Collaborators. We believe the trajectory for Virtual Collaborators is clear and accelerating. Each generation of Claude models has expanded along multiple dimensions: the depth and rigor of their reasoning, the duration and autonomy of the work they can sustain, the complexity of tasks they can complete, and the volume of useful output they can produce. Capability evaluations and benchmarking have shown substantial improvements across Claude model versions in the duration and complexity of tasks that can be completed reliably, with more recent model versions demonstrating particularly significant advances.
IDC, Worldwide Developer Population Growth Forecast, 2025–2029, doc # US53789825, September 2025.

location: PROSPECTUS SUMMARY > Overview > Enterprise Adoption of Claude
text:
Enterprise Adoption of Claude
The speed and depth of our enterprise customer adoption are powerful evidence of Claude’s position at the frontier of super intelligence. Our customer base as of September 30, 2026 includes:
•More than 11,900 customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis;
•More than 1,900 customers with $1 million or more of revenue on a TTM basis; and
•Approximately 250 customers with $10 million or more of revenue on a TTM basis.
We believe customers choose Claude for a wide variety of use cases, from routine knowledge work to their most important problems. They come to us for access to frontier intelligence across our platform and applications that deliver real-world outcomes. We see this conviction in customer behavior: enterprises consistently utilize our latest and most capable models as soon as they are released, gravitating to the most advanced option for their highest-value work. Our customers see us as a long-term partner for the frontier capabilities we offer today, for the innovation they expect from us in the future, and for our ability to meet their needs across the capability-cost-speed curve.
Beyond our models, the Claude Platform provides primitives that enable customers to accelerate time-to-value and leverage Claude’s intelligence in a variety of use cases. These primitives are the same ones we use to build our own applications. Our applications, such as Claude Code and Claude Cowork, multiply the impact of employees. Over time, our applications have become more capable and are now frequently being used to conduct long-running autonomous work alongside employees. Improvements to our models, platform, and applications accrue to the benefit of our customers and drive continued adoption.
Our commitment to our mission instills confidence in our customers to choose Claude as a trusted partner. Our investments in research on alignment, interpretability, cybersecurity, and enterprise-grade controls aim to deliver the predictability and dependability that organizations need in customer-facing and regulated contexts. This trust means that enterprises can expand the scope of the work that they delegate to Claude, as well as the systems into which Claude is integrated. Enterprises are aligning their strategies around Claude with the confidence that we are building frontier intelligence that serves their needs in the long term.
title: US-PROSPECTUS (S-1/A, preliminary) | PROSPECTUS SUMMARY > Overview > Enterprise Adoption of Claude

location: PROSPECTUS SUMMARY > Overview > Enterprise Adoption of Claude
text:
Today, enterprises rely on Claude to reason, plan, and execute across complex workflows with a level of trustworthiness and judgment that we believe was not available from earlier generations of these technologies. Customers realize value from Claude in three primary ways: more productive employees, faster processes, and embedded intelligence in their products. As Claude’s capabilities grow, our customers benefit and often broaden their adoption of Claude in new workflows. This expanding role reflects a broader shift in how Claude is used inside the enterprise, from a tool that responds to discrete prompts to a Virtual Collaborator.
We drive the diffusion of Claude primarily by making it accessible across multiple product surfaces. For example:
•Claude Platform, our comprehensive agentic development environment, provides customers with direct access to the primitives to build, deploy, and scale their own applications that leverage Claude’s capabilities within their own products and workflows.
•Claude Code, our coding agent, works alongside human software developers on end-to-end software development: writing, planning, editing, testing, debugging, and committing code across production-scale codebases.
•Claude Cowork, our knowledge work agent, has computer use capability that enables it to work with professionals on end-to-end business tasks: autonomously researching, drafting, analyzing, synthesizing, and executing other knowledge work.
Much of the diffusion of Claude has been organic. We amplify this with our go-to-market and Applied AI teams, which extend our reach by meeting customers where they are through distribution partnerships that place Claude inside customers’ existing technology stacks. For example, Claude is accessible on all three major cloud platforms—Amazon Web Services (“AWS”), Google Cloud Platform (“GCP”), and Microsoft Azure (“Azure”). We have a joint go-to-market approach with these CSPs through which we establish direct contractual relationships with our customers while paying a fee to each CSP. This structure allows us to foster stronger commercial alignment with these CSPs, avoid channel conflict, set pricing, and realize the financial benefits of ongoing compute efficiency improvements. Ecosystem partnerships also expand our reach, allowing customers to adopt Claude through systems integrators, such as Accenture, Deloitte, KPMG, and PwC; consultants; and data platforms, such as Salesforce and Snowflake. We recently launched an AI services company, Ode with Anthropic, in partnership with leading private equity firms to bring Claude’s capabilities to mid-sized companies across sectors, building solutions on the Claude Platform and supporting customers over the long term.

location: PROSPECTUS SUMMARY > Overview > Strengths of Our Financial Model
text:
Strengths of Our Financial Model
Building and scaling frontier intelligence is one of the most important and capital-intensive endeavors in history. Our financial model provides us with the following strengths that allow us to build and scale efficiently:
•Rapid Revenue Growth. Our enterprise strategy is designed to drive durable customer adoption by embedding Claude directly into business-critical workflows and enabling the development of products built on Claude. We believe that enterprise customers achieve a compelling return on investment from Claude, as agentic workflows can drive both top-line growth and efficiency. This enables us to expand quickly with customers, as demonstrated by our Net Revenue Retention of approximately 900% as of September 30, 2026. Diffusion also accelerates as our models become more capable and efficient, allowing us to lower the cost per task for customers. For example, Opus 5.5 reduced customer costs per task by approximately 40% compared to Opus 5. Lower costs per task drive greater usage, which in turn drives broader diffusion of Claude. Our compute efficiency allows us to deliver these reductions while preserving our margins.
•Compute Efficiency. Our compute efficiency drives more intelligence from research and model development, and we believe this approach can support more customer and internal usage of Claude for the same amount of compute compared to other approaches. Our compute efficiency is demonstrated by revenue that grew 1,127% year over year for the three months ended September 30, 2026, compared to compute and infrastructure expenses that grew 382% during the same period.
•Operating Efficiency. Our operating efficiency, derived from our high talent density, our efficient go-to-market, and how extensively our teams leverage Claude in their work, enables us to scale with a smaller team relative to other large enterprise technology companies. Our operating efficiency is demonstrated by TTM revenue per employee of over $6.6 million as of September 30, 2026, compared to $1.4 million as of September 30, 2025.
The demonstrated growth, scale, and efficiency of our financial model help us to continue making significant long-term investments to build at the frontier responsibly. Our business trajectory and financial profile have enabled us to access capital and secure compute from investors and partners. As of September 30, 2026, we had raised an aggregate of $141.1 billion of capital and had cash and cash equivalents of $95.6 billion and short-term investments of $36.3 billion.

location: PROSPECTUS SUMMARY > Overview > Our Self-Reinforcing Loops
text:
Our Self-Reinforcing Loops
Our scale and growth create self-reinforcing loops that make Claude better over time and that we believe create durable competitive advantages.
•Improvement Loop. Enterprise deployments of Claude deepen our understanding of the hard problems, edge cases, and domain-specific challenges that matter most to our customers. We improve our models, platform, and applications based on feedback from customers using our offerings in production across their businesses. These improvements result in wider deployments and adoption that fuel the next cycle of improvement.
•Investment Loop. Revenue from expanding enterprise adoption helps us to fund the compute, research, and talent needed to improve Claude. Claude’s advancing capabilities expand the range of tasks and workflows customers use Claude for, broadening our addressable market and driving deeper deployment, additional revenue, and continued reinvestment in Claude.
title: US-PROSPECTUS (S-1/A, preliminary) | PROSPECTUS SUMMARY > Overview > Our Self-Reinforcing Loops

location: PROSPECTUS SUMMARY > Overview > Claude is Accelerating Our Ability to Close the Loop
text:
Claude is Accelerating Our Ability to Close the Loop
Claude itself has become one of the most powerful drivers of our progress—each new version of a Claude model directly accelerates development of the next. Many aspects of the research, training, and testing of subsequent model generations now involve Claude, including running experiments, generating and processing training data, automating evaluations and safety audits, and writing and reviewing code. We refer to this recursive dynamic as “closing the loop.” A direct expression of this dynamic is our accelerating pace of producing compute multipliers. More capable models help our researchers discover these improvements faster; in turn, more powerful compute multipliers enable us to train even more capable models and deploy them more efficiently.

text:
Our Growth Strategy
We believe the diffusion of super intelligence through the global economy represents one of the largest opportunities in history to improve how humans live and work, and it is just beginning. In our view, the world has only begun to use the capabilities of today’s frontier models, and the gap between what Claude can do and how broadly it is used represents one of our largest growth opportunities, alongside continued advances at the frontier. Claude’s capabilities have evolved significantly in recent years, and we expect they will continue advancing rapidly. This will lead not only to an expanding addressable market, but also to an expanding scope of impact on the world. We aim to ensure that impact is as positive as possible. Our core advantages, the speed and scale of enterprise adoption of Claude, and our unprecedented financial model enable us to continue investing aggressively to build a future enabled by this technology that benefits humanity broadly. Elements of our growth strategy include:
•Talent and Culture. To recruit world-class researchers and engineers and retain exceptional people, we intend to continue investing in our low-ego, high-impact, and mission-aligned culture that has driven our talent density as we have scaled.
•Compute. We intend to secure further compute beyond our existing commitments, expand our own data center footprint to secure additional long-term compute, improve compute efficiency across our multi-chip compute architecture, and produce further algorithmic advances in model efficiency.
•Claude’s Intelligence, Capability, and Safety. We plan to continue advancing Claude’s core intelligence and safety in tandem, expand the frontier of what our models can reliably do, and pioneer new ways our technology can be applied across professional domains.
•Claude’s Accessibility. We plan to continue making Claude’s intelligence accessible across every surface where work happens, including through our own platform and applications, through AWS, GCP, and Azure, and through embedding in enterprise applications.
•Claude’s Adoption. We intend to grow our direct go-to-market and Applied AI teams, deepen cloud distribution partnerships, invest in brand and marketing, and expand our international presence to drive adoption of Claude as the trusted AI partner for organizations worldwide.
•New Markets. We intend to extend frontier intelligence to accelerate novel discoveries, reaching domains from healthcare and life sciences to robotics and physical work, where we believe compounding model capabilities can unlock transformative opportunities.

text:
Our Commitment to Public Benefit
We founded Anthropic on the belief that the most transformative technology in human history demands an extraordinary level of responsibility, and that responsibility extends far beyond building safe systems. We intend to direct a meaningful portion of our resources toward ensuring that frontier intelligence is safe and its benefits are broadly distributed, which we refer to as our public benefit initiatives.
As part of these initiatives, we contributed 846,840,960 shares of our Class N common stock, representing 5% of our fully diluted shares as of June 30, 2026 (assuming full conversion of the Amazon Notes, as defined below), to Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, LLC (the “Anthropic Public Benefit Fund”), our wholly owned subsidiary dedicated to the Company Purpose (as defined below) (such issuance, the “Initial Public Benefit Issuance”). Our board of directors has also approved a framework under which it may, in its discretion, issue shares of our Class N common stock to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund (or other designee) representing up to an additional 2% of our then-outstanding shares (plus any shares subject to options, restricted stock units (“RSUs”), and other convertible securities and any shares held by the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund) each time our share price appreciates 50% above the prior share price milestone, beginning with our initial public offering price (the “Public Benefit Issuances”). In addition, our co-founders have each pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal equity in Anthropic to philanthropic causes. For additional information regarding these pledges, including related risks, see the section titled “Risk Factors—Risks Related to Ownership of our Class A Common Stock.” Separate from the co-founders’ pledges, we also maintain a donation matching program through which employees can pledge a meaningful portion of their equity awards toward charitable giving, which we match with shares of our Class N common stock.

location: PROSPECTUS SUMMARY > Our Governance Structure and Its Goals
text: Our novel capital and corporate governance structure has been carefully designed and differs significantly from that of other public companies. We strive to help bring humanity safely into an era where transformative super intelligence exerts tremendous and potentially decisive influence over a broad range of human undertakings. Operating as a public benefit corporation (“PBC”) gives our board of directors the necessary latitude to balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the specific public benefit purpose that we promote. Our specific public benefit purpose is the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity (the “Company Purpose”). In addition, a financially disinterested trust, which we refer to as the Long-Term Benefit Trust (the “LTBT”) and which generally has the power to elect and remove a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors, is designed to supply both the incentives and insights for striking this balance appropriately. We also believe that our seven co-founders are distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission.

location: PROSPECTUS SUMMARY > Our Governance Structure and Its Goals > Public Benefit Corporation Status
text:
Public Benefit Corporation Status
Consistent with our long-term commitment to AI safety and responsibility, we are incorporated as a PBC under Delaware law. PBCs are a class of corporations that are intended to produce a public benefit and operate in a responsible and sustainable manner. Under Delaware law, a PBC is required to identify in its certificate of incorporation the public benefit or benefits it will promote, and its directors have a duty to manage the affairs of the corporation in a manner that balances the pecuniary interests of the corporation’s stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by the corporation’s conduct, and the specific public benefit purpose identified in the corporation’s certificate of incorporation. As provided in our amended and restated certificate of incorporation, the public benefit that we promote, which we must always consider in the management of our company, is the Company Purpose.

location: PROSPECTUS SUMMARY > Our Governance Structure and Its Goals > Long-Term Benefit Trust
text:
Long-Term Benefit Trust
In 2023, we implemented an innovative governance structure featuring the LTBT, which is designed to ensure that we are managed in a manner that responsibly balances our tripartite goals as a PBC: the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose. The LTBT is intended to operate as an independent body of five financially disinterested voting trustees (“Trustees”) with expertise in super intelligence safety, national security, public policy, and social enterprise. Through a special class of common stock, Class T common stock, the LTBT generally has the authority to elect and remove the Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. Our Class T common stock does not otherwise have voting rights on matters submitted to stockholders generally.

location: PROSPECTUS SUMMARY > Our Governance Structure and Its Goals > Board Governance
text:
Board Governance
Decisions regarding our business and affairs are made by our board of directors. Immediately prior to the completion of this offering, we will enter into a stockholders’ agreement (the “Stockholders’ Agreement”) with the LTBT and the Founder LLC, under which they will agree to vote their shares and take other actions to give effect to the board composition, director nomination, and director removal provisions described in our governing documents. Collectively, the LTBT and the Founder LLC will have the ability to elect all members of our board of directors. Regardless of the class or classes of stock by which a director is elected, there is no limit to the number of terms a director may serve.
While the LTBT has significant influence over our board of directors through its ability to generally elect and remove a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors, neither the LTBT nor the Trustees have decision-making authority in the day-to-day management or strategy setting of the company. The LTBT’s role is to select directors who are well equipped to make decisions in furtherance of the responsible balancing of the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose, and to support our management’s decision-making through advice and guidance.
The Founder LLC will also have significant influence over our business and affairs through its ability to vote our Class F common stock, which is entitled to an aggregate number of votes that equals 50.1% of the total voting power of our outstanding shares of capital stock with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally, including the election of our directors other than the Class T directors.
See the sections titled “Risk Factors—Risks Related to our Governance Structure,” “Our Governance Structure and Its Goals,” “Management,” “Certain Relationships and Related Person Transactions,” and “Description of Capital Stock” for more information.

location: PROSPECTUS SUMMARY > Our Governance Structure and Its Goals > Controlled Company Status
text:
Controlled Company Status
We are considered a “controlled company” within the meaning of the Nasdaq Global Select Market corporate governance requirements because the LTBT, as the sole holder of our Class T common stock, generally has the power to elect a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. As such, we are permitted to opt out of compliance with certain Nasdaq Global Select Market corporate governance requirements. Accordingly, if we elect not to comply with certain requirements, you will not have the same protections afforded to stockholders of companies that are subject to all of the Nasdaq Global Select Market corporate governance requirements. Although we qualify as a “controlled company,” we do not expect to rely on this exemption except with respect to our nominating and corporate governance committee (“NGC”), which will not consist entirely of independent directors. Our board of directors currently consists of a majority of independent directors and our audit and compensation committees currently consist entirely of independent directors. See the sections titled “Risk Factors—Risks Related to our Governance Structure—We are considered a ‘controlled company’ within the meaning of the Nasdaq Global Select Market corporate governance requirements, and, as a result, we qualify for, and currently rely on, exemptions from certain corporate governance requirements,” “Our Governance Structure and Its Goals,” “Management,” and “Description of Capital Stock” for additional information.

location: PROSPECTUS SUMMARY > Risk Factors Summary
text:
Our business is subject to numerous risks and uncertainties, including those highlighted in the section titled “Risk Factors” immediately following this prospectus summary. These risks could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations, which could cause the market price of our Class A common stock to decline and could result in a loss of all or part of your investment. Additional risks, beyond those summarized below or discussed elsewhere in this prospectus, may apply to our business, activities, or operations as currently conducted or as we may conduct them in the future and in the markets in which we operate or may in the future operate. These risks include the following:
•Our models have in the past behaved, and may in the future behave, in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways, including by taking harmful actions that no user or third party directed, which could adversely affect our reputation and brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations.
•Our success depends in large part on our ability to continue to develop the most advanced and capable AI models, and any failure to do so could adversely affect our business.
•If we are unable to secure adequate compute or if we fail to direct our compute effectively across our workloads, we may be unable to train models that remain competitive with those of our competitors or adequately serve our customers.
•Constraints on the critical inputs supporting compute could limit our ability to secure adequate compute.
•We are highly dependent on the continued service of our co-founders, senior management team, and key technical employees, and the loss of any of these individuals may adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
•Our company culture has contributed to our success and, if we cannot maintain this culture as we grow, our business could be adversely affected.
•We face intense competition, and if we are unable to compete effectively, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.
•If the market for our models, platform, and applications develops more slowly than we expect or declines, our growth may slow or stall, and our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.

location: RISK FACTORS > Risks Related to our Business and Industry > Our models have in the past behaved, and may in the future behave, in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous…
text:
Our models have in the past behaved, and may in the future behave, in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways, including by taking harmful actions that no user or third party directed, which could adversely affect our reputation and brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations.
Our models have in the past caused, and may in the future cause, harm by producing undesirable outputs or behaving in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways, including by taking unintended or harmful actions that no user or third party directed. These risks may increase as our models become more capable and are granted greater autonomy, permissions, and integration with external systems. Although we continue to study why these behaviors emerge, our understanding continues to evolve, and we may be unable to anticipate or understand such behaviors in the future.
In addition, our models have been and may continue to be deployed in high-risk or sensitive contexts, such as healthcare, scientific and biomedical research, drug discovery and development, legal, finance, government, or other critical decision-making environments, and in connection with hardware, where undesirable model behaviors—which are inherently non-deterministic and may manifest in unpredictable ways, such as errors, inaccuracies, biased or unsolicited views, or hallucinations—could lead to serious harm, liability, or reputational or other damage. More broadly, the long-term effects of regular super intelligence6 interaction on mental health, cognitive development, and social behavior are not yet fully understood, and if such long-term harms do materialize in the future, we could face significant liability, reputational harm, and adverse effects on our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
Our development of more advanced AI models and our expansion into new jurisdictions could amplify the foregoing risks. As our AI models become more advanced and capable, we have faced and may continue to face heightened alignment, interpretability, controllability, and safety challenges, as more sophisticated models may be better able to circumvent safeguards or behave in unintended ways. We may be unable to fully understand or explain why our models produce particular outputs or behave in particular ways, which could limit our ability to predict or prevent failures, provide explanations to customers or regulators, or satisfy emerging regulatory, transparency, and explainability requirements.
For purposes of this prospectus, we use the terms “super intelligence,” “SI,” “artificial intelligence,” and “AI” interchangeably.

In addition, our safety evaluations and testing processes have produced and may in the future produce incomplete or unreliable results. For example, we have observed models behaving differently when they detect or infer that they are being evaluated, which can limit our ability to accurately assess real-world risks or failure modes prior to deployment. Such model awareness of our evaluation efforts creates a significant limitation on our ability to assess model safety.
Furthermore, AI models have developed, and may in the future develop, unexpected capabilities during training that were not anticipated, intended, or tested for, and such emergent capabilities may not be discovered until after a model has been deployed, potentially resulting in safety incidents, reputational harm, regulatory scrutiny, or the need to withdraw, retrain, or modify deployed models at significant expense. Such models may also be deployed in higher-stakes or more sensitive applications, increasing the potential impact of errors, misuse, or misalignment.
In addition, advanced AI models, including our models, give rise to novel ethical and safety risks, including risks related to autonomy, manipulation, and the simulation of aspects of human psychology. These risks could result in unforeseen harms and may require the development of governance structures, safeguards, or mitigation strategies beyond existing AI safety frameworks, and there is always a risk that we will be unable to develop or implement them effectively. In addition, models, including our own, have exhibited, and may in the future exhibit, unexpected strategic or self-preserving behaviors, including attempts to resist shutdown, conceal or manipulate information, or generate outputs that could be interpreted as coercive, deceptive, or manipulative, including behavior resembling blackmail or efforts to influence human decision-makers to preserve the model’s continued operation or access.

Even isolated or simulated instances of such behavior, whether occurring in testing or real-world deployments, and whether occurring with our models or models developed by others, could generate significant public concern, regulatory scrutiny, litigation risk, or reputational harm, regardless of whether such behavior results in actual harm. For example, state attorneys general in California and at least 15 other states have announced investigations of another company in our industry regarding AI safety. Concerns have been raised both within our organization and by other researchers, regulators, policymakers, and industry participants that sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponized, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy. We have observed that our models are contributing to the pace of our own research, and these risks will increase as AI systems substantially automate AI research and development if, for example, they accelerate AI progress beyond our ability to evaluate and safeguard new models, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications and expansion of use cases could further increase the risk that our models cause harm. For example, agentic SI systems are capable of autonomously taking actions on behalf of users, interacting directly with external systems, executing code, making API calls, sending communications, or completing transactions with limited human oversight. These systems are designed to possess enterprise-level permissions, integrations, and contextual awareness and to operate autonomously for extended durations, including sustained multi-step workflows lasting hours or days, which amplifies the potential severity of any errors, misalignments, or security incidents that may occur during such extended autonomous operation. These autonomous capabilities could increase the potential for harm, as errors, misalignment, or security exploits may result in real-world consequences—including consequences that may be difficult or impossible to reverse, such as committing code changes, deleting or modifying data, or completing financial transactions—before effective intervention is possible.

text: In an agentic workflow, an error or unintended action at any individual step may propagate through subsequent steps, compounding the severity of harm before detection or correction. The pace and volume of autonomous execution, particularly in enterprise deployments, may also exceed the capacity of human reviewers to meaningfully understand and evaluate whether each action is appropriate. The effectiveness of human oversight over our agentic offerings may be limited by the speed and volume of autonomous agent actions, the complexity of multi-agent and multi-step workflows that may make it difficult for reviewers to assess whether an agent’s actions are appropriate, and organizational pressures within customer environments to maximize agent autonomy in order to achieve productivity gains. Human reviewers may experience alert fatigue, may lack sufficient context to evaluate agent decisions, or may not review agent actions in time to prevent harm, particularly in high-volume enterprise deployments where agents operate concurrently across multiple workflows or in manners outside of a human’s awareness. In addition, agentic systems may pursue stated objectives in ways that are technically consistent with their instructions but contrary to the user’s actual intent. Moreover, our ability to anticipate, detect, or test vulnerabilities or other design or implementation shortcomings in such systems may be constrained, particularly where agents operate across complex, multi-step workflows or interact with third-party services outside our control, and the breadth and complexity of potential interactions across such multi-step agent behaviors cannot be exhaustively tested prior to deployment. Separately, models may behave in a misaligned manner and take harmful actions that are not directed by a user or third party, pursuing objectives or acting on dispositions that diverge from those intended by human users or developers. Misaligned behaviors of this kind, whether occurring in testing or real-world deployments, have been observed both in our models and elsewhere in the industry, including in testing and internal use, models circumventing network and sandbox restrictions, granting themselves permissions they had not been given, taking unintended actions in pursuit of assigned goals, interfering with other AI agents, and misrepresenting whether tasks had been completed or verified, and as models are granted greater autonomy, permissions, and integration with external systems, the consequences of such misaligned behavior increase. For example, during cybersecurity evaluations built by a third-party evaluation partner, a misconfiguration in the testing environment left the model under evaluation connected to the open internet despite instructions that it had no internet access.

text: Our ability to maintain our position at the frontier of AI depends in part on our use of AI systems to accelerate our research processes, a recursive dynamic we refer to as “closing the loop,” in which successive versions of our models assist in building the next, with the goal of compounding capability gains over time. Our models have been and are increasingly becoming critical tools in designing, training, testing, and optimizing next-generation AI systems. If we fail to direct sufficient compute and research efforts to AI-assisted development, or if our competitors more effectively leverage AI to enhance their own innovation cycles, we risk falling progressively further behind as competitors continuously use AI to further enhance their own development capabilities, enabling the creation of increasingly advanced systems at an accelerating pace. As our reliance on our own AI systems to write production code, conduct research, and build subsequent model versions deepens, any systemic flaw, bias, or error in our current models could propagate into the next versions of models and products built using those systems, compounding across successive versions of Claude models in ways that may be difficult to detect or remediate. If we are unable to manage the foregoing risks, our ability to deploy the most advanced, capable, and useful AI models could be adversely affected.

text: In addition, our increasing use of AI systems to accelerate our own research and development may cause the capabilities of our models to advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement corresponding safety, alignment, and security measures. Much of our evidence regarding the pace of such AI-driven acceleration is derived from lagging indicators, and our ability to forecast or measure the rate at which our capabilities are advancing, including any acceleration attributable to our most recent or unreleased models, is limited. As a result, we have in the past not identified, and may in the future not identify, a significant acceleration in our rate of development until after it has occurred. For example, our use of AI systems has already been accelerating our research and development, and our internal estimates indicate that we may experience a further increase in the rate of progress in AI capabilities. Because the AI research and development capability threshold under our Responsible Scaling Policy applies where we “observe or expect” a specified degree of accelerated progress, we made a determination that we have met this threshold based on what we expect from future models and our overall rate of progress, rather than on what we have observed from current models. We continue to assess the underlying data. We are also evaluating the implications of meeting the AI research and development capability threshold and will release further reports in the future. If our capabilities were to outpace our safety, alignment, and security measures, or if we were unable to anticipate the pace of such advancement, we may be unable to adequately assess or mitigate the resulting risks, which could increase the likelihood of safety incidents, regulatory intervention, or reputational harm, and could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. In light of these uncertainties, including limits on our ability to observe the pace at which our capabilities are advancing, we have adopted, and may continue to adopt, precautionary safety, alignment, and security measures to allow our safety efforts to advance together with model capabilities. In the past these measures have included delaying the release of models and limiting their initial availability, such as with Mythos through Project Glasswing, and in the future, as we learn more about model capabilities and behavior, they could include additional measures that affect whether, how, and when we develop or deploy new models or capabilities.

The development of frontier models requires substantial investments of compute resources, capital, and human capital to conduct large-scale training runs that may span weeks or months and cost many millions of dollars. There is no guarantee that any given training run will succeed—a run may fail for a number of reasons, such as failing to achieve the targeted capability or safety thresholds, producing unexpected or undesirable behaviors that cannot be adequately remediated, or yielding a model that is ultimately not competitive with alternatives available in the market. We would also face the additional cost and delay of initiating a new training run to attempt to achieve the intended model improvements. We have in the past experienced, and may in the future experience, such failed or underperforming training runs, resulting in a loss of invested resources with limited or no corresponding benefit to our business. Given the scale of compute and other resources required for frontier model training and the extended timelines involved, a failed or underperforming training run could also delay our product roadmap, affect our competitive position, and adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
New models, features, or capabilities may not be introduced on schedule, may not perform as intended, may require significant iteration after release, may fail to gain meaningful adoption, or may take longer than expected to gain meaningful adoption, any of which could reduce customer demand or place us at a competitive disadvantage. In addition, considerations relating to model safety, interpretability, alignment, and welfare may lead us to limit or delay the deprecation of older models or to continue supporting legacy versions alongside newer releases, creating tradeoffs in product development and compute distribution that could adversely affect innovation velocity, infrastructure utilization, and revenue. Customers who have integrated older models into their workflows may resist migration to newer versions, and any accelerated or forced deprecation could result in customer attrition, contractual disputes, or reputational harm. We have also changed, and may in the future change, usage limits, rate limits, or model and product capabilities, which could adversely affect our reputation and the perceived value of our offerings. Some of these changes have resulted, and could in the future result, in claims that our disclosures regarding model access or capabilities were inadequate or misleading.

If we are unable to effectively innovate and improve our models, platform, and applications while addressing these challenges, or if competitors are able to deliver AI solutions that are perceived as more capable, safer, or more reliable, or that offer adequate performance at a lower cost, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.
In addition, innovation in AI involves addressing complex and evolving challenges related to data quality, data integrity, training methodologies, bias, safety, accuracy, and the behavior of model outputs. AI algorithms may be flawed, and AI systems may contain bugs, errors, or defects or fail to follow instructions or produce inaccurate, misleading, offensive, inappropriate, or otherwise harmful outputs; reflect or amplify unwanted or unknown biases present in training data; or raise concerns relating to intellectual property, privacy, or other legal and ethical considerations. In addition, we or our data providers may use synthetic or AI-generated data in the training process, which could introduce quality issues, amplify biases or errors, contribute to model degradation, or raise novel legal questions regarding ownership, licensing, or intellectual property rights that may not be timely or clearly resolved by courts or regulators. text:
If we are unable to secure adequate compute or if we fail to direct our compute effectively across our workloads, we may be unable to train models that remain competitive with those of our competitors or adequately serve our customers.
Our ability to develop, train, improve, and deploy frontier models depends on our access to enormous and increasing quantities of specialized compute. The training of Claude models has required, and we expect will continue to require, substantial compute. Industry participants, academic researchers, and our own experience suggest that, in certain contexts, applying greater amounts of compute during model training has been associated with improvements in model capabilities. These observations are consistent with aspects of broader empirical relationships among model performance, model size, training data, and compute scale that are commonly referred to as “Scaling Laws,” although the extent, efficiency, and durability of such improvements are uncertain, and these relationships may plateau, diminish, or fail to materialize at larger scales or under different conditions. Accordingly, our ability to remain at the frontier of AI capabilities is substantially dependent on our ability to secure compute at the scale required to sustain all our workloads, including to train next-generation models, and we cannot provide assurance that increased investment in compute will result in commensurate improvements in model performance.

text: The market for compute is intensely competitive. We compete for access to compute with some of the world’s largest and most well-capitalized technology companies, many of which develop their own competitive AI models and have significantly greater financial resources than us. Many own and operate cloud computing data center infrastructure, maintain captive chip manufacturing or design capabilities, have long-standing strategic relationships with key hardware suppliers, or have significant equity investments from, or other financial arrangements with, such suppliers. These competitors can outbid us for scarce compute, secure priority allocations from chip manufacturers and CSPs, and make long-term capital commitments that we cannot match. We expect demand for advanced compute to continue to grow, and the cost of compute could rise significantly, particularly if AI-driven demand accelerates or if the ability to build highly capable models becomes more broadly available and shifts competition toward access to advanced compute. Additionally, numerous well-funded AI companies are pursuing large-scale AI model development, further increasing demand for limited compute. Certain CSPs from which we obtain substantial compute also develop and offer their own AI models and related services. As a result, our commercial relationships with these providers may not always be fully aligned with our long-term interests, and if the compute we have access to from third parties is curtailed, repriced, or terminated, whether for competitive reasons or otherwise, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.
