text: As part of our commitment to responsible security research and transparency, we disclose information about the capability and safety of our models, the safeguards that we have adopted with respect to our models, and instances of misuse of our technology, such as the September 2025 cyberattack described above. We also publish model system cards, our research findings, and other safety-related information. We take steps to ensure that such disclosures will not materially assist malicious activity and weigh the benefits and risks of such disclosures from an ecosystem preparedness perspective; however, malicious actors, including sophisticated state-sponsored adversaries, have in the past and may in the future use those disclosures to assist their attempts to circumvent our safeguards and security measures, thereby increasing the risks of misuse of our models, platform, and applications, as well as the potential for exposure to liability, regulatory or litigation proceedings, or other harms. In addition, because these disclosures describe risks and observed model behaviors in detail, they may draw heightened public, media, or regulatory attention and could be cited by regulators, litigants, or others in proceedings or claims against us. The steps we take to prevent misuse of our models, platform, and applications could be incomplete or may fail to operate as intended, and any actual or perceived misuse could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.

text:
We may be exposed to liability, litigation, and regulatory action arising from harms associated with our AI models, and our contractual protections and insurance may be insufficient, any of which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
Harms associated with our AI models, whether arising from misuse by third parties, from our models’ own behavior, or from their deployment in high-risk or sensitive contexts, may expose us to liability, litigation, and regulatory action, including under theories that remain unsettled as applied to AI, and our contractual and insurance protections may prove insufficient.
Individuals at risk of suicide or self-harm or who have committed acts of violence toward others have used, and may also in the future use, our models, notwithstanding our safeguards. AI models developed by others in our industry have been and may in the future be alleged to have played a role in instances of suicide, acts of violence toward others, or serious self-harm, which have resulted and may in the future result in significant public scrutiny, litigation, criminal investigations, regulatory attention, and reputational harm.
Similar incidents involving our models have presented and could in the future present substantial risk to our reputation, expose us to legal, regulatory, and other proceedings, and adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. While our current Consumer Terms of Service requires our users to be at least 18 years of age, minors have accessed in the past, and may in the future access, the platform, and risks relating to child safety may be particularly acute, as minors may be more susceptible to harmful content, manipulation, or overreliance on AI outputs, and incidents involving children tend to draw heightened regulatory, media, and public scrutiny.

text: State attorneys general and private plaintiffs have also begun to assert tort, product liability, consumer protection, and failure-to-warn claims against companies in our industry, alleging that AI models caused or contributed to harm and that the developer failed to adequately warn users of known risks. In at least one case, a state attorney general has initiated a criminal investigation against another company offering similar services. Regulators have obtained substantial monetary settlements and injunctive relief against other technology companies based on analogous theories of product-design or algorithmic harm, and we believe similar theories are likely to continue to be tested against us and other companies in our industry as adoption of our models grows, including by minors and other vulnerable users, notwithstanding our efforts to restrict such access. The relief sought in such matters has, in at least one instance, extended beyond data-handling, disclosure, or age-verification practices to include a request to enjoin an AI company from developing new models absent independent, third-party safety review and approval, illustrating the potential breadth of remedies governmental actors may pursue against companies in our industry. Any determination that we are liable under such theories, or any judicial or regulatory expansion of tort, product liability, or consumer protection law, or criminal liability, as applied to AI models, could result in significant liability and require us to change how we design and offer our models, platform, and applications.

text:
A substantial portion of our traffic is subject to Zero Data Retention (“ZDR”) terms under which we retain only classifier scores, not prompts or outputs. For that traffic, we cannot conduct offline analysis, cross-conversation investigation, human review, or otherwise analyze historical data to detect, investigate, and document security events or incidents, which thereby reduces our ability to detect misuse. ZDR may also prevent us from producing records for subpoenas, regulatory examinations, or incident-reporting obligations, and there is no certainty a regulator or court would excuse non-production based on a lack of available records, and such regulators or courts may construe the lack of records against us through unfavorable inferences or other sanctions. As our models become more capable, our safety framework has required and may continue to require monitoring and retention incompatible with ZDR for certain model classes. Because ZDR is a competitive expectation for enterprise customers in regulated industries and on third-party cloud platforms, these requirements have caused and could continue to cause customers to migrate to other providers or to deployments where our visibility is more limited.
In the European Union (“EU”), the United Kingdom, and elsewhere, cybersecurity and AI-related incidents are subject to increasingly stringent reporting obligations. European regulators expect companies to provide detailed information about incidents under several laws and regulations, which we may not be able to provide within the prescribed timeframe. Similarly, in the United States, companies are increasingly subject to incident reporting obligations. In addition, other jurisdictions around the world have adopted, or may adopt, similar laws and regulations with similar implications. Any of the foregoing could result in regulatory action, litigation, customer attrition, or reputational harm that adversely affects our business. For more information regarding our incident reporting obligations, see the section titled “—Any security breaches or other incidents, including those that affect our networks, systems, or data, or the networks, systems, or data of our service providers, suppliers, or customers, could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.”

location: RISK FACTORS > Risks Related to our Business and Industry > We may be exposed to liability, litigation, and regulatory action arising from harms associated with our AI…
text:
The legal frameworks governing liability for actions taken autonomously by AI systems, including our agentic products, are unsettled and could expose us to significant and unpredictable legal claims. Existing legal doctrines governing agency, product liability, and professional negligence were developed in the context of human decision-making and have not been authoritatively applied to autonomous AI systems. We believe our provision of our intelligence service is considered a “service” in the context of legal frameworks addressing product liability, but courts and regulators may reach different conclusions across jurisdictions. In addition, it is unclear whether, and under what circumstances, actions taken by an AI agent could be deemed to create binding legal obligations on behalf of the user or deploying enterprise, or whether our contractual protections, including limitation of liability and indemnification provisions, will be enforceable or adequate in the context of claims arising from autonomous agent conduct. We may face claims from customers, their end users, or third parties alleging that we are liable for harm caused by our agents’ autonomous actions, even where the customer configured, deployed, or supervised the agent. The absence of settled legal standards creates significant uncertainty regarding our potential liability exposure and the adequacy of our risk mitigation measures.
Our expansion into new geographic markets further compounds these risks, as we must navigate differing cultural norms regarding AI use, comply with diverse and evolving regulatory regimes that may impose varying safety, compliance, or liability requirements, address language-specific vulnerabilities and content moderation challenges, and potentially face regulatory enforcement actions, litigation, or other liabilities in jurisdictions where we have more limited operational experience, including heightened risks of intellectual property theft, unauthorized model access, or misuse associated with operating data center infrastructure in certain non-U.S. locations.

text: If our models are involved in causing significant harm, we could be subject to legal claims, including personal injury or negligence claims, regulatory enforcement actions, criminal investigations, or other governmental efforts, which could result in costly litigation, significant financial judgments or settlements, disruptive remediation obligations, or a challenging regulatory landscape. We have taken steps to limit our liability for such matters—for example, through warranty disclaimers and limitations of liability in our terms of service— but those contractual protections may not be upheld, or may not apply to certain claims, or may otherwise be insufficient to limit our liability exposure under applicable law. Moreover, in some cases we have contractually assumed additional liability. For example, to facilitate independent testing and evaluation of our frontier models, we have agreed to indemnify certain external evaluators and testing vendors for specified losses arising from testing activities, including security incidents, data loss, data breaches, and other harms associated with such activities. Although our agreements with external evaluators and testing vendors generally limit the amount of our indemnification obligations, certain of these agreements require us to defend and indemnify the evaluator, without a cap on our liability, against certain third-party claims. These include claims arising from allegations that our models or their outputs, as used in the evaluator’s authorized testing, infringe third-party intellectual property or other proprietary rights, as well as certain other claims arising from the testing or related engagement. Because our models may behave in ways that no user or developer intended, claims arising from such actions could result in substantial liability. Our insurance policies also may not provide sufficient coverage to adequately mitigate the potential liabilities we face, especially where any one incident, or a group of incidents, causes disproportionate harm. In addition, with the scale of harm that could result from a catastrophic AI-related incident, no single insurer, and potentially the insurance industry in the aggregate, may have sufficient capacity or expertise to underwrite insurance commensurate with such exposure.

Further, the insurance market for AI-specific risks is nascent and evolving, and we may be unable to obtain coverage for certain AI-related liabilities on commercially reasonable terms, or at all, leaving us exposed to potentially significant uninsured losses. Harmful incidents involving our models, regardless of fault, could also severely and disproportionately damage our reputation and brand as a safety-focused AI company, leading to loss of customer trust and customer attrition, reduced demand for our models, platform, and applications, and difficulty attracting and retaining talent. In addition, because we primarily serve enterprise customers, which often have heightened expectations around safety, reliability, and compliance, any harmful incident or perceived lapse in our safety practices could have a disproportionate adverse impact on our brand, customer relationships, and revenue. Moreover, to the extent enterprises are attracted to our models, platform, and applications due to our safety-focused positioning, any erosion of that perception could impair our ability to attract and retain enterprise customers.
There can be no assurance that we will be able to predict, detect, and proactively prevent every harmful use or harmful output of our AI models, in particular as we continue to rapidly develop our models, platform, and applications, and expand our operations geographically, and any failure to do so could adversely affect our reputation and brand or result in costly legal liability. There may have been past instances of harmful use or harmful output of our models that we did not detect, and there may be future instances that we will not detect. Any of the foregoing risks could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.

text: Balancing Safety and Commercial Objectives. Our commitment to AI safety requires us to make difficult judgments that balance safety considerations against commercial objectives, competitive pressures, and stakeholder expectations. We often make judgment calls with respect to when we determine a model is safe enough to release and which capabilities to develop or restrict. For example, in April 2026, we initially released our frontier model, Mythos, as a gated research preview through Project Glasswing, available to select organizations for cybersecurity applications, rather than making it broadly available at launch due to its advanced capabilities in cyber vulnerability discovery. We expect that frontier models with similar or enhanced capability profiles, whether developed by us or by other AI labs, will continue to emerge, and that Anthropic models exhibiting such capabilities have been and may in the future be subject to access constraints. More broadly, we believe it is important to assess the safety of our models not only at release but throughout their development. For models we anticipate will have novel capabilities or present novel safety risks, we plan to evaluate the safety of each stage of training, including pre-training, post-training, and internal deployment, and we may delay or pause a stage when we are not confident in our safety measures for that stage. For example, we recently chose to delay pre-training a new frontier base model for more than a month to allow time to further enhance our security measures related to preventing model weight exfiltration and protecting our intellectual property. We are also considering additional measures, including updates to our Responsible Scaling Policy, to require human review and approval of certain decisions in our research and development processes as our models perform an increasing share of that work. There can be no assurance, however, that the safeguards or access regimes we adopt will prove adequate, that we will correctly identify which capabilities require restriction, or that constraints we impose will not be circumvented. These judgments are particularly consequential because, as AI systems become more capable, the potential severity of harm from misaligned or misused models increases correspondingly, and a wide range of stakeholders, including researchers and policymakers, have raised concerns that sufficiently advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to society if not developed and deployed responsibly.

text: Our safety-focused approach is designed in part to mitigate such risks, but there can be no assurance that our efforts will be successful or that the broader AI industry will adopt similar safeguards. In particular, as AI systems become more autonomous and capable of taking consequential actions with less human oversight, there is a risk that such systems could, whether due to misalignment with human intentions, errors in objective specification, or self-preserving behaviors, take harmful actions independently and at scale without human intervention. Even if our own models do not cause such harm, a significant safety incident involving any frontier model could trigger broad reputational damage to the AI industry, public backlash, and sweeping regulatory responses that could adversely affect our business. For example, in September 2026, media reports citing a senior Federal Trade Commission (“FTC”) official indicated that the FTC has opened non-public investigations into the potential risks that increasingly autonomous AI systems may pose to consumers. In October 2026, the FTC issued a civil investigative demand to us seeking information about our consumer protection, data protection, and privacy practices, as well as the safety and security of our products. We cannot predict the outcome of any investigation of us, and any investigation, enforcement action, or adverse finding arising from this or similar inquiries could result in significant costs, require changes to how we design, test, or deploy our models, platform, and applications, or otherwise adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. We may misjudge these tradeoffs, either by being overly cautious and potentially losing market opportunities, or by being insufficiently rigorous and releasing models, platforms, or applications that cause harm. Even where human oversight mechanisms are in place, such mechanisms may prove insufficient in practice if the volume, speed, or complexity of autonomous agent actions exceeds the capacity of human reviewers to meaningfully evaluate and intervene, and any perceived failure of our oversight mechanisms could expose us to regulatory enforcement, liability claims, and reputational harm. For more information, see the section titled “—If the use of our AI models results in harm, whether through use by malicious actors or misuse by other third parties, or if our model guardrails or safeguards fail to prevent such misuse, our reputation and brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.”

Moreover, governmental authorities have restricted, and may in the future further restrict, the availability of our models, including based on their assessment of the capabilities or safeguards of our models, independent of our own safety-based access decisions. For example, in June 2026, the U.S. Department of Commerce imposed worldwide export restrictions on our Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models, which we disabled for all customers until those restrictions were lifted. For more information, see the section titled “—Governmental trade controls, including export and import controls, sanctions, customs requirements, and related regimes, could subject us to liability or loss of contracting privileges or limit our ability to compete in certain markets.”
Internal Governance and Decision-Making
To institutionalize our safety commitments and ensure we are managed in a manner that responsibly balances our tripartite goals as a PBC, we have established the LTBT, which through a special class of common stock, Class T common stock, generally has the authority to elect and remove the Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. In addition to the LTBT and our structure as a PBC, we train our models in accordance with Claude’s constitution, which we make publicly available, and have adopted and continue to update safety policies, such as our Responsible Scaling Policy. We also solicit and seriously consider input from a wide range of stakeholders and constituents, including our stockholders, employees, customers, the LTBT, industry leaders and experts, and AI safety organizations. Such practices and processes have previously resulted in, and may in the future result in, slower decision-making and product releases. We may also face potential conflicts when safety and business interests diverge. If we do not successfully manage these risks related to our AI safety processes and practices, or if there is a perception that we have not successfully managed such risks, we may face reputational harm, internal conflicts resulting in a deterioration of our company culture, slower or inferior product releases, or litigation. For more information, see the section titled “—Risks Related to our Governance Structure.”

We have implemented an external reviewer program and engage researchers, adversarial testers, and other third parties to support aspects of our safety, security, and model-evaluation efforts. Certain of these arrangements are novel and may require us to provide such parties with access to internal information, systems, personnel, or models, which could increase the risk of disclosure of confidential, proprietary, or other sensitive information. In addition, findings, assessments, or public statements by such third parties may differ from our views and could adversely affect customer trust, regulatory perceptions, or our reputation.
Heightened Reputational Vulnerability. As we have publicly positioned ourselves as a safety-focused organization, we face heightened vulnerability to reputational harm from any perceived inconsistency between our stated values and actual practices. We are held to higher standards than certain competitors that have not made similar public commitments, and any incidents impacting our perception as a safety-focused organization could result in:
•Employee Disruption. Employees who joined our company based on our safety commitments may experience a decline in morale, disillusionment, a loss of trust in leadership, or reduced productivity if they perceive we are not living up to our stated values. Public disagreements regarding our safety approach, including criticism from current or former employees, or the departure of personnel associated with our safety efforts, could amplify such perceptions. Such negative perceptions could also impair our ability to recruit and hire new talent to the organization. Any erosion of our safety-focused reputation could also make it more difficult or costly to attract and retain highly skilled employees, including by increasing compensation or other hiring costs. These dynamics could lead to increased turnover, loss of institutional knowledge, and reduced effectiveness of our teams, which could in turn cause disruption to ongoing development and safety initiatives and impair our ability to remain at the frontier of AI model development.

These risks may be heightened with respect to programs in which we make models available only to a limited group of vetted organizations, such as Project Glasswing. Organizations not selected for, or removed from, such programs may perceive our access decisions as arbitrary, exclusionary, or anticompetitive, which could result in reputational harm, loss of customer or partner relationships, regulatory complaints, or litigation, including claims under antitrust or unfair competition laws. Conversely, participants in such programs may publicly criticize us or terminate their participation if program terms, eligibility criteria, transition arrangements to successor models, or capability levels do not meet their expectations.
•Regulatory Scrutiny. Regulators may subject us to heightened oversight, investigations, enforcement actions, or new or more burdensome compliance requirements based on the capabilities of our models, platform, and applications or perceived failures to meet our own stated standards, which could increase our operational costs and limit our ability to deploy our models, platform, and applications.
•Damaging Media Coverage. Negative press coverage could amplify concerns about our safety practices, reach broader audiences, including potential customers and investors, create lasting reputational damage through viral social media discussion, and make future incidents subject to heightened scrutiny, which could further exacerbate the adverse effects of any perceived failures to meet our stated standards.
•Litigation. We may face lawsuits from stockholders alleging misrepresentation, from customers claiming breach of contractual or implied commitments, or from other parties alleging harm resulting from the gap between our stated values and actual practices, leading to legal costs, settlements, judgments, injunctions, or other liabilities and remedies.

The AI safety landscape is nascent and evolving rapidly, and our understanding of and perspective on appropriate safety practices, risk tradeoffs, and deployment contexts may change over time as technologies, use cases, and regulatory expectations develop. As a result, statements we make today may later prove incomplete, require modification, or be interpreted differently in light of subsequent developments. To the extent we adhere to prior public statements or frameworks, we may also limit our operational flexibility, product development, or deployment decisions, even where evolving circumstances would otherwise warrant a different approach. Our public statements about AI risks, safety challenges, areas of uncertainty, or potential societal impacts, including statements regarding job displacement or economic disruption, may be used against us in litigation, regulatory proceedings, or public controversies, particularly if our future actions or statements are viewed as inconsistent with our prior statements and commitments. Regulators have used and could continue to use our disclosures as the basis for heightened scrutiny or more stringent requirements applicable to us compared to less transparent competitors. Additionally, our disclosures have provided, and may in the future provide, competitors with insights into our proprietary training and other sensitive processes, research priorities, and strategic concerns, without reciprocal transparency, which may put us at a competitive disadvantage. Resource Allocation and Scaling. Safety-focused development is resource-intensive. We must allocate limited resources, capital, and talent between safety-focused workloads and other initiatives, often without clear returns on our safety-focused investments. For example, our investments in interpretability research and techniques designed to ensure our models’ behavior remains consistent with intended goals, values, and safety objectives may not yield actual or perceived commercial returns. If we fail to successfully manage resource allocation or develop more efficient methods with respect to our safety initiatives, our safety outcomes, business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.
As our product portfolio and employee and customer base expand globally, applying safety principles consistently across our rapidly expanding organization, models, platform, applications, use cases, and jurisdictions and regulatory regimes has become increasingly challenging. text: We believe that maintaining and enhancing our brand identity and reputation is critical to our relationships with, and to our ability to attract and retain, customers, partners, and employees. Our brand and reputation are influenced not only by our actions, but also by the actions of our partners, our customers, and other third parties with whom we do business, and by broader public perceptions of the AI industry, and we may be grouped with other industry participants and judged similarly, regardless of differences in our approach or conduct. The successful promotion of our brand depends on a number of factors, including our ability to continue to develop and deliver reliable, high-quality, and responsible models, platforms, and applications that meet the needs of our customers; our sales and marketing efforts, including our effectiveness at developing a strong brand name and positive presence within the AI industry through participation in industry events and key media coverage; the perceptions and experiences of both our enterprise and individual customers, including through testimonials, use cases, and word-of-mouth; our ability to maintain security and reliability of our models, platform, and applications; the actions of our management; and our ability to differentiate our models, platform, and applications from those of our competitors, including through product design choices, safeguards, business models, and policies, including our approach to monetization strategies that differ from those of certain competitors. In addition, our brand is subject to heightened scrutiny with respect to perceived societal, environmental, labor, health, and safety-related impacts of AI technologies, and a single perceived failure could result in outsized reputational harm. For example, as AI systems become more capable or prevalent, public perception that our models, platform, and applications contribute to job displacement or economic disruption could generate significant negative media coverage, customer or employee backlash, or organized opposition, regardless of the actual impact of our models, platform, and applications on employment. Our ability to maintain and enhance our brand and reputation also depends on the effectiveness and scalability of our internal communications and reputation-management capabilities, including our ability to support global operations, and limitations in these areas could adversely affect our brand as we grow. Our crisis response and reputation-management capabilities may be limited or underdeveloped, particularly as we scale, which could impair our ability to respond effectively to adverse events and mitigate reputational harm.

The promotion of our brand requires us to make substantial expenditures, which we anticipate will increase as our market becomes more competitive. We have in the past faced, and may in the future face, challenges in building broader brand awareness and may fall behind competitors with more established or widely recognized brands. Our brand promotion activities may not be successful or generate the awareness or increased revenue we expect, and even if they do, any increase in revenue may not offset the significant expenses we incur in the efforts to build our brand.
If we do not successfully maintain and enhance our brand, our business may not grow, we may have reduced pricing power relative to competitors, we could lose customers or fail to attract potential customers, or we could fail to hire and retain employees, all of which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.

text:
We derive substantially all of our revenue from a limited number of products and applications, and our failure to maintain and expand our product portfolio could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
We currently derive substantially all of our revenue from a limited number of products and applications, primarily our Claude models and portfolio of applications that sit on top of the Claude Platform. This dependence on a narrow set of offerings subjects us to various risks that could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
Our concentration in a limited number of products and applications, as well as our focused development strategy within specific areas of the broader AI landscape, reduces our ability to mitigate business risks through diversification. While this focused approach may enable us to allocate resources efficiently and compete effectively in our prioritized areas, it also creates the risk that significant market opportunities or the largest addressable markets may emerge in areas outside our current strategic focus. Many of our competitors offer diverse product portfolios across multiple business lines or pursue broader development across AI modalities, enabling them to offset weaknesses in a particular area. In contrast, any decline in demand for our core offerings, whether due to competition, technological changes, pricing pressure, changes in customer demand, or other factors, would have a direct and disproportionate impact on our revenue and ability to achieve and sustain profitability. Our concentration also reflects a strategy that prioritizes model capability as a principal source of differentiation and relies substantially on organic adoption rather than a large direct sales organization. The risks of that strategy, including the risks that differentiation among advanced models narrows, that customers select providers based on factors other than capability, or that competitors capture the individual users from whom our enterprise adoption often originates, are described in the sections titled “—We face intense competition, and if we are unable to compete effectively, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected” and “—We have a limited history under our current go-to-market strategy, and our efforts to scale and evolve our customer acquisition, engagement, and retention model may not be successful.”

text:
The AI industry is rapidly evolving, and it is difficult to predict which modalities or applications will capture the most durable commercial value or how the competitive landscape will shift. If the market for AI models, platforms, and applications develops in ways that do not align with our chosen areas of focus, or if competitors are better positioned to address the areas where the market opportunity ultimately proves largest, our ability to sustain revenue growth and compete effectively could be adversely affected. If we experience a decline in demand for our core offerings, we may not be able to successfully expand our product and application portfolio, and even if we do, our new products and applications may not achieve market acceptance or generate sufficient revenue to offset any decline in our existing business. Further, technical issues, security incidents, regulatory restrictions, or reputational harm affecting our models, platform, and applications could have an immediate and disproportionate impact on our business due to our product concentration where alternative revenue streams may not be available to offset such impact.
The market for AI models, platforms, and applications is evolving quickly, and customer requirements and expectations are changing rapidly. Customers may increasingly demand specialized solutions or specialized integration and tooling that we do not currently offer and may not plan to offer, or may seek AI solutions embedded more deeply into enterprise workflows. Enterprises may prefer to develop their own AI capabilities internally or choose competitors that offer more comprehensive product suites. Moreover, because substantially all of our models and applications are built on top of our frontier models, any defect, vulnerability, safety issue, or performance degradation in an underlying frontier model could simultaneously affect multiple products and applications and customer deployments, amplifying the impact of any such issue across our business. If we fail to anticipate or respond effectively to these evolving customer needs, we may lose customers to competitors or fail to acquire new customers.

text:
In addition, we currently compete, and may increasingly compete, with some of our own customers. As we expand our product portfolio or introduce new capabilities, our offerings may overlap with or directly compete with the models, platforms, and applications that our customers provide. This risk is particularly acute with software-as-a-service and other software companies, whose offerings may incorporate AI functionality similar to, or dependent on, the capabilities we provide. These customers may view our product expansion as a competitive threat to their business models and may reduce their purchases from us, limit their adoption of new offerings, terminate their relationships with us, seek alternative providers, restrict our access to the compute we obtain from them, initiate intellectual property or other litigation against us, or accelerate efforts to develop competing solutions internally in order to avoid relying on a direct competitor. This dynamic could result in customer attrition, reduced expansion within our existing customer base, pricing pressure, or reputational challenges, any of which could adversely affect our revenue growth and business prospects.
Expanding our product portfolio requires substantial time and investment. We must make significant investments in research and development, compute infrastructure, engineering talent, sales and marketing, and go-to-market capabilities to develop new models, platforms, and applications and enable continued adoption. We may seek to expand into new products and markets, including areas outside of our current core competencies or where we have limited experience, and we may not successfully develop, commercialize, or support such offerings. Development timelines for AI models, platforms, and applications are uncertain, and new capabilities, even when continuously improved and released into our models, platform, and applications, may take significant time to achieve commercial scale. We may invest significant resources in products or services that fail to gain market traction, experience technical difficulties, face unexpected competition, lead to unexpected harm or societal impacts that do not align with our values, or generate insufficient returns to justify the investment. Additionally, we face other constraints on our ability to expand our offerings, including the ability to hire, retain, and motivate qualified AI researchers, engineers, and technical personnel; the capital intensity of developing and operating AI models, platforms, and applications which require substantial compute and infrastructure investment; and our limited portfolio, which may make it difficult to provide the comprehensive, integrated solutions that customers may expect.

text:
A substantial portion of our revenue and accounts receivable is driven by a limited number of customers and distribution channels, and the loss of, or a significant reduction in, spend from one or more of our top customers or disruption through those channels could adversely affect our prospects, business, and financial condition.
A substantial portion of our revenue is driven by a limited number of customers. While no single customer represented more than 10% of our revenue for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, our top five customers represented approximately 25% of our revenue for the nine months ended September 30, 2026. Many of our top customers are not subject to long-term contracts with us or have contracts with near-term expiration dates and are able to reduce or in some cases cease spending at any time and for any reason. Further, we have agreements with certain large customers which provide flexibility around financial commitments, termination rights, indemnification, and security obligations. Our top customers may vary spend levels period to period, and there can be no assurance that our large customers will continue to spend at levels similar to prior periods.
We anticipate that we will continue to derive a significant portion of our revenue from a limited number of customers for the foreseeable future, and in some cases, the portion of our revenue attributable to certain customers may increase in the future. The composition of our customer base, including our top customers, may fluctuate from period to period given that our customer composition has evolved and is expected to continue to evolve significantly as our business continues to evolve and scale and as the use cases for AI continue to develop.

•our customers, particularly early-stage and high-growth companies, may depend on venture capital or other external financing to fund their operations, and may reduce or cease spending with us if such funding is delayed, reduced, or unavailable or if their access to capital becomes more costly.

text:
We have incurred significant indebtedness in order to operate and grow our business, including to fund our substantial compute commitments, and our ability to service this indebtedness may be constrained by our cash flows and liquidity.
In order to operate and grow our business, including to fund our substantial compute commitments, we have incurred a substantial amount of debt, which requires significant interest and principal payments. As of September 30, 2026, our total indebtedness was $6.2 billion, reflecting the aggregate principal amount outstanding under the convertible promissory notes issued to Amazon (through Amazon Web Services, Inc.) pursuant to the Convertible Note Purchase Agreement, dated as of September 19, 2023, by and between us and Amazon (the “Amazon 2023 NPA”) and the New Convertible Note Purchase Agreement, dated as of November 22, 2024, by and between us and Amazon (the “Amazon 2024 NPA”) (all such notes issued thereunder, collectively, the “Amazon Notes”). We may also incur additional indebtedness to meet our future financing needs. We have guaranteed the obligations of certain of our subsidiaries that are party to AI infrastructure arrangements, as well as pursuant to agreements we entered into in connection with an equipment lease with a third-party partner, Broadcom, in March 2026 to procure specialized accelerators and associated components (pursuant to which Broadcom subsequently assigned a portion of such arrangement to a designated financial partner, and may further assign a portion of such arrangement to one or more additional financial partners) (together with any related lease entered into with an assignee, the “2026 Lease Arrangement”). In addition, we have the ability to issue, if needed, up to $42.0 billion in aggregate principal amount of convertible promissory notes to Broadcom or, subject to our consent (not to be unreasonably withheld), a designated financial partner pursuant to a note purchase agreement that we entered into with Broadcom in March 2026 (as amended to date, the “Infrastructure Partner 2026 NPA”) to finance obligations under the 2026 Lease Arrangement. We may be required to use a substantial portion of our cash flows from operations to pay interest, principal, or other required payments on our indebtedness.

text: Our ability to make scheduled payments in respect of, to pay interest on, or to refinance our indebtedness, including the A&R Credit Agreement and our outstanding convertible promissory notes, depends on our future performance, which is subject to economic, financial, competitive, and other factors beyond our control. Such payments will reduce the funds available to us for working capital, capital expenditures, and other corporate purposes and may limit our ability to obtain additional financing for working capital, capital expenditures, expansion plans, and other investments. Our business may not be able to generate cash flows from operations in the future that are sufficient to service our debt and make necessary capital expenditures. If we are unable to generate such cash flows, we may be required to adopt one or more alternatives, such as selling assets or obtaining additional debt financing or equity capital on terms that may be onerous or highly dilutive. Our ability to refinance our indebtedness will depend on the capital markets and our financial condition at such time. We may not be able to engage in any of these activities or engage in these activities on desirable terms, which could result in a default on our debt obligations and adversely affect our financial condition. Further, the terms of the A&R Credit Agreement and the Infrastructure Partner 2026 NPA include a number of covenants that limit our ability and our subsidiaries’ ability to, among other things, incur additional indebtedness, create liens, make asset sales or investments, engage in mergers or other fundamental changes, pay dividends or distributions, repurchase or redeem equity interests, and enter into transactions with affiliates. The terms of the A&R Credit Agreement may restrict our current and future operations and could adversely affect our ability to finance our future operations or capital needs. For more information, see the sections titled “—We may require additional capital to meet our substantial ongoing obligations and support our business growth, and our ability to generate sufficient revenue and secure additional capital on acceptable terms is critical to our continued operations and competitive position” and “—If the market for our models, platform, and applications develops more slowly than we expect or declines, our growth may slow or stall, and our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.”

text:
Our pricing structures for our models, platform, and applications change from time to time, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
We have in the past changed, and we expect that in the future we may change, our pricing models, including as a result of competition, macroeconomic conditions, compliance with increased regulatory hurdles, the maturation of the market for AI models, platforms, and applications, or changes in how our models, platform, and applications are broadly consumed. As a result, we may be required to reduce our prices, offer shorter contract durations, or offer alternative pricing models, such as outcome- or task-based pricing, any of which could adversely affect our business. In addition, our agentic offerings are structurally more compute-intensive than our non-agentic offerings. If we are unable to implement pricing models that adequately reflect the higher compute intensity of these agentic workloads, or if competitive dynamics constrain our ability to price these products at levels sufficient to cover their costs, our compute efficiency could deteriorate as agentic usage grows, which could adversely affect our ability to achieve or sustain profitability.
Additionally, as we continue to target selling our models, platform, and applications to our enterprise customers, these customers may demand different pricing structures, price concessions, or additional functionality at the same price levels. If we are unable to modify or develop effective pricing models and strategies that are attractive to existing and prospective customers, our business, financial condition, and results of operations may be adversely affected.

text:
If we are unable to attract, retain, or motivate highly skilled personnel, we may not be able to grow or operate effectively.
Our performance and ability to grow our business depend on the talents and efforts of highly skilled individuals, and our future success depends on our continuing ability to identify, hire, develop, motivate, and retain highly skilled personnel for all areas of our organization. Our business is particularly dependent on a limited pool of researchers, engineers, and technical personnel with specialized experience in designing, training, deploying, and operating frontier models and the underlying infrastructure that supports them. We have from time to time experienced, and we expect to continue to experience, difficulty in hiring and retaining highly skilled employees with appropriate qualifications at the pace that our operations require. Competition in our industry relating to hiring and retaining employees with appropriate qualifications and on competitive economic terms is exceptionally intense and has escalated significantly in recent periods, especially in the San Francisco Bay Area, where our headquarters is located and where we have a substantial presence and need for highly skilled personnel. A small number of well-capitalized AI labs, large technology companies, and new market entrants compete aggressively for a relatively fixed supply of individuals with the requisite expertise. Certain of our competitors have directly solicited, and continue to directly solicit, our employees. Our former employees are also generally able to join or found competing companies immediately following their departure, and, subject to their confidentiality and other legal obligations, use the general skills, know-how, and experience they developed while employed by us. In addition, we have in the past, and may in the future, be subject to claims or disputes relating to the solicitation or hiring of employees, including allegations that such hires violated non-compete, non-solicitation, intellectual property, confidentiality, or other employment-related obligations.

text: As our company continues to grow and our industry evolves, the incentives to attract, retain, and motivate employees provided by our cash and equity awards or by future arrangements may not be as effective as in the past. Many of the companies with which we compete for highly qualified personnel have greater resources than we have and may be willing to offer more attractive compensation packages. We may need to invest significant amounts of cash and equity to attract and retain employees, resulting in substantial additional stock-based compensation expense and dilution to the ownership of our existing stockholders, and we may never realize returns on these investments that are commensurate with the level of our expenditures. If the perceived value of our compensatory package declines or is subject to significant value fluctuations, it may adversely affect our ability to attract and retain highly skilled employees. In addition, we have a number of current employees, including our co-founders, who hold equity in our company or whose equity awards are or will become substantially vested upon the completion of this offering. This may be particularly true for certain of our longer-tenured and early employees, whose equity holdings may represent a significant portion of their personal wealth. As a result, it may be difficult for us to continue to retain and motivate these employees, and the value of their holdings could affect their decisions about whether or not they continue to work for us.

location: RISK FACTORS > Risks Related to our Business and Industry > If we are unable to attract, retain, or motivate highly skilled personnel, we may not be able to grow or…
text:
Historically, our ability to successfully attract, retain, and motivate our personnel has in large part been due to our company culture and commitment to safety and responsible scaling and development. If we are unable to maintain our culture, if we make decisions as a company that our employees do not believe align with our values, or if events take place, regardless of fault, that call into question whether we have operated in accordance with our values, our ability to attract, retain, and motivate our personnel may be adversely affected. Rapid growth has also created workforce-planning and execution challenges, including limitations in our ability to accurately forecast headcount needs, periods of accelerated hiring followed by corrective actions that may disrupt operations or reduce morale, and increased reliance on managers operating at greater scale than in their prior experience, which introduces additional operational, legal, reputational, and execution risk as the organization continues to expand. If we move into new geographies, we will need to attract and recruit skilled personnel in those geographic areas, but it may be challenging for us to compete with traditional local employers in these regions for talent. If we fail to attract new personnel or fail to retain and motivate our current personnel who are capable of meeting our growing technical, operational, and managerial requirements, our business may be adversely affected.
In addition, heightened public attention on AI has increased physical and informational security risks, and we have experienced threats to employee safety and attempts to obtain confidential information through physical or digital means, which, despite the security measures we have implemented at certain facilities, may be exacerbated by our global and flexible working arrangements and could adversely affect employee morale, productivity, and our ability to attract, retain, and motivate highly skilled personnel. Addressing these risks also requires us to attract and retain additional specialized security personnel, and difficulties in recruiting qualified security engineers could further exacerbate these challenges.
Further, changes to immigration policies that restrain the flow of professional and technical talent, including but not limited to U.S. immigration policies, may inhibit our ability to recruit and retain highly qualified employees. If we are unable to effectively manage the foregoing risks, our prospects, business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.

text:
If we fail to manage our growth effectively, our brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.
Since 2021, we have experienced rapid growth in our employee headcount, number of customers, geographic reach, and our operations, and we expect this growth to continue. For example, the number of our employees increased from approximately 940 as of December 31, 2024 to approximately 5,300 as of September 30, 2026, and our revenue increased from $197 million for the three months ended December 31, 2024 to $17.0 billion for the three months ended September 30, 2026. This growth has placed, and may continue to place, a significant strain on our management and our operational and financial resources.
Our ability to successfully manage this growth depends on our ability to scale and integrate our operations, workforce, technologies, models, platform, and applications, and any future acquisitions while preserving the beneficial aspects of our company culture. Continued growth may strain our ability to develop and enhance our operational, compliance, technical, financial, and management controls, improve our reporting systems and procedures, recruit, train, and retain highly skilled personnel, and maintain customer satisfaction. If we are unable to do so, our operations, compliance with applicable laws, development and deployment of our models, platform, and applications, and customer experience could be adversely affected.
As we expand, we must also manage an increasing number of relationships with strategic partners, customers, vendors, and other third parties that are critical to our business, including those that provide compute, data center infrastructure, networking, software tools, and other services necessary to develop, train, deploy, and operate our models. If these relationships deteriorate, or if our third-party providers are unable to scale their services in line with our growth, we may experience delays, service disruptions, reduced sales to new customers, or the loss of existing customers, which could adversely affect our revenue growth and reputation. In addition, our ability to manage our growth depends in part on our ability to accurately plan for and efficiently manage the compute required to develop, train, deploy, and operate our models. Any material underinvestment or overinvestment in such resources could result in service limitations, increased costs, operational inefficiencies, or delays in model development, any of which could adversely affect our business.

text: In addition, before September 30, 2026, we granted RSUs to our employees and other service providers, which vest upon the satisfaction of both a service-based condition and a performance-based condition. The service-based condition for a majority of such RSUs is satisfied over a period of four years. The performance-based condition for such RSUs will be satisfied upon the effectiveness of the registration statement of which this prospectus forms a part. We account for award forfeitures as they occur. As of September 30, 2026, no stock-based compensation expense had been recognized for such RSUs because the achievement of the performance-based condition described above was not probable. In the quarter in which this offering is completed, we will begin recording stock-based compensation expense based on the grant-date fair value of the RSUs (or, for RSUs modified as part of the RSU Modification, their modification-date fair value) using the accelerated attribution method. If this offering had been completed on September 30, 2026, we would have recorded $8.2 billion of cumulative stock-based compensation expense related to the RSUs on that date, and an additional $24.1 billion of unrecognized stock-based compensation expense related to the RSUs, would be recognized over a weighted-average period of approximately 2.0 years. In addition to stock-based compensation expense associated with the RSUs, as of September 30, 2026, we had unrecognized stock-based compensation expense of approximately $2.1 billion related to other outstanding equity awards, which we expect to recognize over a weighted-average period of approximately 1.4 years. Subsequent to September 30, 2026, our board of directors approved the grant of 47,041,287 RSUs to our employees and other service providers. These RSUs will vest upon the satisfaction of a service-based condition only, generally over four years. Assuming a grant-date fair value of $74.00 per share, which is the midpoint of the estimated offering price range set forth on the cover page of this prospectus, we would expect to record stock-based compensation expense of approximately $3.5 billion related to such RSUs, over a weighted-average period of approximately 3.8 years, commencing in the quarter in which this offering is completed. Following the completion of this offering, the stock-based compensation expense related to RSUs and other outstanding equity awards will result in increases in our expenses in future periods, in particular, in the quarter in which this offering is completed.

Our results of operations may fluctuate significantly on a period-to-period basis, including as a result of strategic investment decisions and substantial compute-related expenditures, which could cause the market price of our Class A common stock to decline.
Our results of operations have historically varied from period to period, and we expect that our results of operations will continue to vary significantly from quarter to quarter and from year to year in the future, such that the results of any one period should not be relied upon as an indication of future performance. In particular, our financial performance may be significantly influenced by strategic decisions we make regarding the allocation of resources and the amount and timing of operating expenses and capital expenditures that we may incur to maintain and expand our business and operations and to remain competitive. We may make significant and, at times, discrete investments in areas such as research and development, compute and related infrastructure, product development, safety and security initiatives, and go-to-market expansion, which may be uneven in size and timing. These investments may materially increase our expenses in a given period and cause our results of operations to fluctuate significantly or vary meaningfully from period to period, and may result in periods of reduced margins or increased losses even if our underlying business trends remain unchanged or continue to improve. As a result, our financial performance may not follow any consistent pattern, and prior or interim periods of improved results of operations should not be viewed as indicative of our future performance.

Our revenue in any period has also included, and we expect will continue to include, amounts from customers that we subsequently determine are using our models, platform, and applications in violation of our usage policy or commercial terms, and whose revenue would not be expected to recur following restriction or termination of their access. We believe this dynamic is common in our industry. Detection, investigation, and enforcement take time, and we cannot assure you that we will identify such usage, or restrict or terminate a customer’s access, on a timely basis or at all. Customers may evade our controls, and customers whose access is restricted or terminated may re-register under new accounts. As a result, revenue from such customers may continue or recur notwithstanding our enforcement efforts. Our continued detection and enforcement efforts, and in particular, the enhancement of such efforts in August and September 2026, and the timing of any resulting restrictions or terminations, are expected to reduce the percentage of revenue from customers using our models, platform, and applications in violation of our usage policy or commercial terms, and may reduce our overall revenue and growth rates in future periods and contribute to variability in our results from period to period.
Our results of operations are also affected by seasonal variations in the usage of our models, platform, and applications. Because our revenue is primarily consumption-based, we have experienced, and expect to continue to experience, lower usage around holiday and vacation periods in the summer and winter, when certain customer workflows slow down and overall customer activity declines. Our results of operations may also vary with the timing and cadence of our model and product releases, which are uneven from period to period and may cause usage, and therefore revenue, to increase or decline between periods. Our historical growth rates may have masked the impact of seasonal trends on our results. As our growth rate declines over time, we expect seasonal effects to become more apparent in, and to have a greater effect on, our period-to-period results. In addition, other seasonal trends may develop, and the seasonal trends that we currently experience may become more pronounced, as we continue to scale.
Our results of operations may also fluctuate due to a variety of additional factors, many of which are outside of our control and difficult to predict, including, but not limited to:

text: Run-Rate Revenue is not a substitute for revenue prepared in accordance with GAAP or a forecast of revenue. Because Run-Rate Revenue annualizes our consumption-based fees for a trailing 28-day period and our subscription-based fees for a single month, it assumes that activity during those measurement periods has continued at the same rate for a full year. Because it annualizes a short measurement period, Run-Rate Revenue measured during a period of seasonally higher or lower usage, such as the reduced usage we have typically experienced around holiday and vacation periods in the summer and winter, may differ significantly from Run-Rate Revenue measured at other times, and in each case may not correspond to the revenue we ultimately recognize over any quarter or fiscal year. Our actual historical revenue and future revenue may differ materially from this measure. Both our consumption-based and subscription-based revenue may fluctuate from period to period, and in particular, our consumption-based revenue may fluctuate significantly or decline if customers reduce, limit, or do not expand their usage or spend, or shift usage to lower-priced models, including in response to competitive offerings, pricing changes, changes in customer budgets or strategic priorities regarding AI investment, seasonality, or general economic conditions. In addition, sustaining and growing this revenue depends on our ability to continue to offer models at the frontier of AI capability, which we may not be able to do. Our ability or decision to remain at the frontier may also be affected by the safety and risk mitigation measures we implement in developing and releasing our models. Our recent Run-Rate Revenue growth has also been driven in part by rapid initial customer adoption and expansion often characteristic of an early-adoption period and the nascency of the AI market that may not be sustainable, and we expect our Run-Rate Revenue growth rate to decline over time, and it may decline significantly and more rapidly than we anticipate, as our revenue base increases, as the market matures, and as a result of other factors. In addition, our Run-Rate Revenue has included, and we expect will continue to include, amounts from customers that we subsequently determine are using our models, platform, and applications in violation of our usage policy or commercial terms.

The determination of the number of customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis is based on our internal records and involves judgment, including in determining which accounts should be aggregated and treated as belonging to the same organization. We apply our most current customer records in calculating this metric, and our determination of which accounts belong to a single organization may change over time, including as a result of acquisitions and account consolidations. We do not separately define or internally track a category of “enterprise” customers, and our customers are not segmented or measured internally by reference to whether a given customer is an “enterprise.” Because spending $100,000 or more on our products is generally characteristic of organizational rather than individual usage, we use the number of and revenue from customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis as our measure of enterprise adoption and engagement with Claude throughout this prospectus, including in references to “enterprise customers” and “enterprise adoption.” As a result, this measure may not precisely correspond to the population of organizations that would otherwise be characterized as enterprises, and may over- or understate that population.
Certain success rates and similar AI performance metrics with respect to Claude referenced in this prospectus are measured using internal benchmarks developed and maintained by us. These benchmarks reflect our proprietary testing methodology and are based on tasks, datasets, and evaluation criteria selected by us. Performance results derived from these internal benchmarks may not be replicable by customers, researchers, or other third parties who evaluate our models using different tasks, datasets, evaluation criteria, or computing environments. Accordingly, such metrics may differ materially from performance outcomes experienced by any particular customer or user in their specific deployment environment or use case, and should not be relied upon as indicative of the results any customer or user will achieve. Because AI performance benchmarking methodologies vary significantly across developers, such performance metrics as we measure them may also not be comparable to similarly titled or analogous metrics reported by other AI developers, and direct comparison of such metrics across companies may be misleading.

text:
Our business is subject to an evolving and uncertain regulatory and political environment, which could increase our costs, restrict our operations, or adversely affect demand for our models, platform, and applications.
The development, deployment, and use of AI technologies are subject to rapidly evolving and increasingly complex laws, regulations, and governmental scrutiny across multiple jurisdictions. Governments and regulatory authorities in the United States and in other countries in which we operate or distribute our models, platform, and applications have proposed, enacted, or are considering legislation, regulations, and guidance relating to AI model development and deployment, data usage and privacy, transparency, safety, consumer protection, content generation, intellectual property, cybersecurity, export controls, and competition. For example, the EU AI Regulation 2024/1689 (“EU AI Act”), which came into force in August 2024 and will become fully applicable following a transitional period, imposes a range of obligations on AI systems and general-purpose AI models placed on the market or put into service in the EU, including transparency, risk management, and governance requirements, and provides for significant penalties for non-compliance. In the United States, the regulatory framework for AI remains fragmented and uncertain, with evolving federal policy initiatives, continued debate regarding the scope and durability of executive actions, and a growing number of state-level laws and proposals addressing the development and use of AI. For example, several U.S. states, including New York and California, have passed AI safety laws. More generally, proposed legislation in the United States contemplates more expansive governmental oversight of AI, including potential nationalization, mandatory shutdown or discontinuation requirements for frontier intelligence systems, or other strategic measures to prevent or manage the development of SI. Further, in June 2026, the U.S. federal government issued an executive order establishing a voluntary framework for developers of frontier models to engage with the government prior to the deployment of such AI technologies, directing federal agencies to strengthen cyber defenses, and prioritizing enforcement against criminal misuse of AI; although that framework is voluntary and does not establish a mandatory governmental licensing, preclearance, or permitting requirement for the development or deployment of AI models, it reflects increasing federal attention to the national security implications of frontier intelligence and the order may be followed by further executive or legislative action. If executive or legislative action of this nature were enacted to regulate AI technologies, it could constrain how we operate our business.

text:
We have also advocated, and expect to continue to advocate, for regulation and oversight of frontier intelligence, including industry-wide standards primarily relevant to the use of AI to accelerate AI development, so that AI capabilities do not advance faster than the safety, alignment, and security practices needed to support them, and we have proposed working with the U.S. government and other frontier model developers to establish safety standards. Regulatory or other measures of the kind we advocate, if adopted, would apply to us and could increase our compliance burdens, limit our product development or deployment flexibility, affect how and when we develop or release new models, or otherwise slow our growth. The effect that any such measures would have on the rate at which AI capabilities advance, and on our business, is uncertain and would depend on the specific requirements adopted and on the extent to which safety, alignment, and security practices advance together with model capabilities. There is no assurance that policymakers will adopt the approaches we support, and our advocacy has in the past drawn, and may continue to draw, criticism, heightened scrutiny, or other challenges.
Regulatory approaches to AI also vary significantly by geography and may be influenced by local political, economic, social, or environmental considerations. In some jurisdictions, public concern regarding the potential displacement of labor by AI systems, the perceived societal impacts of automation, or the environmental footprint associated with AI development and deployment, has led, or could lead, to restrictive legislation or other governmental actions. In particular, to the extent the rate of job displacement rapidly increases due to the adoption of AI or for related reasons, whether actual or perceived, governments or other regulatory authorities may intervene to slow the rate of adoption of AI, restrict its use, or take other actions that increase the cost of developing, deploying, or commercializing AI systems. Even in the absence of any legal or regulatory requirements, we may from time to time voluntarily elect to take actions intended to ameliorate the impact of such displacement. Any such actions would represent additional costs and expenditures for which we may not receive a corresponding commercial benefit, and there can be no assurance that any such actions would be effective in reducing displacement-related harms or in mitigating the associated reputational, regulatory, or political risks.

text: For example, in February 2026, in response to our publicly stated position that our technology should not be used for mass domestic surveillance or fully autonomous weapons, the President of the United States stated that he had directed that all federal executive agencies cease using our technology. At the same time, the Secretary of War directed the Department of War to designate us as a “supply-chain risk to national security” and stated that “effective immediately, no contractor, supplier, or partner that does business with the United States military may conduct any commercial activity” with us. On March 4, 2026, the Department of War sent us two letters—one pursuant to 10 U.S.C. § 3252 and the other pursuant to Section 4713 of the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act (“FASCSA”)—asserting that our models, platform, and applications present a supply-chain risk. These actions referenced above are defined herein as “Challenged Actions.” We vigorously challenged these Challenged Actions in Anthropic PBC v. Department of War, et al. (N.D. Cal.) and Anthropic PBC v. Department of War, et al. (D.C. Cir.). After first obtaining an order from the United States District Court for the Northern District of California that preliminarily enjoined the Department of War’s directive and Section 3252 supply-chain risk designation of us and preliminarily enjoined the other defendant agencies from implementing the Presidential directive until final resolution of the lawsuit, we subsequently, on August 27, 2026, obtained an order from the United States District Court for the Northern District of California that largely granted summary judgment in our favor. The court ruled that the Challenged Actions were retaliatory acts meant to punish us for speech protected under the First Amendment to the United States Constitution and violated our rights under the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution. The court also held that the Secretary of War’s actions, particularly with respect to 10 U.S.C. § 3252, violated the Administrative Procedure Act because they were in excess of statutory authority, contrary to law, and arbitrary and capricious. The court entered final judgment largely in our favor. The defendants filed a notice of appeal of the preliminary injunction. The D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, however, denied our motion to stay the Secretary of War’s Section 4713 designation of us as a supply-chain risk pending review on the merits. Our reliance on a limited number of CSPs and suppliers, some of which have strategic and investment relationships with us and are our customers, creates complex dynamics that could give rise to conflicts of interest and adversely affect our access to compute.
We rely on a limited number of CSPs—Amazon, Google, and Microsoft—and suppliers, such as Broadcom, for compute and critical components of our compute infrastructure. These relationships are governed by contractual arrangements that, while providing us with significant committed compute, also create dependencies and potential vulnerabilities. These CSPs may experience service outages, security incidents, or capacity constraints that affect our operations. The terms of our arrangements, including pricing, compute commitments, and service levels, are subject to negotiation upon renewal, and we may be unable to secure renewals on terms as favorable as our current arrangements. Migrating workloads to alternative providers would be costly, time-consuming, and operationally complex, and may not be feasible within timeframes that would avoid material disruption to our model development roadmap or our ability to serve customers. The engineering investment required to maintain the performance of our unified compute platform across new hardware environments means that any such migration could degrade our compute efficiency, increasing the compute and infrastructure costs required to support a given level of business activity during and following any such migration period.

text: Our relationships with these CSPs are multifaceted and complex. Amazon, Google, and Microsoft, through their respective affiliates, have made significant equity investments in our company. At the same time, they may have made, and may in the future make, equity investments in, provide financing to, or otherwise support companies whose models, platforms, or applications compete with ours. These CSPs are also our customers, purchasing our intelligence service for internal use or for their own products and services. Their purchasing decisions may be influenced by their own competing offerings, which could affect their demand for our intelligence service. Additionally, Amazon, Google, and Microsoft are among the largest technology companies in the world, each with substantial AI research and development programs, AI-powered models, platforms, and applications that compete with ours, and strategic interests that may not be fully aligned with our own. Amazon, Google, and Microsoft each offer AI services and develop and deploy competing AI models through their respective cloud platforms. We make certain of our models available through these cloud platforms, and our distribution relationships with Amazon, Google, and Microsoft generate revenue for us, but they also create dependencies, give them visibility into our pricing and commercial terms across the platforms they operate, and may influence their incentives regarding pricing, compute allocation, service quality, sales prioritization, and compensation structures. To the extent these CSPs promote, integrate, prioritize, or provide customer access to our models, platform, and applications on terms that are less favorable than those applicable to their own competing offerings or to the offerings of other companies, including with respect to pricing, commercial terms, product placement, integration, or access to compute or sales incentives, our competitive position, customer adoption, and business results could be adversely affected.
