text:
If we or our payment processing partners fail to manage the risks related to our payment processing activities, we could be subject to fines, regulatory scrutiny, disruptions to our business, or reputational harm.
A portion of our customers authorize us to bill their credit card accounts through our third-party payment processing partners for our paid subscriptions. We have experienced, and expect to continue to experience, fraudulent activity, including the creation of accounts using false identities and the use of stolen or otherwise unauthorized payment credentials, which has resulted, and may in the future result, in losses, including payment processing fees, chargeback fees, and fines and penalties imposed by our payment processors or card networks, for which we may not be reimbursed. We maintain fraud-detection and identity-verification measures, but these measures have not identified, and may not identify, all such activity. Further, our customers provide us with credit card billing information online, and we do not verify the physical identity of cardholders or conduct additional verification beyond what we collect online, which increases our risk of exposure to fraudulent activity.
We also incur chargebacks when customers or card issuers claim that a transaction was unauthorized or otherwise improper. If the volume of chargebacks were to become excessive, we could be subject to higher processing fees, additional fines, fraud mitigation requirements, or the termination or suspension of our ability to accept certain payment methods, including credit cards, through one or more payment processors.
In addition, payment processors, card networks, and financial institutions periodically revise their rules, standards, and practices, including data protection and documentation standards, required to utilize their services. Our compliance with these evolving requirements, and the continued compliance of our third-party payment processing partners, may require additional operational resources and expense. Failure by us or our payment processing partners to comply with applicable standards could result in fines, increased scrutiny, disruptions to our business and our ability to process payments for our intelligence service, or reputational harm.

text:
Our ability to use our net operating loss carryforwards and certain other tax attributes may be limited.
We have incurred substantial net operating losses (“NOLs”) during our history. In general, under Sections 382 and 383 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended (the “Code”), a corporation that undergoes an “ownership change” is subject to annual limitations on its ability to utilize its pre-change U.S. federal NOL carryforwards and certain other tax attributes, including tax credit carryforwards, to offset its future taxable income or tax liabilities. For these purposes, an ownership change generally occurs if the percentage of a corporation’s stock (by value) owned by one or more “5-percent shareholders” increases by more than 50 percentage points over a rolling three-year period. We have experienced ownership changes in the past, and we may experience ownership changes in the future, including as a result of this offering or subsequent shifts in our stock ownership, some of which may be outside our control. NOLs and other tax attributes of companies we have acquired are, and of companies we may acquire may be, subject to similar limitations. Similar provisions of state tax law and the tax laws of non-U.S. jurisdictions may also limit our ability to utilize state and non-U.S. NOL carryforwards and other tax attributes. In addition, certain states, including California, have suspended or otherwise limited the use of NOL carryforwards and other tax attributes, which could accelerate or permanently increase our state income tax liabilities. Separately, under current law, U.S. federal NOLs arising in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2017 may be used to offset only 80% of taxable income in any year, whether or not an ownership change occurs. As a result of the foregoing, even if we attain profitability, we may be unable to use all or a material portion of our NOLs and other tax attributes, which could adversely affect our future cash flows and results of operations.

Our corporate structure and intercompany arrangements are subject to the tax laws of multiple jurisdictions, and we could be required to pay additional taxes, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
As we continue to expand our non-U.S. operations, we are, and may increasingly be, required to report taxable income in various jurisdictions around the world based on our business activities in those jurisdictions. Our corporate structure and associated transfer pricing policies reflect the functions, risks, and assets of the entities involved in our intercompany transactions. However, our tax position is subject to various risks, including increases in tax rates, new or revised tax laws (which may apply retroactively), and new interpretations of existing tax laws and policies by taxing authorities or courts, any of which could increase our overall tax obligations.
Our intercompany transactions are subject to complex transfer pricing rules administered by tax authorities in the jurisdictions in which we operate, many of which apply divergent, and sometimes conflicting, legal standards. Tax authorities may take inconsistent positions regarding the application of the arm’s-length principle, the characterization or valuation of our intellectual property, or the pricing of intercompany services and other transactions. If a tax authority successfully challenges our transfer pricing or the allocation of income and expenses among jurisdictions, we could be required to reallocate income or pay additional taxes, interest, and penalties. If the jurisdiction from which income is reallocated does not agree with the adjustment, we could also be subject to double taxation. In addition, certain of our cross-border contracting arrangements, including infrastructure-related agreements entered into by U.S. entities pending the formation of local subsidiaries, may give rise to non-recoverable value-added or similar indirect taxes or other tax costs, which could be material depending on the jurisdiction.
Although we believe our tax positions are reasonable, our tax reserves are adequate, and our transfer pricing practices reflect arm’s-length terms, tax authorities may disagree with our assumptions, judgments, and estimates. If a tax authority were to prevail in asserting that our intercompany arrangements do not satisfy applicable transfer pricing requirements, we could be required to pay additional taxes, interest, and penalties that exceed our reserves. Such an outcome could increase our effective tax rate, reduce our cash flows, and adversely affect our ability to achieve and sustain profitability.

We base our estimates in part on historical experience, market observable inputs, if available, and various other assumptions that we believe to be reasonable under the circumstances, as provided in the section titled “Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations—Critical Accounting Estimates.” Significant accounting policies, estimates, and assumptions used in preparing our consolidated financial statements include, but are not limited to, revenue recognition, stock-based compensation, common stock valuations, fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs, leases, income taxes, and loss contingencies. In addition, we engage in complex and novel transactions and may be required to consolidate certain assets or entities on our financial statements, which may involve significant judgment and could result in volatility in our reported results of operations. Our results of operations may be adversely affected if our assumptions change or if actual circumstances differ from those in our assumptions, which may cause our results of operations to fall below the expectations of securities analysts and investors and cause a decline in the market price of our Class A common stock.

If we fail to maintain an effective system of disclosure controls and internal control over financial reporting, our ability to produce timely and accurate financial statements or comply with applicable regulations may be impaired, which may adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
As a public company, we will be subject to the reporting requirements of the Exchange Act, the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, and the listing standards of the Nasdaq Global Select Market. The Sarbanes-Oxley Act and related Exchange Act rules require, among other things, that we maintain effective disclosure controls and procedures and internal control over financial reporting. We are continuing to develop and refine our disclosure controls and other procedures that are designed to assure that information required to be disclosed by us in the reports that we will file with the SEC is recorded, processed, summarized, and reported within the time periods specified in SEC rules and forms and that information required to be disclosed in reports under the Exchange Act is accumulated and communicated to management, including our principal executive and financial officers, to allow timely decisions regarding disclosure. We are also continuing to improve our internal control over financial reporting. We have expended, and anticipate that we will continue to expend, significant resources to maintain and improve the effectiveness of our disclosure controls and procedures and internal control over financial reporting.
Our current controls and any new controls that we develop may become inadequate because of changes in the conditions in our business. Further, weaknesses in our disclosure controls, procedures, or internal control over financial reporting may be discovered in the future. Any failure to develop or maintain effective controls, or any difficulties encountered in their implementation or improvement, may adversely affect our results of operations or cause us to fail to meet our reporting obligations and may result in a restatement of our financial statements for prior periods. We also rely on distribution partners and other third-party service providers to process and store data underlying our financial reporting. Our ability to maintain effective internal controls therefore depends in part on the design and operating effectiveness of controls maintained by these third parties, and our ability to audit or remediate deficiencies in such third-party control environments is limited.

Ineffective disclosure controls and procedures and internal control over financial reporting may also cause investors to lose confidence in our reported financial and other information, which would likely adversely affect the market price of our Class A common stock. text:
We are exposed to fluctuations in interest rates and currency exchange rates, which could negatively affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
We hold a significant amount of cash, cash equivalents, and investments, a substantial portion of which is invested in instruments with variable or market-based interest rates. As a result, our investment income is sensitive to changes in prevailing interest rates. A decline in interest rates could reduce the income we earn on these investments, which could adversely affect our financial condition and results of operations. In addition, volatility in interest rates may impact the fair value of our investment portfolio and could affect our overall financial performance.
Our sales are currently denominated in U.S. dollars, euros, and British pounds, and will likely be denominated in other currencies in the future. Because we report our results of operations and revenue in U.S. dollars, we are exposed to foreign currency translation risk and may in the future face additional foreign currency risks. For example, a strengthening of the U.S. dollar compared to these foreign currencies could increase the real cost of our models, platform, and applications to non-U.S. customers, which could reduce demand for our models, platform, and applications and adversely affect our results of operations. In addition, as our non-U.S. operations expand, an increasing portion of our operating expenses may be denominated in foreign currencies and subject to fluctuations due to changes in foreign currency exchange rates. If we are not able to effectively manage these risks, including through any hedging activities, our financial condition and results of operations could be adversely affected.

Our capital stock structure features certain provisions that are novel or otherwise not common among other corporations with multiple-class structures, and may effectively eliminate the ability of holders of our Class A common stock to influence important decisions, including a change in control.
We have a novel capital and corporate governance structure that has no direct public company precedent. We are incorporated as a PBC under Delaware law. As a PBC, we are required to balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose identified in our amended and restated certificate of incorporation. In addition, the LTBT possesses certain rights that are designed to help ensure that we are managed in a manner that responsibly balances our goals as a PBC. Through a special class of common stock, Class T common stock, the LTBT generally has the authority to elect and remove the Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. See the section titled “Our Governance Structure and Its Goals—Long-Term Benefit Trust— Election and Removal of Directors” for more information. The LTBT is intended to operate as an independent body of five financially disinterested Trustees, and our Class T common stock has no economic rights. As a result, the LTBT may have interests that differ from yours, and it may exercise its power in a way with which you disagree or in a way that may be adverse to your interests. Immediately prior to the completion of this offering, we will also issue a single share of Class F common stock, a special class of our common stock, to the Founder LLC. Our Class F common stock will be entitled to an aggregate number of votes that equals 50.1% of the total voting power of our outstanding shares of capital stock as of the applicable record date with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally, including the election of our directors other than the Class T directors. Immediately prior to the completion of this offering, we will also authorize a special class of our common stock, Class E common stock, which we will issue to our employees, excluding our co-founders. Our Class E common stock will be entitled to vote only on certain limited matters and will not have any economic rights.

Accordingly, holders of our Class A common stock generally will not be able to affect the outcome of any matter submitted to a vote of our stockholders or the election of our directors, regardless of how they vote, unless a majority of the Continuing Founders (as defined below) cannot agree on how our Class F common stock will be voted (in which case our Class F common stock will generally be voted proportionately with the votes of our Class A common stock cast on the matter).

Our governance structure is likely to have the effect of limiting the likelihood of an unsolicited merger proposal, unsolicited tender offer, or proxy contest for the removal of directors. As a result, our governance structure may make it more difficult to replace our directors and management and may have the effect of depriving our stockholders of an opportunity to sell their shares at a premium over prevailing market prices.
We cannot predict whether our structure will result in lower demand for our Class A common stock, increased volatility, adverse publicity, or other adverse consequences. In particular, the absence of judicial precedent interpreting this structure increases the risk and unpredictability of governance-related litigation, and courts may interpret the obligations inherent in our structure in ways that we might not anticipate.

text:
Our capital structure will concentrate voting power with the LTBT and the Founder LLC for the foreseeable future and will result in the LTBT and the Founder LLC having voting power that is not derived from or proportionate to economic interests in our company.
Our Class T common stock will generally entitle the LTBT to elect and remove the Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. Our Class T common stock will remain outstanding indefinitely, subject to the right of our board of directors and the Trustees or specified majorities of our Class A common stock, Class E common stock, and Class F common stock to amend or terminate the terms of the LTBT or the rights of our Class T common stock or to redeem our Class T common stock (such time as no share of Class T common stock is outstanding, the “Class T Sunset Time”). The Class T common stock may also be transferred without restriction upon the receipt of the same approvals required to amend, terminate, or redeem it. We intentionally structured the Class T common stock in this manner to preserve long-term flexibility if circumstances change. If the Class T common stock were transferred to a person or entity that is not affiliated with the LTBT or is not otherwise required to consider the Company Purpose, for so long as we remain a PBC, all of our directors, regardless of how they are elected, would continue to be obligated to act in accordance with Delaware law and our certificate of incorporation, bylaws, and other governing documents as then in effect, including those provisions relating to our public benefit purpose. The Trust Agreement (as defined below) limits Trustee compensation to a reasonable cash amount fixed annually by the Trustees. Trustee compensation will not vary with or be conditioned upon the profits or any action or inaction of our company. The policies of the LTBT prohibit a Trustee from directly purchasing or holding any of our securities.

Certain aspects of our governance structure, such as our multi-class capital structure, may limit the ability of certain institutional investors to invest in us as a result of their investment policies or may make such an investment less attractive to the portfolio managers of certain institutional investors.

These policies may depress our valuation compared to those of other similar companies that are able to be included in such indices.

text:
We are considered a “controlled company” within the meaning of the Nasdaq Global Select Market corporate governance requirements, and, as a result, we qualify for, and currently rely on, exemptions from certain corporate governance requirements.
We are considered a “controlled company” within the meaning of the Nasdaq Global Select Market corporate governance requirements because the LTBT, as the sole holder of our Class T common stock, generally has the power to elect a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. As a result, we may elect not to comply with certain corporate governance requirements, including:
•the requirement that a majority of our board of directors consist of independent directors;
•the requirement that our board of directors have a nominating and corporate governance committee that is comprised entirely of independent directors with a written charter addressing the committee’s purpose and responsibilities; and •the requirement that we have a compensation committee that is comprised entirely of independent directors with a written charter addressing the committee’s purpose and responsibilities.
If we elect not to comply with certain requirements, you will not have the same protections afforded to stockholders of companies that are subject to all of the Nasdaq Global Select Market corporate governance requirements. Although we qualify as a “controlled company,” we do not expect to rely on this exemption except with respect to our NGC, which will not consist entirely of independent directors. Our board of directors currently consists of a majority of independent directors and our audit and compensation committees currently consist entirely of independent directors. In the event that we cease to be a “controlled company” and our Class A common stock continues to be listed on the Nasdaq Global Select Market, we will be required to comply with the provision that our NGC be comprised entirely of independent directors within the applicable transition period.

We operate as a Delaware public benefit corporation. As a public benefit corporation, we cannot provide any assurance that we will achieve the Company Purpose.
As a PBC, we are intended to produce a public benefit or benefits and to operate in a responsible and sustainable manner, balancing our stockholders’ pecuniary interests, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose identified in our amended and restated certificate of incorporation. We cannot assure you that we will achieve the Company Purpose or that the expected positive impact from being a PBC will be realized, which could adversely affect our reputation, business, financial condition, and results of operations. As a PBC, we are required, under Section 366 of the Delaware General Corporation Law (“DGCL”) and pursuant to our amended and restated bylaws, to disclose to stockholders a report at least biennially on our overall performance in promoting the public benefit identified in our amended and restated certificate of incorporation and the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct and on our assessment of our success in achieving the Company Purpose and in promoting those interests. If we are not timely or are unable to provide this report, or if the report is not viewed favorably by parties doing business with us, regulators, others reviewing our credentials, or other stakeholders, including holders of our Class A common stock, our reputation as a PBC may be adversely affected.

text:
Our focus on the long-term best interests of our company as a PBC, and the duty of our directors to balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those stakeholders materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose, may conflict with short-, medium-, or long-term financial interests and business performance, which may negatively impact the value of our Class A common stock.
We have made, and may in the future make, decisions that we believe balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose set forth in our amended and restated certificate of incorporation, even if such decisions may negatively impact the short-, medium-, or long-term performance of our business, financial condition, and results of operations or the short-, medium-, or long-term performance of our Class A common stock. This may impact the value of our Class A common stock and make owning our Class A common stock less appealing to investors who are focused on returns. Our decisions and actions in pursuit of long-term success may not result in the long-term benefits we expect, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations, as well as the market price of our Class A common stock. Such decisions and actions may include changes to our models, platform, and applications; limitations on certain uses of our models, platform, and applications; moderating the pace of the development of our models for safety-related reasons; adjustments to the timing of new offerings; changes in how we deliver customer support; investments in our relationships with partners and employees; investments in and introductions of new models, platforms, and applications; investments in social impact initiatives consistent with our public benefit objectives; and changes in our approach to working with local or national jurisdictions on laws and regulations governing our business.

text: Our policies, including those on usage, currently prohibit, or may be revised in the future to prohibit, certain usage or other actions, which may have adverse commercial consequences to us. For example, our usage policy prohibits the use of our models, platform, and applications to develop or operate fully autonomous weapons or to conduct mass surveillance, including mass domestic surveillance, and we have declined to permit such uses based on the Company Purpose, notwithstanding the revenue those or similar uses could generate. Maintaining these limitations has had, and may continue to have, adverse commercial and financial consequences. We have also restricted or delayed the availability of certain capabilities for safety reasons. For example, we initially released our Mythos model only as a gated research preview through Project Glasswing rather than making it broadly available to the public. Similarly, we have chosen not to develop certain commercially attractive offerings, such as image and video generation models, in order to direct our compute toward our research and safety priorities. Our public advocacy, and the decisions we make to moderate the pace of AI development, delay or restrict the release of models or features, or forgo commercial opportunities for safety-related reasons, may not maximize stockholder value, could have a negative impact on the value of our Class A common stock, and could result in litigation. Each of these decisions reflects our directors’ balancing of the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose. While we believe these decisions are consistent with the Company Purpose, as a result of these decisions, we may forgo revenue, customers, or growth opportunities that a corporation managed solely to maximize stockholder value might pursue.

text: Further, while directors of traditional corporations typically have a fiduciary duty to focus on maximizing stockholder value, directors of a PBC have a duty to consider not only the stockholders’ financial interests but also the company’s specific public benefit purpose and the best interests of those stakeholders materially affected by the company’s actions. Thus, our directors are not merely permitted, but obligated, to consider the Company Purpose and the interests of other stakeholders. Under Delaware law, directors are shielded from liability for breach of these obligations if they make informed and disinterested decisions that serve a rational purpose. In the event of a conflict among the interests of our stockholders, the Company Purpose, or the interests of our other stakeholders, our directors must only make informed and disinterested decisions that serve a rational purpose; thus, we cannot guarantee that such a conflict would be resolved in favor of our stockholders’ monetary interests, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations and cause the market price of our Class A common stock to decline. In addition, there is very limited judicial precedent interpreting the balancing requirement applicable to PBCs under Delaware law, particularly for companies with significant scale or visibility, or with a scope of PBC purpose similar to ours. As a result, the scope of directors’ obligations, the standards by which their decisions may be reviewed, and the nature and availability of stockholder remedies in connection with alleged failures to responsibly balance these interests remain uncertain. Future judicial interpretations of these provisions could be more expansive than we currently anticipate and could result in increased litigation risk, greater scrutiny of board decision-making, or outcomes that differ from our expectations.

text:
Additionally, as a PBC, we are less vulnerable to an unsolicited takeover effort than a traditional company would be and, therefore, your ability to realize your investment through an acquisition may be limited. We may also not be an attractive target for activists or hedge fund investors because new directors must consider and give appropriate weight to the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose, and stockholders may be able to enforce this obligation through litigation. Further, by requiring that our board of directors consider additional stakeholders and the Company Purpose, and not just maximizing stockholder value, Delaware law could make it easier for our board of directors to reject a hostile bid, even where the acceptance of such a bid would provide the greatest short-term financial yield to investors.
In addition, we intend to direct a meaningful portion of our resources toward our public benefit initiatives, which may include contributions to nonprofit organizations, research institutions, underserved communities, and other third parties that may not otherwise have access to frontier intelligence capabilities. These initiatives, which include the Initial Public Benefit Issuance and the future Public Benefit Issuances, have been, and may continue to be, substantial in scale, and we expect to significantly grow these efforts over time. The benefits of such expenditures may be difficult or impossible to measure in financial terms and may not result in any direct or measurable benefit to our business or our stockholders. The amount of resources directed toward these initiatives may, in any given period, reduce our revenue, increase our expenses, or otherwise affect our results of operations.

text:
As a Delaware public benefit corporation, we may be subject to increased litigation concerning our board of directors’ obligation to balance our stockholders’ pecuniary interests, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose, the occurrence of which may have an adverse impact on our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
Section 367 of the DGCL provides that stockholders of a Delaware PBC with shares listed on a national securities exchange may only file an action to enforce the statutory balancing requirement imposed on the board of directors by the DGCL if they, individually or collectively, own the lesser of at least two percent of the corporation’s outstanding shares or shares of the corporation with a market value of at least $2,000,000 as of the date the action is instituted and, in the case of a derivative action, such stockholders satisfy any other conditions applicable to filing a derivative action. This potential liability for enforcement of the statutory balancing requirement does not exist for traditional corporations. Therefore, we may be subject to the possibility of increased litigation, which would require the attention of our management, and, as a result, may adversely affect our management’s ability to effectively execute our strategy. There is limited judicial precedent for this type of balancing litigation, which may create uncertainty around the scope of our directors’ obligations or the remedies available to stockholders. Additionally, any such litigation may be costly, which may adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.

Our amended and restated bylaws will designate a state or federal court located within the State of Delaware as the exclusive forum for substantially all disputes between us and our stockholders, and also provide that the federal district courts will be the exclusive forum for resolving any complaint asserting a cause of action arising under the Securities Act of 1933, as amended, each of which may limit our stockholders’ ability to choose the judicial forum for disputes with us or our directors, officers, stockholders, or employees.
Our amended and restated bylaws, which will become effective immediately prior to the completion of this offering, will provide that, unless we consent in writing to the selection of an alternative forum, the Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware (or, if the Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware does not have jurisdiction, another State court in Delaware or the federal district court for the District of Delaware) will, to the fullest extent permitted by law, be the sole and exclusive forum for (i) any derivative action or proceeding brought on our behalf, (ii) any action asserting a claim of breach of a fiduciary duty owed by any of our current or former directors, stockholders, or officers or other employees to us or our stockholders, (iii) any action arising pursuant to any provision of the DGCL, or as to which the DGCL confers jurisdiction upon the Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware, (iv) any action arising pursuant to or to interpret, apply, enforce, or determine the validity of our amended and restated certificate of incorporation, or our amended and restated bylaws, or (v) any action asserting a claim governed by the internal affairs doctrine, except for, in all cases, any claim as to which such court determines that there is an indispensable party not subject to the jurisdiction of such court (and the indispensable party does not consent to the personal jurisdiction of such court within 10 days following such determination).

text:
Section 22 of the Securities Act establishes concurrent jurisdiction for federal and state courts over Securities Act claims. Accordingly, both state and federal courts have jurisdiction to hear such claims. To prevent having to litigate claims in multiple jurisdictions and the threat of inconsistent or contrary rulings by different courts, among other considerations, our amended and restated bylaws will also provide that, unless we consent in writing to the selection of an alternative forum, the federal district courts of the United States will, to the fullest extent permitted by applicable law, be the sole and exclusive forum for resolving any complaint asserting a cause or causes of action arising under the Securities Act against any person in connection with any offering of our securities, including, without limitation, any auditor, underwriter, expert, control person, or other defendant. Unless we consent in writing to the selection of an alternative forum, the United States District Court for the District of Delaware will, to the fullest extent permitted by applicable law, be the sole and exclusive forum for the resolution of any derivative action or proceeding brought to enforce any duty or liability created by the Exchange Act or the rules or regulations thereunder. All other claims arising under the Exchange Act may be brought in any federal court of competent jurisdiction.
Any person or entity purchasing, holding, or otherwise acquiring any interest in any of our securities shall be deemed to have notice of and consented to the foregoing bylaw provisions. Although we believe these exclusive forum provisions benefit us by providing increased consistency in the application of Delaware law and federal securities laws in the types of lawsuits to which each applies, the exclusive forum provisions may limit a stockholder’s ability to bring a claim in a judicial forum of its choosing for disputes with us or our current or former directors, officers, stockholders, or other employees, which may discourage lawsuits with respect to such claims against us and our current and former directors, officers, stockholders, or other employees. text:
Although our Class N common stock is not entitled to vote, it is entitled to economic rights equivalent to those of our Class A common stock, including the right to participate ratably with our Class A common stock in any dividends we may declare and in distributions upon a liquidation, dissolution, or winding up. As a result, the shares of Class N common stock issued in connection with the completion of this offering as a result of the Preferred Stock Conversion, Convertible Notes Conversion, and the concurrent private placement will dilute the economic interests, including any dividends and any proceeds available for distribution to stockholders, of the holders of our Class A common stock, and such shares are included together with our Class A common stock in determining net tangible book value per share. See the section titled “Dilution.”
The shares of Class N common stock will automatically convert into an equal number of shares of Class A common stock upon a transfer effected through: (i) a registered offering or an open market sale of such shares or (ii) a transfer to an unaffiliated third party, subject to certain limitations described in the section titled “Description of Capital Stock.” While held as Class N common stock, these shares are non-voting and therefore do not impact the voting power of the holders of our Class A common stock. Upon the conversion of shares of Class N common stock into Class A common stock, however, the resulting shares of Class A common stock will be entitled to one vote per share and the issuance of such shares will dilute the voting power of the existing holders of our Class A common stock. Any shares of Class N common stock that we issue in the future would have the same effect, diluting the economic interests of the holders of our Class A common stock while outstanding, as well as diluting their voting power upon conversion into Class A common stock.

Future issuances of our Class A common stock, including upon conversion of our Class N common stock, and our Class N common stock will not dilute the voting power of our Class F common stock because our Class F common stock is entitled to a fixed 50.1% of the total voting power of our outstanding shares of capital stock as of the applicable record date with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally. For example, if we were to issue 1,000,000 additional shares of Class A common stock, our Class F common stock would automatically be entitled to an incremental number of votes sufficient to cause the aggregate voting power of our Class F common stock to equal 50.1% of the total voting power of our outstanding shares of capital stock as of the applicable record date with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally, or approximately 1,004,008 additional votes. Any future issuances of additional shares of Class A common stock, including upon conversion of our Class N common stock, and Class N common stock will not be subject to approval by our stockholders except as required by the listing standards of the Nasdaq Global Select Market.

location: USE OF PROCEEDS
text:
The principal purposes of this offering and the concurrent private placement are to increase our capitalization and financial flexibility, create a public market for our Class A common stock, facilitate an orderly distribution of shares for the selling stockholders, and enable access to the public equity markets for us and our stockholders.
We intend to use the net proceeds from this offering and the concurrent private placement for general corporate purposes, including working capital, operating expenses, and capital expenditures, including investments in compute and infrastructure, as well as hiring and retention of highly skilled personnel. Additionally, we may use a portion of the net proceeds we receive from this offering and the concurrent private placement to acquire or invest in businesses, products, services, or technologies. However, we do not have agreements or commitments for any material acquisitions or investments at this time.
We also intend to use a portion of the net proceeds we receive from this offering and the concurrent private placement to satisfy our anticipated tax withholding and remittance obligations of $3.8 billion related to the RSU Settlement. This amount is based upon the assumed initial public offering price of $74.00 per share, which is the midpoint of the estimated offering price range set forth on the cover page of this prospectus, and an assumed 50.90% tax withholding rate. Each $1.00 increase or decrease in the assumed initial public offering price of $74.00 per share would increase or decrease, as applicable, the amount we would be required to pay to satisfy our tax withholding and remittance obligations related to the RSU Settlement by $52 million.
We cannot further specify with certainty the particular uses of the net proceeds that we will receive from this offering and the concurrent private placement. Accordingly, we will have broad discretion in using these proceeds. Pending the use of proceeds from this offering and the concurrent private placement as described above, we may invest the net proceeds that we receive in this offering and the concurrent private placement in short-term, investment-grade, interest-bearing instruments.

location: MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS > Overview
text: Anthropic was founded in 2021 by a team of researchers responsible for many of the breakthroughs that define super intelligence.8 We are first and foremost a research lab—our mission is the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity. This mission directs our focus—along with our talent and culture, our frontier and safety research, our approach to compute, and our enterprise strategy, it is one of the core advantages that set us apart. These advantages enable us to continuously advance frontier intelligence and shape the standards for its safe and responsible development. Our frontier intelligence, Claude, is delivered to customers through our models, platform, and applications. Claude has experienced the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history, as demonstrated by revenue growing from $0 at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $17.0 billion for the three months ended September 30, 2026.

meta.section: MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS

location: MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS > Our Financial Model
text:
Our financial model is built on four primary drivers that define the trajectory of our results:
•Adoption of Claude. The advancing intelligence and capabilities of each successive version of a Claude model drive the diffusion of Claude across the global economy. As new customers adopt Claude and existing customers expand their usage into new workflows, our revenue grows.
•Compute Efficiency. We are focused on increasing the intelligence produced and revenue generated per dollar of compute invested and have delivered significant efficiency improvements.
•Operating Efficiency. Our high talent density, efficient go-to-market, and how extensively our teams leverage Claude in their work help to drive improved operating margin, Adjusted Operating Margin, and revenue per employee.
•Compute Investments. Investing in compute is critical to support our long-term growth, and we intend to continue making substantial investments in compute.
The drivers of our financial model materialize on different timelines. The adoption of Claude and associated revenue growth, compute efficiency, and operating efficiency have each increased rapidly over time. Compute is procured and committed in advance and the expense is incurred as it is brought online and added to our fungible pool, often in large, discrete steps. The fungible pool can support all workloads dynamically, including research, model development, serving customers, and internal usage of Claude. As a result, there is a lag between when investment is committed and when the full revenue associated with such investment is realized.
This dynamic has produced a financial model in which our operating margin and Adjusted Operating Margin for the nine months ended September 30, 2026 have expanded significantly year over year. As significant incremental compute is brought online in future periods, the associated expense will be recognized in advance of the full revenue that the compute will ultimately support, and we expect operating margin and Adjusted Operating Margin may compress in those periods. At our current stage, this cycle is an inherent aspect of our business and will cause operating margins to fluctuate from period to period, at times meaningfully, even if the underlying economics of the business continue to improve.

text: In addition, the majority of our compute is contracted under multi-year commitments that we typically procure 12 to 18 months in advance of availability. When customer demand or research needs exceed this long-term capacity, we procure short-term compute that currently costs significantly more than comparable compute procured under our multi-year commitments. We expect our use of short-term compute to continue to increase in the near term and to in turn compress our operating margin and Adjusted Operating Margin as a result.

location: MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS > Adoption of Claude
text:
Each successive version of a Claude model is designed to advance the frontier with capabilities that customers value most, including coding, agentic workflows, computer use, and complex reasoning, which unlock new categories of use and drive compounding demand from new and existing customers. Claude’s intelligence is a primary driver of its diffusion and our revenue growth: because Claude leads at the AI frontier, customers rapidly adopt it, quickly see real value, and organically expand their use. We complement this intelligence-led growth with direct go-to-market and Applied AI teams and extend our reach through native availability across all three major cloud platforms—AWS, GCP, and Azure—and through partnerships with systems integrators, consultants, and data platforms.
We deliver this intelligence through an integrated approach. Our Claude model family is the foundation, with model classes optimized for different points along the capability-cost-speed curve. On top of our models, Claude Platform gives developers access to the primitives we use ourselves, which they can use to build their own AI solutions. We have also built first-party applications on Claude Platform for customers that prefer a ready-to-deploy option. We believe the value of this integrated approach is reflected in the increasing number of customers that use both Claude Platform and our first-party applications. For the three months ended September 30, 2026, over 50% of our customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis used Claude Platform and at least one of our first-party applications, up from approximately 30% for the three months ended December 31, 2025.
As more customers adopt Claude and expand their usage, we have rapidly grown our base of customers that generate meaningful revenue. We had more than 11,900 customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis as of September 30, 2026, up from more than 950 as of September 30, 2025. In addition, as customers further embed Claude into their most critical workflows and growth initiatives, many rapidly expand their deployments into higher revenue tiers. As of September 30, 2026, we had more than 1,900 customers with $1 million or more of revenue on a TTM basis and approximately 250 customers with $10 million or more of revenue on a TTM basis.
title: US-PROSPECTUS (S-1/A, preliminary) | MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS > Adoption of Claude

location: MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS > Adoption of Claude
text:
This customer momentum is driven by significant usage expansion as customers realize the value of deploying Claude across their organizations. The value that Claude delivers to customers has helped drive our Net Revenue Retention of approximately 900% as of September 30, 2026.
The growth in our business reflects the degree to which enterprises are embedding Claude directly into their business-critical workflows. Despite these trends, adoption across the global economy remains nascent. As Claude’s capabilities continue to advance, we believe the addressable opportunity will expand, and Claude will continue its rapid diffusion across more enterprises.

meta.section: MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS

location: MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS > Compute Efficiency
text:
Compute is the most significant operating cost in our business, and compute efficiency is a critical determinant of our operating efficiency and revenue. Our research-driven algorithmic improvements in training and inference optimization and multi-chip compute architecture have combined to dramatically increase our compute efficiency as our revenue has scaled. The result is that we are able to continue increasing the intelligence our research can produce and the revenue our business can generate per dollar of compute investment.
We define compute efficiency as maximizing the intelligence produced and revenue generated per dollar of compute invested. Three pillars drive our compute efficiency:
•Training Efficiency. Our researchers regularly innovate compute multipliers. Increasingly, Claude itself assists in the research and engineering that produce each successive version of our models, which is a recursive dynamic we refer to as “closing the loop,” with successive versions of our models accelerating the development of the next and compounding these gains across model generations.
•Inference Efficiency. Our researchers have delivered meaningful compute multipliers for inference —reducing the compute required to serve a given level of model performance—while our engineering teams have driven significant optimizations in how efficiently that compute is utilized in production. This allows us to provide greater value for customers and generate greater revenue from our compute base over time, which is critical as we have consistently operated in a compute-constrained environment where customer demand exceeds available compute.
•Multi-Chip Compute Approach. We train and serve Claude natively across four major chip families (AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs) using a proprietary orchestration layer that enables us to optimize workloads for price and performance. This flexibility, which took years and significant investment to build and we believe is difficult to replicate at scale, expands our available compute, reduces dependence on any single vendor, and enables us to continuously route workloads to the most optimal hardware for those workloads. This foundation, paired with Claude’s increasing understanding of chip and model architectures, allows us to onboard new chip platforms in a fraction of the time this once required.
title: US-PROSPECTUS (S-1/A, preliminary) | MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS > Compute Efficiency

location: MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS > Compute Efficiency
text:
Revenue per dollar of compute has expanded meaningfully, even as we have accelerated research and product velocity and expanded our internal Claude usage. For example, our revenue grew 1,127% year over year for the three months ended September 30, 2026, compared to our compute and infrastructure expenses that grew 382% during the same period. While serving our growing customer demand, we also advanced the frontier with new leading models, including Mythos 5, Fable 5, and Opus 5, and launched new products, including Claude Cowork, Claude Security, and Claude Design.
In the three months ended September 30, 2026, our underlying compute efficiency improvements were partially offset by the delivery of additional compute, including $5.0 billion of compute under short-term commitments, which currently costs significantly more than comparable compute procured under our multi-year commitments. This reduced revenue per dollar of compute compared to the preceding quarter.

location: MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS > Operating Efficiency
text:
Our operating efficiency is derived from our high talent density, our efficient go-to-market, and how extensively our teams leverage Claude in their work. Claude is the common thread, amplifying the output of our employees. For example, over 90% of the contributions to our codebase in September 2026 were written by Claude.
Additionally, the average daily volume of code contributed to our codebase per engineer in the three months ended September 30, 2026 was over 45 times the average daily volume in the year ended December 31, 2024.
From September 30, 2025 to September 30, 2026, TTM revenue increased approximately 1,200% while headcount increased approximately 170%, driving TTM revenue per employee from $1.4 million to over $6.6 million, a reflection of extraordinary talent density and a culture built to compound it.
Our go-to-market model reflects this as well—intelligence-led growth and broad distribution partnerships enable us to rapidly expand customer adoption and revenue without being limited by the rate at which we can grow our sales and marketing organization, resulting in greater sales efficiency as compared to typical enterprise technology companies.
Our revenue was $33.2 billion for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, up from $2.5 billion for the nine months ended September 30, 2025. Our operating loss was $1.3 billion for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, down from $5.2 billion for the nine months ended September 30, 2025. The result of our revenue growth, compute efficiency, and operating efficiency has been a significant improvement in Adjusted Operating Income, which was $4.1 billion for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, up from an Adjusted Operating Loss of $3.1 billion for the nine months ended September 30, 2025. We expect operating margin and Adjusted Operating Margin to fluctuate over time, particularly in periods when substantial incremental compute is delivered to us and we incur the associated expenses. See the section titled “—Non-GAAP Financial Measures” for a description of and information about Adjusted Operating Income (Loss) and Adjusted Operating Margin, as well as a reconciliation of these measures to the most directly comparable financial measures calculated in accordance with GAAP.

location: MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS > Compute Investments
text:
Investing in compute is a prerequisite for long-term growth. We invest in compute for research, model development, serving customers, and internal usage of Claude. Our commercial traction, research progress, and the scale of the opportunity ahead give us the conviction to continue investing aggressively in compute. An increasing portion of these investments relates to building out our own compute and infrastructure and vertically integrating across the compute supply chain to secure long-term compute at the scale required for frontier model development. These investments take the form of capital expenditures and other commitments, including lease obligations, that we incur well in advance of the related compute becoming operational and generating revenue. As a result, we expect this build-out to change the cash flow profile of our business and to be a significant use of net cash in operating and investing activities for the foreseeable future. See the section titled “—Liquidity and Capital Resources” for more information.
In addition, as our compute needs have grown substantially, we are shifting from sourcing compute solely through fixed-term cloud agreements to a hybrid model that also includes leasing chips directly and hosting them in dedicated facilities operated on our behalf. We refer to this additional source of compute as Anthropic Direct, which helps to address our scaling compute requirements and we believe will provide long-term economic advantages. Anthropic Direct represents a more flexible use of capital by allowing us to separate our commitments for data center capacity from our commitments for the compute infrastructure deployed inside them. Because data centers require longer lead times but represent a smaller fraction of total compute costs, this approach enables us to secure data center capacity early while deferring larger accelerator investments until our specific compute needs are more certain.

text:
As of and subsequent to September 30, 2026, we have entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements, including short-term commitments, as well as leases not yet commenced, with an aggregate committed spend of approximately $900.9 billion. The flexibility from Anthropic Direct allows us to backfill the short-term compute we procure during periods of high demand with more cost-effective, long-term compute as our dedicated infrastructure comes online.
We intend to fund these investments through the revenue we generate and the capital that we raise. As of September 30, 2026, and prior to taking into account the net proceeds to us from this offering and the concurrent private placement, we had $146.6 billion of liquidity, consisting of $95.6 billion of cash and cash equivalents, $36.3 billion of short-term investments, and $14.8 billion of availability under our A&R Credit Facility (as defined below). location: MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS > How We Generate Revenue
text:
At the foundation of our business is our family of four Claude model classes—Mythos (including Fable), Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku—each optimized for a different point on the capability-cost-speed curve. Our frontier models allow customers to match the right model to each use case. Customers typically use higher-capability models for complex reasoning, coding, and agentic workflows where greater model intelligence is required. Customers also frequently adopt our full range of models, routing individual tasks to the models that are most optimized to meet their needs along the capability-cost-speed curve. The model a customer uses and the volume of usage are the primary drivers of customer spend. We establish a direct contractual relationship with the customer and offer customers the flexibility to purchase directly from us or through CSP marketplaces, and many customers utilize both channels.
Pay-for-intelligence, our consumption-based revenue model, is our primary revenue model and currently represents the substantial majority of our total revenue. Under this model, customers pay for usage, which is metered in tokens and priced according to the model selected. Our pay-for-intelligence revenue is primarily generated from customers building applications incorporating Claude or utilizing our first-party applications.
In addition, we offer certain of our applications on a subscription basis, serving both enterprises and prosumers. Under this model, customers pay a subscription fee for a specified level of usage and capabilities during the subscription term, which is generally 12 months or less.
Depending on the model, platform, or applications chosen by our customers, they enter into pay-for-intelligence pricing, subscription-based pricing, or both. For example, when subscribers approach or exhaust the usage capacity included in their tier, they may utilize a higher subscription tier or purchase more intelligence directly, creating a seamless bridge from subscription to incremental pay-for-intelligence revenue.
A growing number of enterprise customers agree to non-cancelable annual or multi-year contracts with minimum spend commitments in exchange for a committed price list. These contracts result primarily in consumption-based revenue.

text:
Consumption-based revenue increased from $288 million, or 75% of total revenue, for the year ended December 31, 2024, to $3.8 billion, or 83% of total revenue, for the year ended December 31, 2025, to $26.3 billion, or 79% of total revenue, for the nine months ended September 30, 2026. Subscription-based revenue increased from $98 million, or 25% of total revenue, to $789 million, or 17% of total revenue, to $6.9 billion, or 21% of total revenue, over the same periods. The larger dollar increase in consumption-based revenue reflects the growth in customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis. For 2023, our revenue of $41 million was substantially all consumption-based, reflecting our early operations. We expect consumption-based revenue to continue to represent the substantial majority of total revenue for the foreseeable future.
Our recent growth may reflect early-stage adoption dynamics, the nascency of the AI market, and rapid initial customer expansion that may not be sustainable over time. We expect our revenue growth rate to decline over time, and it may decline significantly and more rapidly than we anticipate as our revenue base increases and as the market matures.

text:
Our Customers
We serve enterprises of all sizes and across industries, in nearly every region of the world. Organizations that use Claude range from the world’s largest enterprises to AI-native startups, research institutions, and mission-driven organizations working on some of the world’s most consequential problems. Customers realize value from Claude in three primary ways: more productive employees, faster processes, and embedded intelligence in their products. As enterprise customers push Claude into increasingly complex workflows, we engage with them to understand their evolving requirements, which helps shape our product roadmap. This feedback loop deepens customer relationships with each release and makes Claude more capable for all customers.
Software developers have been core to our strategy: they are simultaneously the architects of applications built on our platform, and they encode their workflows and institutional knowledge into Claude-powered agents. Developers have been our earliest adopters and often most discerning users: they apply models to unanticipated use cases quickly and surface the edge cases that sharpen each successive version of a Claude model. Claude Code is now embedded in software development workflows across major organizations, with these relationships often beginning with individual engineers who recognized the value of autonomous coding agents and accelerated adoption across their enterprises.
The same intelligence and capabilities we deliver to enterprises are also valuable to prosumers in their personal endeavors. These users provide strategic value as a top-of-funnel engine for our enterprise business— individuals who utilize Claude for their personal work and then champion it inside their organizations.
We are seeing broad-based growth across customer use cases, from software development to financial analysis, content creation, and complex knowledge work. Claude is extensible: regardless of entry point, enterprises quickly discover that frontier intelligence applies to a wide and expanding range of tasks across their organizations. As a result, what sometimes begins as a single use case frequently expands into broader adoption spanning coding, legal analysis, financial modeling, customer operations, and other knowledge-intensive work.

text:
Our Approach to Claude Diffusion
A core driver of Claude’s diffusion is its intelligence—as Claude’s capabilities advance, value to customers expands, and that value drives greater adoption. Ensuring the accessibility of such intelligence is also critical, and we do that in the following ways: through our composable platform and applications that meet customers where they are, through our go-to-market and Applied AI teams directly, and through partnerships that extend our reach at scale.
Intelligence-Led Growth. Our platform and applications are the primary mechanism through which Claude’s intelligence can reach users. As users begin building, brainstorming, and problem-solving with Claude, they quickly come to rely on it as a trusted partner in their work. As Claude becomes part of how people work, they experience firsthand what frontier intelligence makes possible, and such individual adoption reshapes how entire organizations operate. This pattern repeats across organizations: prosumers become internal champions, teams expand their use of Claude, and what begins as a single workflow grows into something that impacts how an entire organization operates. This pattern has been core to our revenue growth.
Direct Teams. This organic adoption is complemented and enhanced through our direct go-to-market teams who help scale Claude to organizations with complex workflows and business processes. By the time our direct teams engage a customer, Claude is often already in use. Our go-to-market teams use this organic momentum to build executive sponsorship and drive enterprise-wide adoption.
Applied AI Teams. Our Applied AI teams embed more deeply with select customers, building solutions that make it easier for organizations to benefit from Claude’s intelligence. They work with enterprises to design and deploy custom solutions, specialized workflows, and domain-specific implementations tailored to the customer’s own requirements. This work drives deeper adoption within individual customers and generates the feedback and information from users that help to shape our platform and product roadmap.

location: MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS > Our Customers and Approach to Claude Diffusion > Our Approach to Claude Diffusion
text:
Cloud Partnerships. Claude is accessible on all three major cloud platforms, AWS, GCP, and Azure, allowing enterprises to deploy Claude within the infrastructure, security perimeters, and commitment structures they already operate. These CSPs extend our reach through their large combined field teams that are empowered to sell our platform and applications, accelerating market adoption at a scale we believe would be difficult for any single organization to directly replicate. We have a joint go-to-market approach with these CSPs through which we establish direct contractual relationships with our customers while paying a fee to each CSP. This structure allows us to foster stronger commercial alignment with these CSPs, avoid channel conflict, set pricing, and realize the financial benefits of ongoing compute efficiency improvements.
Ecosystem Partnerships. Major global systems integrators have built dedicated Claude practices with teams trained to deploy our platform and applications. Go-to-market alliances with leading data platforms embed Claude into data infrastructure that enterprises already operate, facilitating adoption of Claude within existing workflows and making it easier for enterprises to realize value from Claude.
Ode with Anthropic. We recently launched an AI services company in partnership with leading private equity firms to bring Claude’s capabilities to mid-sized companies across sectors, building solutions on the Claude Platform and supporting customers over the long term. Ode with Anthropic will partner closely with our Applied AI and go-to-market teams.
Together, these approaches have led to a structurally efficient approach to facilitating the diffusion of Claude in the economy, with our sales, marketing, and partnerships expenses representing 17% of revenue for the nine months ended September 30, 2026.

text:
Remaining at the Frontier of AI
We believe enterprises consistently choose the most capable and trustworthy AI systems, making our position at the frontier an important driver of our success. Our ability to rapidly grow our revenue is partially dependent on our continued delivery of more intelligent and capable models. Our experience is that as we deliver models with meaningfully improved capabilities that deliver higher intelligence per dollar spent, customers find new applications for AI across their businesses, accelerating adoption and revenue growth.
This can be seen in the trajectory of our model family adoption. Successive versions of our most intelligent generally available model have delivered meaningfully greater intelligence and capabilities. With each release, we have seen most customers utilize the latest version of our models, reinforcing the direct relationship between frontier model quality and revenue generation. As we deliver more capable models, customers have expanded their usage into new use cases and increased their spending accordingly.
We expect our ability to deliver innovation in intelligence and capability at the frontier to remain a key driver of revenue growth in future periods, and maintaining a leading position requires continued investment in research and compute, top technical talent, and access to capital sufficient to support our growth trajectory.

text:
Securing Sufficient Compute and Optimizing Its Utilization
Our ability to continue advancing intelligence at the frontier depends on securing sufficient compute for research, model development, serving customers, and internal usage of Claude. Our ability to leverage heterogeneous compute helps us to secure compute at sufficient scale and optimal price-performance. If any of our chip partners are unable to deliver committed compute or experience delays, or if we need to procure incremental compute, we benefit from having a range of partners as opposed to being overly reliant on any one partner. The availability, timing, and cost of compute are subject to factors largely outside our control, including the concentration of chip and memory manufacturing among a limited number of suppliers and geographies, constraints on the availability of power and data center capacity, and evolving export controls. We have historically operated in a compute-constrained environment in which demand for compute has exceeded the supply available to us. In addition, certain of the CSPs on which we rely for compute are also strategic investors in us, are our customers, and offer AI models and services that compete with ours. These multifaceted relationships could give rise to conflicts of interest or competitive dynamics that adversely affect our access to compute, its cost, or the prioritization of our workloads.
As our compute needs have grown substantially, we are shifting from sourcing compute solely through fixed-term cloud agreements to a hybrid model that also includes leasing chips directly and hosting them in dedicated facilities operated on our behalf. We refer to this additional source of compute as Anthropic Direct, which helps to address our scaling compute requirements and provides potential long-term economic advantages of direct hosting. Anthropic Direct provides us with a more flexible use of capital by allowing us to separate our commitments for data center capacity from our commitments for the accelerators deployed inside them. Because data centers require longer lead times but represent a smaller fraction of total compute costs, this approach enables us to secure data center capacity early while deferring larger accelerator investments until our specific compute needs are more certain.

We rely on compute efficiencies, such as the discovery of compute multipliers, to get the most out of the compute that we procure. Our ability to effectively direct compute and drive compute efficiencies will be an important determinant of both our pace of innovation and our financial results over time.

Attracting and Retaining Technical Talent
Advancing the frontier and maximizing the return on our compute investment require that we attract, hire, and retain top technical talent. Talent attraction and retention start with our seven co-founders, all of whom have remained with the company. We believe our culture and mission alignment enable us to hire and retain the talent required to continuously push the frontier of AI forward in a safe and responsible way. We expect our ability to continue attracting and retaining top technical talent to remain a key determinant of our pace of innovation and our financial results in future periods.

text:
Our Continued Access to Capital
We must make significant investments in compute for research, model development, serving customers, and internal usage of Claude. Our compute requires substantial upfront commitments and ongoing payments as the compute becomes available to us. Our compute commitments will continue to grow as we scale our business. Our ability to secure sufficient compute is directly linked to our ability to access capital on favorable terms, such as through equity or debt financing or cash flow from operations.
In order to maintain our access to capital, we must continue to demonstrate that we are able to invest that capital in a highly productive way. The best measures of our progress are Claude’s intelligence and capability, and customer adoption of Claude. Our ability to convert compute investment into frontier model performance, and then increase customer adoption, will be a key determinant of our access to capital.
Our ability to sustain access to capital depends in part on demonstrating a credible trajectory toward profitability. Our revenue growth, compute efficiency, and operating efficiency have significantly improved our operating margin and Adjusted Operating Margin, but we plan to keep investing heavily, which will adversely impact our results of operations. Our compute commitments are substantial and generally must be satisfied regardless of our revenue or utilization, while our access to additional capital depends on a number of conditions, many of which are outside our control, including market conditions and investor demand. In addition, a portion of our compute and infrastructure build-out has been funded or supported by capital or credit support provided or facilitated by certain of our CSPs and chip partners. Our ability to reduce this reliance over time depends in part on our ability to obtain financing from independent sources on our own credit.

text:
Our Ability to Diffuse Claude in the Enterprise
Our financial performance depends on the pace and breadth at which AI, and in particular Claude, is adopted across the global economy. While Claude’s capabilities already address a wide range of enterprise use cases, we believe that enterprise adoption remains nascent. We believe that our ability to capture this opportunity and drive revenue growth in future periods will depend on three dynamics:
First, our ability to translate model improvements into accessible products and platform capabilities.
In the nine months ended September 30, 2026, we launched an aggregate of 250 new model versions, platform features, and applications, including new capabilities in Claude Code, Claude Cowork, and vertical solutions for key industries. Our growth depends on continuing this pace of product innovation and reducing the friction between Claude’s capabilities and customer workflows. Our growth also depends on how quickly new capabilities reach customers, which in turn depends on the steps we take to assess and mitigate the risks of each model during development and before and after release. In the past, these steps have included delaying the release of new models and limiting their initial availability, such as our initial release of Mythos through Project Glasswing and our later release of Fable 5 as a generally-available model with safety restrictions, and in the future, as we learn more about model capabilities and behavior, could include additional measures that affect whether, how, and when we develop or release new models or capabilities. We evaluate whether to delay or restrict a release based on the results of our pre-release capability and safety evaluations and our assessment of whether available safeguards adequately mitigate the identified risks, and we may also take such steps where those evaluations are inconclusive. For more information, see the section titled “Business—Safety Research is Core to Our Business—Our Approach to Model Releases.” These measures, and any laws, regulations, or standards governing frontier model development that may be adopted, could cause new use cases to emerge more slowly and slow the enterprise adoption and expansion on which our revenue growth depends. We believe that enterprises prefer models that are safe and aligned, and that our continued investment in safety strengthens customer trust and supports long-term adoption.
expenses as reported in their publicly available financial statements.
Second, our ability to expand and diversify distribution.

text:
A large portion of our growth to date has been self-service and organic. As AI adoption extends further into enterprises and more regulated industries, we are investing in direct go-to-market, Applied AI teams, and partnerships across all three major cloud platforms, systems integrators, consultants, and data platforms. We are also expanding our ability to serve international customers through the growth of regional offices and partnerships in key markets, and we expect international expansion to be a meaningful driver of revenue growth as global demand for AI accelerates. The effectiveness of these investments, and our ability to hire and retain go-to-market talent, will be a meaningful determinant of growth.
Third, our ability to land new customers and expand within existing accounts.
The number of customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis grew from approximately 20 as of December 31, 2023, to approximately 200 as of December 31, 2024, to approximately 1,500 as of December 31, 2025, and to more than 11,900 as of September 30, 2026. Total revenue from these customers grew from approximately $37 million to $220 million to $3.5 billion to $26.1 billion and represented 90%, 57%, 76%, and 74% of total revenue for the years ended December 31, 2023, 2024, and 2025, and the TTM period ended September 30, 2026, respectively. The remaining 26% of total revenue for the TTM period ended September 30, 2026 was generated by approximately 40 million customers, each with less than $100,000 of revenue on a TTM basis.
In addition, as of September 30, 2026, we had more than 1,900 customers with $1 million or more of revenue on a TTM basis and approximately 250 customers with $10 million or more of revenue on a TTM basis. Despite this growth, our penetration into the largest enterprises remains early. Over 50% of the Fortune 500 and over 30% of the Global 2000 were customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis as of September 30, 2026. We believe we are in the early stages of our expansion within these customers, with our revenue from these Fortune 500 customers representing, on average, less than 0.1% of their total expenses for the three months ended September 30, 2026.
