text:
Customer Usage Patterns
Our revenue is influenced by customer usage patterns, which are impacted by the frequency and capability of new model version releases, as well as seasonal trends, each of which can create variability in our results from period to period. The continuous and overlapping cadence of new model version releases is inherent to remaining at the frontier of AI development. For example, model versions released in the six months ended September 30, 2026 accounted for over 80% of our revenue for the three months ended September 30, 2026. As we have released successive versions of Claude models, we have continued to see revenue growth as new capabilities unlock additional use cases, prompting new customers to adopt Claude and existing customers to expand their usage.
For purposes of this measure, we include only Fortune 500 customers that are publicly traded and calculate the measure using total
Our customer usage patterns have also typically exhibited seasonality, particularly around holiday and vacation periods in the summer and winter, when certain workflows slow down and overall customer activity declines. For example, developer commits and feature launches are typically slower during the code freezes that many companies schedule over holidays. Consistent with this pattern, for the two weeks ended January 2, 2026, total customer spend declined by approximately 20% compared to the prior two weeks ended December 19, 2025. However, our historical growth rates may mask the impact of seasonal trends on our results. These dynamics are inherent aspects of a pay-for-intelligence revenue model and may be important determinants of our financial results in future periods.
Because of these seasonal patterns, our results of operations have varied, and are expected to continue to vary, from period to period, and our results for any one period may not be indicative of our results for any future period. As our revenue growth rate declines over time, we expect seasonal effects to become more apparent in, and to have a greater effect on, our period-to-period results, and to make it more difficult to forecast our results of operations.

Our Commitment to Public Benefit
Our commitment to public benefit extends to how we deploy our resources. We intend to direct a meaningful portion of our resources toward ensuring that frontier intelligence is safe and its benefits are broadly distributed, which we refer to as our public benefit initiatives. This may include significant contributions to nonprofit organizations, research institutions, and other third parties working on problems where AI can have the greatest positive impact, as well as programs designed to make Claude accessible to underserved communities, educators, and public institutions.

text: As part of these initiatives, we contributed 846,840,960 shares of our Class N common stock, representing 5% of our fully diluted shares as of June 30, 2026 (assuming full conversion of the Amazon Notes), to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, our wholly owned subsidiary dedicated to the Company Purpose, which we refer to as the Initial Public Benefit Issuance. As the value we create grows, we intend for the public benefit to share meaningfully in that growth as well. To that end, our board of directors has approved a framework for additional contributions tied to future increases in our share price. Following this offering and the concurrent private placement, our board of directors, in its discretion, may issue shares of our Class N common stock to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund (or other designee) representing up to an additional 2% of our then-outstanding shares (plus any shares subject to options, RSUs, and other convertible securities and any shares held by the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund) each time our share price appreciates 50% above the prior share price milestone, beginning with our initial public offering price. A share price milestone is reached only when our closing share price has exceeded the applicable threshold on at least 90 of the trailing 120 consecutive trading days, and our average closing share price over the 10 trading days prior to such issuance also exceeds that threshold. Although our board of directors has approved this framework, any future contributions will be made at the discretion of our board of directors. The shares that are contributed to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, including the Initial Public Benefit Issuance, may be transferred or donated to a third party, or otherwise sold in a registered public offering or private placement transaction in furtherance of our public benefit initiatives. Our board of directors will determine the allocations and distributions from the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund until it approves a specific governance structure for the entity, at which point decision-making authority is expected to transition to designated managers of the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund operating under that structure. The initial managers are [Co-founder 1 (CEO)], [Co-founder 2 (President)], [Co-founder 4], and [LTBT Trustee 1 (Chair)]. The Initial Public Benefit Issuance and the additional share contribution framework represent one of the ways in which we intend to pursue the Company Purpose, but they are not the exclusive means of doing so.

text:
We expect to dedicate additional resources, and to make other business and operational decisions, in furtherance of the Company Purpose outside of, and in addition to, these equity contributions.
In addition, we maintain a donation matching program through which employees can pledge a meaningful portion of their equity awards or equivalent cash proceeds to a donor-advised fund or other nonprofit organization, and we match those donations with shares of our Class N common stock. In the same way the Company Purpose defines how we direct our work as an organization, our donation matching program reflects a parallel commitment by our employees to direct the personal financial value created by that work toward the public good. We view our donation matching program as a meaningful expression of the Company Purpose and a reflection of the values that define our culture. In addition, our co-founders have each pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal equity in Anthropic to philanthropic causes, separate from and not eligible for our donation matching program.
Decisions we make to advance our public benefit initiatives may, in any given period, reduce our revenue, increase our expenses, lower our Adjusted Operating Margin, contribute to dilution, and reduce our profitability on a per share basis relative to what we would otherwise report. Our public benefit-related expenses, which currently consist primarily of charitable donations under our donation matching program, were not significant before the three months ended September 30, 2026. For the nine months ended September 30, 2026, expenses related to our donation matching program were $2.1 billion, representing approximately 6% of our total operating expenses for that period. However, we expect the cadence and magnitude of resources directed toward our public benefit initiatives to increase in future periods and remain a factor affecting our results of operations.

text:
Revenue
We generate revenue as customers use Claude through our platform and applications, including Claude Code, Claude Cowork, and vertical solutions for key industries. Claude is powered by our proprietary Claude model family, a set of frontier models, each with varying levels of capability, cost, and speed. Enterprise customers access our intelligence service directly from us or through CSP marketplaces, where we maintain direct contractual relationships with our customers.
Depending on the model, platform, or applications chosen by our customers, they enter into pay-for-intelligence pricing, subscription-based pricing, or both. A growing number of enterprise customers agree to annual or multi-year contracts with minimum spend commitments.
Revenue is recognized when customers use our intelligence service, based on the quantity of tokens consumed. Subscriptions are generally prepaid on a monthly or annual basis, and are subject to usage limits that reset over short periods, which results in revenue being recognized on a ratable basis over the subscription period, which is generally 12 months or less.
We expect our revenue growth rate to decline over time and to fluctuate from period to period. Revenue growth in any period may be affected by customer usage patterns, customer adoption, the deployment of our models, platform, and applications, the pricing of our offerings, the timing and success of new model and product releases, measures we decide to implement to safely deploy new capabilities, our ability to continue meeting customer requirements, and other factors affecting demand for our models, platform, and applications, including those described in the section titled “Risk Factors—We are at an early stage of our revenue growth, we have experienced rapid growth in recent periods, and our historical growth rates are not indicative of future performance or our ability to sustain or forecast future revenue growth.”

text: In addition, our revenue has included, and we expect will continue to include, amounts from customers that we subsequently determine are using our models, platform, and applications in violation of our usage policy or commercial terms. We believe this dynamic is common in our industry. Because detection, investigation, and enforcement take time, we recognize revenue from such customers when the related services are provided, before restricting or terminating their access. Based on our detection and review process, we estimate that revenue from such customers represented approximately 5% to 7% of our revenue for the nine months ended September 30, 2026. This estimate requires judgment and may change as our detection methodologies evolve and we identify previously undetected usage. We expect the percentage of revenue from customers using our models, platform, and applications in violation of our usage policy or commercial terms to decline in future periods as we have enhanced our detection and enforcement efforts, in particular in August and September 2026; however, the timing and magnitude of any resulting adverse effect on our revenue and revenue growth are uncertain.

text:
Operating Expenses
Compute and Infrastructure
Compute and infrastructure expenses primarily consist of costs attributable to operating our technology infrastructure, which supports the full range of workloads for our models, including research, model development, serving customers, and internal usage of Claude. These costs primarily consist of compute fees paid to CSPs under committed and on-demand arrangements, including storage, networking, and connectivity, and related support costs, infrastructure costs associated with serving customer workloads through partner channels, colocation facility costs, equipment leases and committed power costs associated with our data center operations, and third-party application infrastructure software costs directly related to our compute operations. Beginning in 2026, as our obligations commence under compute and infrastructure leases, these expenses also include operating lease costs, amortization of finance lease assets, variable lease costs, and depreciation and amortization on owned servers, networking equipment, and related data center assets. See Note 8 to our consolidated financial statements included elsewhere in this prospectus for a functional presentation of our operating expenses, including cost of revenue, and a description of the workloads underlying the compute and infrastructure expenses within each functional caption. Within that functional presentation, substantially all of the cost of revenue consists of compute and infrastructure expenses associated with customer-serving workloads. Additionally, cost of revenue includes certain personnel-related costs and allocated overhead costs.
Customers adopt and retain our technology based on whether our models are at the frontier of AI capability and maintaining that frontier position is essential to revenue generation. Each model release represents continuous intelligence improvements, making ongoing model development a critical factor in revenue generation. We operate an iterative cycle in which compute deployed to model development yields more capable and efficient models. Those efficiency gains free compute to serve additional customer workloads. In turn, serving our customers at scale generates feedback that informs research and model development. In this cycle, customer-serving activity and model development are each a direct input that informs the other, and we therefore view compute and infrastructure costs as critical to our ability to generate revenue within a short time of incurring such costs.

location: MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS > Components of Results of Operations > Operating Expenses
text:
We expect compute and infrastructure expenses to increase in absolute dollars and remain our largest operating expense for the foreseeable future as additional committed compute becomes available to us under multi-year arrangements with CSPs, and as we continue to invest in additional compute. These expenses are paid and recognized as compute becomes available to us, rather than when committed, and are generally fixed in the near term given the majority of our compute is contracted under multi-year commitments that we typically procure 12 to 18 months in advance of availability. When customer demand or research needs exceed this long-term capacity, we procure short-term compute that currently costs significantly more than comparable compute procured under our multi-year commitments. We deploy this committed compute as a single, shared resource across all workloads, and thus plan, incur, and assess it on a total basis rather than by individual workload. As a result, compute and infrastructure expenses as a percentage of revenue will depend primarily on how our revenue scales relative to our total committed compute cost base. In addition, as part of our public benefit initiatives, we intend to direct a meaningful portion of our resources, which may include compute, toward ensuring that the benefits of frontier intelligence are broadly accessible, and we expect to significantly scale these efforts over time.
Personnel
Personnel expenses primarily consist of stock-based compensation, including expense related to stock options, RSUs, and restricted stock awards (“RSAs”), cash compensation, including base salaries and bonuses, employee benefits, including health and welfare benefits, and employer payroll taxes.
We expect personnel expenses to increase in absolute dollars as we continue to expand our headcount to support the growth of our business. We also expect to incur additional stock-based compensation expense in connection with this offering, including for certain RSUs for which the performance condition will be satisfied upon the effectiveness of the registration statement of which this prospectus forms a part. We expect that personnel expenses may fluctuate as a percentage of revenue depending on the timing and magnitude of stock-based compensation expense, and the pace of hiring across our organization.
Bartz Settlement
Bartz settlement consists of the charge we recorded in 2025 to settle the Bartz litigation. See Note 13 to our consolidated financial statements included elsewhere in this prospectus for additional information.

Sales, marketing, and partnerships expenses primarily consist of fees paid to channel partners and marketing and advertising costs, including media and public relations spend.
We expect sales, marketing, and partnerships expenses to increase in absolute dollars as we continue to invest in activities to drive continued adoption and expanded usage of our models. We expect that sales, marketing, and partnerships expenses may fluctuate as a percentage of revenue depending on the timing of and spend on marketing campaigns and changes in the terms of our channel partner distribution arrangements and the cost to deliver our intelligence service.
Other Operating and Administrative
Other operating and administrative expenses primarily consist of charitable donations expense related to our donation matching program, vendor costs related to data quality and performance evaluation services, information technology and cloud software costs, payment processing and platform fees, facility and occupancy costs, non-income taxes, professional services costs, bad debt expense, and depreciation and amortization related to non-data center assets.
We expect that other operating and administrative expenses will increase in absolute dollars as our business grows and as a result of operating as a public company, including expenses related to compliance with SEC rules and regulations, the listing standards of the Nasdaq Global Select Market, additional costs for directors’ and officers’ liability insurance, and professional services. We also expect other operating and administrative expenses to fluctuate as a percentage of our revenue over time as our business grows, in part as we significantly scale our public benefit initiatives, including expanded programs to make Claude accessible to underserved communities, increased charitable donation matching, contributions to philanthropic vehicles or foundations we may establish or support in the future, and other efforts aligned with our mission.

Change in Fair Value of Convertible Notes, Derivative Liabilities, and SAFEs
Change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs consists of gains and losses as a result of recording our convertible promissory notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFE liabilities at fair value at the end of each reporting period. Because these instruments are marked to market, increases in our enterprise valuation drive increases in this expense. We will continue to recognize changes in the fair value of our convertible notes until they are converted into equity, repaid, or otherwise settled. For more information, see Note 4 to our consolidated financial statements included elsewhere in this prospectus.

location: MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS > Non-GAAP Financial Measures
text:
To supplement our consolidated financial statements prepared and presented in accordance with GAAP, we use certain non-GAAP financial measures, as described below, to facilitate analysis of our operating performance and for internal planning and forecasting purposes.
We use Adjusted Operating Income (Loss), Adjusted Operating Margin, and Adjusted Net Income (Loss) to evaluate our operating performance, formulate business plans, prepare budgets and forecasts, and make strategic decisions, including those relating to operating expenses and the allocation of internal resources. By excluding certain items that management believes are not directly reflective of the ongoing operating performance of our business, we believe these non-GAAP financial measures provide investors, analysts, and others with meaningful insight and enhance their overall understanding of our business and financial performance by providing a more consistent and comparable overview of our financial performance across periods.
Other companies in our industry, including those with similar business models, may define or calculate similarly titled measures in different ways, which may limit the usefulness of these measures for direct comparison. In addition, other companies may not publish these or similar metrics. Further, these metrics have certain limitations in that they do not include the impact of certain expenses that are reflected on our consolidated statements of operations. Thus, our non-GAAP financial measures should not be viewed in isolation or as a replacement for the most directly comparable measures prepared in accordance with GAAP. We encourage investors and others to review our business, financial condition, and results of operations in their entirety, not to rely on any single financial measure, and to view our non-GAAP financial measures in conjunction with their respective most directly comparable financial measures calculated in accordance with GAAP, as well as our consolidated financial statements and accompanying notes included elsewhere in this prospectus.

text:
Revenue
Revenue increased sequentially in each of the quarters presented, from $376 million for the three months ended March 31, 2025 to $17.0 billion for the three months ended September 30, 2026. The increases in each quarter were driven by successive model and product releases that drove higher usage, expansion, and broader adoption across our offerings, with both consumption-based and subscription-based revenue contributing. The number of customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis grew from approximately 400 as of March 31, 2025 to more than 11,900 as of September 30, 2026.
For the three months ended September 30, 2025 to the three months ended December 31, 2025, the increase in revenue due to higher usage was partially offset by a decrease of approximately $70 million from price reductions introduced as part of new model versions and contractual discounts. For the three months ended June 30, 2026 to the three months ended September 30, 2026, the increase in revenue due to higher usage was partially offset by a decrease of approximately $600 million from price reductions introduced as part of new model versions and contractual discounts. Price changes did not have a material impact on the other quarterly revenue trends presented.

location: MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS > Quarterly Trends > Operating Expenses
text:
Operating Expenses
Compute and Infrastructure
Compute and infrastructure expenses increased sequentially in each of the quarters presented, from $944 million for the three months ended March 31, 2025 to $9.9 billion for the three months ended September 30, 2026, driven by the delivery of committed compute under our multi-year arrangements. Because we typically procure compute 12 to 18 months in advance of availability, these expenses are generally fixed in the near term and increase as committed compute becomes available to us. Compute and infrastructure expenses as a percentage of revenue decreased from 251% for the three months ended March 31, 2025 to 48% for the three months ended June 30, 2026, as revenue growth outpaced the growth of our committed compute cost base, and increased to 58% for the three months ended September 30, 2026, reflecting the delivery of additional compute. This includes $5.0 billion of compute under short-term commitments, which currently costs significantly more than comparable compute procured under our multi-year commitments.
Personnel
Personnel expenses increased sequentially in each of the quarters presented through the three months ended June 30, 2026, driven by headcount growth and the associated increases in compensation, including stock-based compensation. Personnel expenses decreased in the three months ended September 30, 2026, primarily driven by lower stock-based compensation expense due to certain option awards becoming fully vested, partially offset by higher cash compensation resulting from headcount growth.
Bartz settlement
In the three months ended September 30, 2025, we recorded a $1.5 billion charge to settle the Bartz litigation. See Note 13 to our consolidated financial statements included elsewhere in this prospectus.
Sales, Marketing, and Partnerships
Sales, marketing, and partnerships expenses increased sequentially in each of the quarters presented, with the most significant increases observed in the three months ended March 31, 2026 and June 30, 2026. The increases were primarily driven by fees paid to channel partners, reflecting the growth of our business, and increased marketing and advertising expenses, driven by higher media spend to support product launches.
Sales, marketing, and partnerships expenses as a percentage of revenue decreased from 22% for the three months ended March 31, 2026 to 14% for the three months ended September 30, 2026, primarily driven by a decrease in revenue generated from sales through channel partners as a percentage of total revenue and changes in the terms of our channel partner distribution arrangements.

Our operating loss widened in the three months ended June 30, 2025, primarily driven by the delivery of additional committed compute under our CSP arrangements, the associated expenses of which increased by more in dollars than our revenue in the period, and in the three months ended September 30, 2025, which included the Bartz settlement. Our operating loss narrowed in the three months ended December 31, 2025 and March 31, 2026, and we generated operating income of $1.0 billion for the three months ended June 30, 2026, as revenue growth outpaced the growth in total operating expenses. We incurred an operating loss of $567 million for the three months ended September 30, 2026, primarily driven by $5.0 billion of compute under short-term commitments and $2.0 billion of non-cash charges related to our donation matching program. We expect our operating results to continue to fluctuate from quarter to quarter, particularly as the amount of incremental compute we receive, and the associated expenses we incur, may vary from period to period.

text: Since inception, we have financed our operations, corporate investments, and capital expenditures primarily through proceeds from the issuance of convertible promissory notes, redeemable convertible preferred stock, cash generated from sales, and SAFEs. To date, we have financed our compute and infrastructure primarily under arrangements with our CSPs, as well as through proceeds from the financing activities described above and cash generated from operations. As of September 30, 2026, we had cash and cash equivalents of $95.6 billion, $36.3 billion of short-term investments, and $14.8 billion available under the A&R Credit Facility, as described below. Cash and cash equivalents consist of cash held in checking and interest-bearing accounts, money market funds, and other highly liquid investments with original maturities of three months or less from the date of purchase.

meta.section: MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS

location: MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: We have generated losses from our operations, as reflected in our accumulated deficit of $156.2 billion, which includes $135.1 billion related to changes in the fair value of our convertible notes driven by increases in our enterprise valuation and derivative liabilities since 2023, including $94.3 billion during the nine months ended September 30, 2026. Additionally, we have generated negative cash flows from operating and investing activities in 2023, 2024, and 2025, driven by ongoing expenditures to support business growth including investments to secure access to more compute and infrastructure capacity. We generated positive cash flows from operating activities of $6.6 billion for the nine months ended September 30, 2026. We continue to invest in our own data center infrastructure and enter into compute and infrastructure capacity arrangements to support anticipated demand for our intelligence service. Given the long lead times between contracting for, purchasing, or leasing compute and that compute becoming available to serve workloads, we secure these arrangements well in advance of anticipated demand. To secure certain data center development projects, which require significant capital commitments in advance of deployment, we have in some cases relied, and expect to continue to rely, on arrangements with financing sources or partners who guarantee the lease obligations to support the development of data center capacity that is expected to host such partners’ chips or computing infrastructure. Our ability to expand compute and infrastructure capacity through these arrangements in the future may depend on the continued willingness and ability of a limited number of CSPs, partners, and financing sources to enter into and perform under such arrangements. In some cases, we may also make payments in advance of the delivery of the equipment or infrastructure. We anticipate making significant and increased investments for the foreseeable future, including for owned or leased compute and infrastructure in advance of delivery. These investments help ensure we have the technological resources to maintain and expand our position at the frontier of AI.
title: US-PROSPECTUS (S-1/A, preliminary) | MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS > Liquidity and Capital Resources

meta.section: MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS

location: MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: Our increasing efforts to build out our compute and infrastructure require substantial capital expenditures and are changing the cash flow profile of our business. Whereas the compute purchased through our CSP arrangements is generally paid for as the compute becomes available to us, we expect an increasing portion of our compute and infrastructure investment to take the form of capital expenditures and other commitments, including lease obligations, that require significant upfront payments well in advance of the related compute becoming operational. We expect our capital expenditures to increase significantly as we expand our build-out, and we expect these investments to result in significant net cash used in operating and investing activities for the foreseeable future. Our net cash used in these activities may increase regardless of whether our financial performance improves. The magnitude and timing of these investments are inherently uncertain and may change materially over short periods, including as a result of decisions to accelerate or expand our build-out, and such changes could rapidly and significantly affect our cash flows for a given period. In addition, these investments are subject to known trends and uncertainties that could adversely affect our results of operations. The compute and chips necessary for frontier model development are available from a limited number of suppliers and geographies and are subject to intense competition, supply constraints, and evolving export controls, and we have historically operated in a compute-constrained environment in which demand for compute has exceeded the supply available to us. In addition, certain of the CSPs and chip partners on which we rely provide us capital or credit support, serve as our infrastructure vendors, and develop and offer AI models and services that compete with ours. These relationships could give rise to conflicts of interest that affect our access to compute, its cost, the prioritization of our workloads, or the terms on which such capital or credit support is provided. For a discussion of these and other risks, see the section titled “Risk Factors.”
title: US-PROSPECTUS (S-1/A, preliminary) | MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS > Liquidity and Capital Resources

meta.section: MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS

location: MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text:
We also intend to use a portion of the net proceeds we receive from this offering and the concurrent private placement to satisfy our anticipated tax withholding and remittance obligations of $3.8 billion related to the RSU Settlement. This amount is based upon the assumed initial public offering price of $74.00 per share, which is the midpoint of the estimated offering price range set forth on the cover page of this prospectus, and an assumed 50.90% tax withholding rate. Each $1.00 increase or decrease in the assumed initial public offering price of $74.00 per share would increase or decrease, as applicable, the amount we would be required to pay to satisfy our tax withholding and remittance obligations related to the RSU Settlement by $52 million.
We believe our existing available cash and cash equivalents and short-term investments, together with cash generated from sales and amounts available under our A&R Credit Facility, will be sufficient to support working capital, operating and finance lease payments, and capital expenditure requirements for at least the next 12 months from the date of this prospectus. However, our future capital requirements will depend on many factors, including our revenue growth, the timing and extent of our investments in compute and infrastructure capacity, including additional or expanded CSP, equipment lease, and data center arrangements, the success and expansion of our sales, marketing, and business development strategies, any potential future investment in complementary businesses, products, technologies, assets, and talent, risks associated with the AI industry, and other factors described under “—Key Factors Affecting Our Performance.” As a result of these and other factors, we may be required to seek additional financing sooner than we currently anticipate. If we determine that additional financing is required, we may not be able to raise it on terms acceptable to us or at all. Any such financing, if completed, may be costly, dilutive, or lead to restrictions on how we operate our business. If we are unable to raise additional capital when required, or if we cannot expand our operations or otherwise capitalize on our business opportunities because we lack sufficient capital, our business, financial condition, results of operations, and cash flows would be adversely affected.

Revolving Credit Agreement
In May 2025, we entered into a Credit Agreement (as amended from time to time prior to the A&R Credit Agreement (as defined below), the “Credit Agreement”) with certain lenders from time to time party thereto and Morgan Stanley Senior Funding, Inc., as administrative agent and collateral agent for the lenders, which initially provided for a $2.5 billion senior secured revolving credit facility with a $400 million letter of credit sublimit (the “Initial Credit Facility”). In September 2025, we amended the Initial Credit Facility to increase the aggregate revolving commitments to $2.75 billion, and in November 2025, we further amended the Initial Credit Facility to increase the aggregate revolving commitments to $3.25 billion.
In September 2026, we entered into an Amended and Restated Credit Agreement (the “A&R Credit Agreement”), which amended and restated the Credit Agreement to provide for a $15.0 billion senior secured revolving credit facility with the full amount thereof available for letters of credit (the “A&R Credit Facility”). The A&R Credit Facility will mature on September 4, 2031, subject to earlier springing maturity if more than $500 million in aggregate scheduled cash principal payments on certain of our indebtedness are required within the 91-day period preceding the date on which any such scheduled principal payment is due, and we do not have sufficient liquidity to make all such payments then due and remain in pro forma compliance with our financial covenant, subject to certain other exceptions and conditions set forth in the A&R Credit Agreement. The proceeds of the A&R Credit Facility may be used for working capital, general corporate purposes, and other lawful purposes. We may request borrowings in U.S. dollars or certain other agreed currencies, subject to the terms of the A&R Credit Agreement. As of September 30, 2026, we had no borrowings drawn under the A&R Credit Facility and $205 million of standby letters of credit outstanding. As of September 30, 2026, we were in compliance with all covenants under the A&R Credit Agreement.

AMD Agreement
In July 2026, we entered into a hardware supply framework agreement (the “Hardware Supply Agreement”) with AMD to purchase, lease, or access AMD-based Helios rack-scale systems featuring AMD Instinct™ MI450 series GPUs. Pursuant to the terms of the Hardware Supply Agreement, AMD has provided a commitment to purchase up to $5.0 billion of our Class N common stock (the “AMD Equity Commitment”), which becomes available for us to draw on in increments following the achievement of specified AMD GPU delivery and deployment milestones. In connection with the concurrent private placement, we entered into a letter agreement with AMD under which, upon the closing of the concurrent private placement, the $2.5 billion purchase price paid by AMD for shares of our Class N common stock in the concurrent private placement will satisfy a portion of the AMD Equity Commitment by reducing, on a dollar-for-dollar basis, the amount available for us to draw. As a result, following the closing of the concurrent private placement, up to $2.5 billion of the AMD Equity Commitment will remain, which will become available for us to draw only to the extent that the cumulative amount accrued based on AMD GPU delivery and deployment milestones exceeds the aggregate purchase price paid by AMD in the concurrent private placement. Based on the deployment schedule contemplated by the Hardware Supply Agreement, we expect the first of the AMD GPU delivery and deployment milestones to be achieved in 2027. Following the completion of this offering, any subsequent purchases of our Class N common stock by AMD pursuant to the Hardware Supply Agreement will be made at a price per share equal to the volume-weighted average price of our Class A common stock over the 30 trading days immediately preceding the applicable closing date of such purchase, and we must make any draw request within 12 months following the final delivery and deployment of AMD GPU capacity under the Hardware Supply Agreement.

Overview
We have entered into NPAs with each of Google (through Google LLC), Amazon (through Amazon Web Services, Inc.), and Broadcom that provide for the issuance of convertible promissory notes and, in certain cases, shares of our non-voting capital stock. Our NPAs with Google consist of agreements entered into in September 2023 and August 2024, pursuant to which all convertible promissory notes previously issued thereunder have been fully converted into non-voting redeemable convertible preferred stock and under which no additional notes may be issued, and an agreement entered into in March 2026 (“Google 2026 NPA”), which provides for potential future financing capacity, subject to certain conditions described below. Our NPAs with Amazon consist of the Amazon 2023 NPA and the Amazon 2024 NPA, pursuant to which we previously issued convertible promissory notes, approximately $6.2 billion aggregate principal amount of which remains outstanding as described below under “—Convertible Notes—Outstanding Notes,” and under which no additional notes may be issued, and the 2026 Stock Purchase and Convertible Note Facility Agreement, dated as of April 20, 2026, by and between us and Amazon (“Amazon 2026 NPA”), which provides for potential future financing capacity, subject to certain conditions described below. The Infrastructure Partner 2026 NPA provides for potential future financing capacity, if needed, subject to certain conditions described below. The principal economic terms of the NPAs that relate to our outstanding notes and potential future financing capacity are summarized in the tables below. To the extent an NPA creates an obligation to issue notes in the future, that obligation is accounted for as a derivative liability on our consolidated balance sheets until the related note is issued. For additional information, including the historical issuance and conversion of notes under these agreements, see Notes 9 and 16 to our consolidated financial statements included elsewhere in this prospectus.

Operating Activities
Net cash used in operating activities for the year ended December 31, 2025 decreased by $3.1 billion compared to the year ended December 31, 2024. The decrease was primarily driven by a decrease in prepaid hosting services reflecting the consumption during 2025 of hosting capacity that had been prepaid in prior periods and an increase in accounts payable, accrued expenses, and other current liabilities due to increased CSP costs and the timing of related payments. The decrease was partially offset by higher cash payments, including a payment related to the Bartz settlement, higher cash compensation costs from headcount growth, and an increase in accounts receivable.
Net cash used in operating activities for the year ended December 31, 2024 increased by $4.1 billion compared to the year ended December 31, 2023. The increase was primarily driven by an increase in prepaid hosting services due to business expansion requiring additional hosting capacity.
Net cash provided by operating activities was $6.6 billion for the nine months ended September 30, 2026 as compared to cash used in operating activities of $2.0 billion for the nine months ended September 30, 2025. Our operating cash flows result primarily from cash received from our customers, offset by cash payments we make for products and services, employee compensation, operating leases, and interest. The increase in operating cash flow was primarily driven by an improvement in net loss adjusted for non-cash items, partially offset by a lower benefit from changes in working capital, primarily reflecting the timing of payments to vendors and cash receipts from customers. Working capital at any point in time is subject to many variables, including the timing of billings and cash collections, vendor payment terms, and the timing of invoice receipt and payment.

Our international revenue, as well as costs and expenses denominated in foreign currencies, and intercompany transactions with our foreign subsidiaries, expose us to the risk of fluctuations in foreign currency exchange rates against the U.S. dollar. A hypothetical 10% change in foreign currency exchange rates applicable to our business would not have had a material impact on our consolidated financial statements as of September 30, 2026. We have not entered into derivative or hedging transactions, but we may enter into such arrangements in the future if our exposure to foreign currency becomes more significant.

location: MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS > Critical Accounting Estimates > Stock-Based Compensation
text:
Stock-Based Compensation
We measure compensation expense for all stock-based payment awards, including stock options and RSUs, granted to employees, directors, and other service providers, based on the estimated fair value of the awards on the date of grant. The most significant input in determining the fair value of a stock option is the estimated fair value of our common stock. The estimated fair value of our common stock is also used to measure the grant-date fair value of RSUs and RSAs, including those subject to performance-based vesting conditions.
Stock Options
We estimate the fair value of stock options granted to employees, consultants, officers, and directors using the Black-Scholes-Merton option pricing model on the date of grant. The fair value of stock options that are expected to vest is recognized as compensation expense on a straight-line basis over the requisite service period. Forfeitures are accounted for when they occur.
The Black-Scholes-Merton model considers several variables and assumptions in estimating the fair value of stock-based awards. These variables include:
•Fair Value of Common Stock. Because our common stock is not yet publicly traded, we must estimate the fair value of our common stock. Our board of directors considers numerous objective and subjective factors to determine the fair value of our common stock as discussed in the section titled “— Common Stock Valuations” below.
•Expected Volatility. Since we have no trading history of our common stock, the expected volatility of our underlying common stock is estimated by taking the weighted-average historical volatility of a group of comparable publicly traded companies over a period equal to the expected life of the options.
•Expected Term. Expected term represents the period over which we anticipate stock-based awards to be outstanding. We estimate the expected term based on the options’ vesting term and contractual terms, such that the expected life is equal to the average of the stock-based award’s weighted-average vesting period and its contractual term.
•Risk-Free Rate. The expected risk-free rate assumption is based on the U.S. Treasury instruments whose term is consistent with the expected term of the stock options.
•Expected Dividend Yield. The expected dividend yield is zero, as we have never declared or paid any dividends and have no current plans to do so.

We have granted RSUs to our employees and non-employee service providers under our 2021 Plan. RSUs outstanding as of September 30, 2026 have both service-based and performance-based vesting conditions. The service-based vesting period for these awards is typically four years. Upon satisfaction of the performance-based condition, RSUs for which the service-based vesting condition has also been satisfied will vest immediately, and any remaining unvested RSUs will vest ratably over the remaining service period. The performance-based condition is generally satisfied upon the occurrence of a change in control event or the effective date of the registration statement of which this prospectus forms a part.

After the allocation of enterprise value to the various classes of stock, a discount for lack of marketability (“DLOM”) is applied to arrive at a fair value of the common stock. A DLOM is meant to account for the lack of opportunity to sell private company stock that is not traded on public exchanges. In making the final determination of common stock value, consideration is also given to the recent sales and/or expected sales of common stock.
Application of these approaches involves the use of estimates, judgment, and assumptions that are complex and subjective, such as those regarding our expected future revenue, expenses, and future cash flows, discount rates, market multiples, the selection of comparable companies, and the probability of possible future events. Changes in any or all of these estimates and assumptions or the relationships between those assumptions impact our valuations as of each valuation date and may have a material impact on the valuation of our common stock.
Following this offering, it will not be necessary to determine the fair value of our common stock, as the shares of our common stock will be traded in the public market.

text:
Fair Value of Convertible Notes, Derivative Liabilities, and SAFEs
We elected to account for our convertible notes at fair value pursuant to Accounting Standards Codification (“ASC”) Topic 825, Financial Instruments. The convertible notes are recognized at their estimated fair value on our consolidated balance sheet, and changes in fair value are recorded in change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs in our consolidated statement of operations. We elected the fair value option to eliminate the accounting complexity that would otherwise result from separately accounting for the liability and equity components of the convertible notes under the traditional bifurcation model.
In connection with the 2023 and 2024 note purchase agreements with both Amazon and Google, we recognized derivative liabilities representing obligations to issue future convertible notes pursuant to the terms of those agreements. The derivative liabilities were measured at estimated fair value, with changes in fair value recorded in change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs in the consolidated statement of operations.
The estimated fair value of the convertible promissory notes is determined using a hybrid approach comprising a CCA and a CSE method. The analysis estimates the fair value of the convertible promissory notes using a scenario-based analysis that considers the probability-weighted present value of the instruments across the range of possible outcomes available to the note holders, including conversion into redeemable convertible preferred stock or Class N common stock, cash repayment at maturity, and cash settlement at a premium upon a change of control. The scenarios included consider the probability-weighted value of the instruments in the CCA and CSE framework.

text:
The application of this methodology involves the use of complex and subjective estimates, judgments, and assumptions, including the probability and timing of each settlement scenario such as a qualified equity financing, initial public offering, direct listing, or change of control; the estimated fair value of our equity securities into which the notes may convert; the applicable conversion prices, which vary by note series and are contingent on factors such as elapsed time since issuance and contractual caps and percentage discounts; and the ownership thresholds and rollover provisions that determine the extent to which principal balances convert into equity versus being reissued as rollover notes. In particular, the ownership cap and rollover mechanism— whereby conversion is capped at specified ownership thresholds and any unconverted principal balance is re-issued as a non-interest bearing rollover note that remains subject to fair value measurement—requires significant judgment in estimating what proportion of each note financing will convert versus roll over, because this determination depends on the size and structure of future equity financings that are inherently uncertain. Changes in any or all of these estimates and assumptions, or the relationships between those assumptions, impact our valuations as of each measurement date and may have a material impact on the amounts recognized in our consolidated statement of operations.
The fair value option election described above also applied to the SAFEs that we issued during the year ended December 31, 2023. The SAFEs were measured at estimated fair value using the same scenario-based framework, with the monetary settlement amount fixed at inception and the number of equity shares received upon conversion being variable; consistent with the convertible notes, changes in fair value were recorded in change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs in the consolidated statement of operations. All SAFEs were converted into redeemable convertible preferred stock during the years ended December 31, 2023 and 2024, and no SAFEs remained outstanding as of December 31, 2024 or 2025. No SAFEs were outstanding at any point during the nine months ended September 30, 2026. Accordingly, the primary ongoing estimation exposure under the fair value option relates to the convertible notes and rollover notes described above.

Leases
We lease facilities and equipment, including compute and infrastructure capacity, under operating and finance leases. We determine whether an arrangement is or contains a lease at inception and evaluate the classification of our leases at lease commencement and, as necessary, upon modification. Accounting for leases requires significant judgment, including determining whether an arrangement is or contains a lease, and significant estimates, including the expected lease term, the fair value of the leased property, and our incremental borrowing rate.

text:
Income Taxes
We account for income taxes using the asset and liability method, recognizing deferred tax assets and liabilities for temporary differences between the financial reporting and tax bases of assets and liabilities, as well as for net operating loss and credit carryforwards, measured at enacted tax rates applicable in the years of expected reversals. We establish valuation allowances when necessary to reduce deferred tax assets to amounts more-likely-than-not expected to be realized, based on the weighting of positive and negative evidence.
Assessing the realizability of our deferred tax assets is an area of significant management judgment. We evaluate our deferred tax assets for recoverability based on historical taxable income, projected future taxable income, reversal patterns of existing temporary differences, and available tax planning strategies. As an AI company operating in a rapidly evolving market with significant ongoing investment in compute and infrastructure, our projections of future taxable income are inherently uncertain. Should our assessment of the recoverability of deferred tax assets change, our income tax provision would be adjusted in that period, which could materially impact our results of operations.
We account for uncertain tax positions in accordance with ASC Topic 740, Income Taxes. Tax benefits from uncertain positions are recognized when it is more likely than not that the position will be sustained on examination based on its technical merits, measured at the amount that is more likely than not to be realized upon settlement. These assessments require judgment, particularly with respect to the qualification and documentation of research and development tax credits, where supporting evidence may be subject to differing interpretations. The actual outcome of these matters may differ materially from our current estimates. We recognize interest and penalties related to unrecognized tax benefits within our provision for income taxes.

Loss Contingencies
We are involved in legal claims, proceedings, and other regulatory and administrative matters that arise in the ordinary course of business, certain of which may include speculative claims for substantial or indeterminate amounts of damages.
We routinely assess each significant matter and its potential financial exposure. We record a liability when we believe it is both probable that a loss has been incurred and the amount can be reasonably estimated, and we disclose matters for which a loss is reasonably possible and the loss or range of loss can be estimated. These assessments require significant judgment in determining both the likelihood and estimated amount of potential losses. We base our accruals on the best information available at the time, taking into account the specific facts and circumstances of each matter, the merits of our defenses, and the impact of negotiations, settlements, regulatory proceedings, rulings, and advice of legal counsel. Our estimates are subject to change as additional information becomes available and as matters develop, and we have in prior periods revised our assessments based on updated information.

location: BUSINESS > Overview
text:
For the first time in history, intelligence is something humans can build. The cognitive capability to reason, analyze, synthesize, decide, and create is producible at scale and accessible on demand. We believe this abundance of super intelligence10 will rapidly transform every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet. If this technology truly delivers on its potential—with the risks well managed—it could significantly accelerate global growth and dramatically improve quality of life for people around the world.
Anthropic was founded in 2021 by a team of researchers responsible for many of the breakthroughs that define AI. We are first and foremost a research lab—our mission is the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity. This mission directs our focus—along with our talent and culture, our frontier and safety research, our approach to compute, and our enterprise strategy, it is one of the core advantages that set us apart. These advantages enable us to continuously advance frontier intelligence and shape the standards for its safe and responsible development. Our frontier intelligence, Claude, is delivered to customers through our models, platform, and applications. Claude has experienced the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history, as demonstrated by revenue growing from $0 at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $17.0 billion for the three months ended September 30, 2026. This rapid and growing adoption generates two self-reinforcing dynamics—an improvement loop that advances Claude and an investment loop that helps fund our continued research at the frontier.
For purposes of this prospectus, we use the terms “super intelligence,” “SI,” “artificial intelligence,” and “AI” interchangeably.

location: BUSINESS > Overview
text: We believe the diffusion of AI through the global economy represents one of the largest opportunities in history to improve how humans live and work, and it is just beginning. In our view, the world has only begun to use the capabilities of today’s frontier models, and the gap between what Claude can do and how broadly it is used represents one of our largest growth opportunities, alongside continued advances at the frontier. Claude’s capabilities have evolved significantly in recent years, and we expect they will continue advancing rapidly. This will lead not only to an expanding addressable market, but also to an expanding scope of impact on the world. We aim to ensure that impact is as positive as possible.

text:
Our Core Advantages
Mission & Focus. All of our efforts are guided by a singular focus on our mission. This focus enables us to concentrate talent, research, and compute investment on the highest-value work for humanity and to avoid conflicting priorities. Achieving our mission means the world gains the enormous benefits of frontier intelligence while mitigating the most significant risks, and we believe this requires safety and capability to advance together.
Talent & Culture. Our mission and focus enable us to attract and retain world-class talent, including researchers and engineers who want their work to shape a better future. We also have a culture that promotes a low-ego, truth-seeking environment, where frontier capability and safety are mutually reinforcing. We believe our culture has driven our talent density as we have scaled.
Frontier & Safety Research. We believe that sustained, focused research at the frontier of intelligence is required to build the most capable and safest AI systems. Our frontier capabilities and safety research are deeply integrated and directly shape model design, training, and deployment, helping us produce systems that are more reliable, steerable, and well suited for real-world deployment, particularly in demanding enterprise environments. We translate our research leadership into innovation velocity and have consistently released better models, platform capabilities, and applications. Each version of a Claude model assists in building the next, helping to compress development timelines and produce compounding improvements in the speed at which we innovate. We refer to this recursive dynamic as “closing the loop,” and we believe it is one of the most significant structural advantages in frontier intelligence and can greatly accelerate the rate at which capabilities advance. We believe that model capabilities must be advanced together with safety, alignment, and security practices, particularly as the speed of AI development accelerates. We assess the risks of each model during development and before and after release, and take the steps we believe are appropriate to balance model capabilities with safety, alignment, and security, even where doing so may moderate the rate at which we release new capabilities. We view decisions of this kind as deliberate tradeoffs that we make because they serve the Company Purpose, the long-term interests of our mission, and our customers’ demand for safe and aligned models.
title: US-PROSPECTUS (S-1/A, preliminary) | BUSINESS > Overview > Our Core Advantages

location: BUSINESS > Overview > Our Core Advantages
text:
Our Approach to Compute. We manage compute as a single, fungible pool from multiple strategic partners, and we dynamically direct available compute between workloads based on where the marginal unit is expected to be most productive at any given time. We believe that this approach to compute enables us to deliver superior models, serve more customers, and achieve greater productivity from our compute investment. This compute efficiency creates the foundation for us to advance frontier capabilities through research and model development, meet growing demand from customers, and provide for internal usage of Claude. We have achieved this through our research breakthroughs and our multi-chip compute architecture across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs, enabling us to orchestrate workloads to optimize for price and performance. To support our research, model development, customer demand, and internal usage of Claude, we continue to invest at scale. As of and subsequent to September 30, 2026, we have entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements, including short-term commitments, as well as leases not yet commenced, with an aggregate committed spend of approximately $900.9 billion, substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure. These commitments include approximately $451.6 billion expected to be incurred before December 31, 2030, and substantially all of the remainder is expected to be incurred between 2031 and 2045. Approximately $70.7 billion of these commitments are due in the 12 months following September 30, 2026. See the section titled “Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations—Liquidity and Capital Resources—Contractual Obligations” for more information.
Enterprise Strategy. Our enterprise strategy is built on the belief that frontier intelligence is most valuable in real-world settings, as deployment across enterprises is where economic impact is greatest and where the improvement loop from customer feedback is richest. Accordingly, we have organized our research priorities, our product roadmap, and our go-to-market and Applied AI teams around enterprise use cases, which range from routine knowledge work to the most complex problems. The customer feedback we gather directs our research focus and makes Claude more capable over time. This broadens where Claude can be deployed and further expands enterprise adoption, which helps ensure that the benefits of our technology reach people and organizations at scale.

text:
Enterprise Adoption of Claude
The speed and depth of our enterprise customer adoption are powerful evidence of Claude’s position at the frontier of AI. Our customer base as of September 30, 2026 includes:
•More than 11,900 customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis;
•More than 1,900 customers with $1 million or more of revenue on a TTM basis; and
•Approximately 250 customers with $10 million or more of revenue on a TTM basis.
Unlike a static product that serves a single use case, Claude is frontier intelligence with rapidly advancing capabilities. We build at three layers of the stack: the models themselves, the platform for building on those models, and the applications that place Claude directly in the hands of our users. An advance at any layer compounds across all three layers, accelerating the pace at which we can deliver more capable intelligence. We believe the value of this integrated approach is reflected in the increasing number of customers that use both Claude Platform and our first-party applications. For the three months ended September 30, 2026, over 50% of our customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis used Claude Platform and at least one of our first-party applications, up from approximately 30% for the three months ended December 31, 2025.
Today, enterprises rely on Claude to reason, plan, and execute across complex workflows with a level of trustworthiness and judgment that we believe was not available from earlier generations of these technologies. Customers realize value from Claude in three primary ways: more productive employees, faster processes, and embedded intelligence in their products. As Claude’s capabilities grow, our customers benefit and often broaden their adoption of Claude in new workflows. This expanding role reflects a broader shift in how Claude is used inside the enterprise, from a tool that responds to discrete prompts to what we call a Virtual Collaborator: an AI system that works alongside humans to perform complex, multi-step work at professional levels.
We drive the diffusion of Claude primarily by making it accessible across multiple product surfaces. For example:
•Claude Platform, our comprehensive agentic development environment, provides customers with direct access to the primitives to build, deploy, and scale their own applications that leverage Claude’s capabilities within their own products and workflows.

text:
•Claude Code, our coding agent, works alongside human software developers on end-to-end software development: writing, planning, editing, testing, debugging, and committing code across production-scale codebases.
•Claude Cowork, our knowledge work agent, has computer use capability that enables it to work with professionals on end-to-end business tasks: autonomously researching, drafting, analyzing, synthesizing, and executing other knowledge work.
Much of the diffusion of Claude has been organic. We amplify this with our go-to-market and Applied AI teams, which extend our reach by meeting customers where they are through distribution partnerships that place Claude inside customers’ existing technology stacks. For example, Claude is accessible on all three major cloud platforms—AWS, GCP, and Azure. We have a joint go-to-market approach with these CSPs through which we establish direct contractual relationships with our customers while paying a fee to each CSP. This structure allows us to foster stronger commercial alignment with these CSPs, avoid channel conflict, set pricing, and realize the financial benefits of ongoing compute efficiency improvements. Ecosystem partnerships also expand our reach, allowing customers to adopt Claude through systems integrators, such as Accenture, Deloitte, KPMG, and PwC; consultants; and data platforms, such as Salesforce and Snowflake. We recently launched Ode with Anthropic, an AI services company, in partnership with leading private equity firms to bring Claude’s capabilities to mid-sized companies across sectors, building solutions on the Claude Platform and supporting customers over the long term.

Strengths of Our Financial Model
Building and scaling frontier intelligence is one of the most important and capital-intensive endeavors in history. Our financial model provides us with the following strengths that allow us to build and scale efficiently:
•Rapid Revenue Growth. Our enterprise strategy is designed to drive durable customer adoption by embedding Claude directly into business-critical workflows and enabling the development of products built on Claude. We believe that enterprise customers achieve a compelling return on investment from Claude, as agentic workflows can drive both top-line growth and efficiency. This enables us to expand quickly with customers, as demonstrated by our Net Revenue Retention of approximately 900% as of September 30, 2026.
•Compute Efficiency. Our compute efficiency drives more intelligence from research and model development, and we believe this approach can support more customer and internal usage of Claude for the same amount of compute compared to other approaches. •Our revenue was $17.0 billion for the three months ended September 30, 2026, up from $1.4 billion for the three months ended September 30, 2025.

Our Self-Reinforcing Loops
Our scale and growth create self-reinforcing loops that make Claude better over time and that we believe create durable competitive advantages.
•Improvement Loop. Enterprise deployments of Claude deepen our understanding of the hard problems, edge cases, and domain-specific challenges that matter most to our customers. We improve our models, platform, and applications based on feedback from customers using our offerings in production across their businesses. These improvements result in wider deployments and adoption that fuel the next cycle of improvement.
•Investment Loop. Revenue from expanding enterprise adoption helps us to fund the compute, research, and talent needed to improve Claude. Claude’s advancing capabilities expand the range of tasks and workflows customers use Claude for, broadening our addressable market and driving deeper deployment, additional revenue, and continued reinvestment in Claude.

location: BUSINESS > Overview > Claude is Accelerating Our Ability to Close the Loop
text:
Claude is Accelerating Our Ability to Close the Loop
Claude itself has become one of the most powerful drivers of our progress—each new version of a Claude model directly accelerates development of the next. Many aspects of the research, training, and testing of subsequent model generations now involve Claude, including running experiments, generating and processing training data, automating evaluations and safety audits, and writing and reviewing code. We refer to this recursive dynamic as “closing the loop.” A direct expression of this dynamic is our accelerating pace of producing compute multipliers. More capable models help our researchers discover these improvements faster; in turn, more powerful compute multipliers enable us to train even more capable models and deploy them more efficiently.
A clear example of our ability to close the loop is the deployment of Claude Code, our agentic coding product, across our engineering organization. As our models have advanced, we have seen significant improvement in Claude’s capability on more challenging, open-ended engineering problems that lack a clear specification and have historically depended on experienced human judgment. Claude’s success rate on these problems reached approximately 90% in September 2026, up approximately 50 percentage points in nine months, based on our internal benchmarks. Claude Code has progressed from suggesting code to writing and running it directly and working autonomously over long time horizons on complex, multi-step engineering tasks. This has enabled our engineers to increasingly direct and review its work rather than write code line by line. As a result, the average daily volume of code contributed to our codebase per engineer in the three months ended September 30, 2026 was over 45 times the average daily volume in the year ended December 31, 2024. Over 90% of the contributions to our codebase in September 2026 were written by Claude.
The impact of Claude extends beyond research and engineering. From December 31, 2024 to September 30, 2026, our headcount grew over five times, while our revenue for the three months ended September 30, 2026 was 86 times our revenue for the three months ended December 31, 2024.
title: US-PROSPECTUS (S-1/A, preliminary) | BUSINESS > Overview > Claude is Accelerating Our Ability to Close the Loop

location: BUSINESS > Overview > Claude is Accelerating Our Ability to Close the Loop
text:
We believe this operating leverage has been driven by the use of Claude throughout our organization. Across our research, engineering, go-to-market, and operations teams, Claude allows employees to leverage a team of agents in their daily work, enabling a comparatively small team to take on work that would traditionally require a far larger one by multiplying the impact of each person.
The expansion of our own use of Claude reflects this leverage directly. The value of our own internal Claude usage at list prices has grown by over 250 times from January 2026 to September 2026, and in April 2026, this monthly value first exceeded our monthly personnel expense, excluding stock-based compensation. Because each version of Claude is used to help build the next and because Claude makes our teams more productive across the company, we believe the compute we devote to internal usage compounds these gains, continuously accelerating our pace of development and further strengthening our leadership position.
Using AI to help build more capable AI could also pose a considerable safety risk, particularly if it sharply accelerates the pace of progress. This is one of the areas covered by our Responsible Scaling Policy, which sets out our plans to monitor and mitigate the risks as we approach what has been termed “recursive self-improvement.” We believe our investments in safety techniques will enable us to manage these risks and responsibly realize substantially more leverage from Claude than we do today in developing AI models. However, we do not anticipate being able to safely use Claude to fully autonomously design and build successive generations of frontier models without meaningful human supervision or understanding, if and when that becomes technically possible. Accordingly, we are considering updates to our Responsible Scaling Policy to keep humans in control of frontier model development at Anthropic.

Scaling Laws and the Predictability of Progress
The intelligence and capabilities of AI systems have advanced dramatically. Tasks that were beyond the reach of AI systems just a few years ago, such as complex mathematical reasoning, designing scientific experiments, and executing substantial portions of software development, are now routinely performed by AI.
These advances have followed empirical “Scaling Laws,” the finding that AI model performance improves predictably with increases in model size, training data, and compute. The foundational paper, Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models, whose lead authors (including [Co-founder 1 (CEO)], [Co-founder 5], [Co-founder 6], and [Co-founder 3]) later co-founded Anthropic, was critical in establishing these relationships and helped guide the wave of modern LLMs.
to knowledge workers globally. IDC, The Economic Impact of AI: 2026 Edition, doc # US54452226, April 2026. Reflects cumulative economic impact as the sum of the annual impact estimated for each year from 2025 through 2031. Includes the annual value created across AI solutions and services, investments in the AI infrastructure supply chain, and enhancements in enterprise productivity and efficiency unlocked by AI. IDC, Worldwide Black Book: Live Edition V2 2026 Forecast, July 2026.
We expect AI capabilities—across language, reasoning, mathematics, coding, scientific analysis, and an expanding range of agentic tasks and knowledge work—to continue advancing for many years. We believe this will drive demand for AI that outstrips supply for the foreseeable future, limited principally by the availability of compute. We believe that the majority of this demand will be concentrated at the frontier: our experience has been that enterprises gravitate to our most capable models across a wide variety of workloads, including their highest-value work. In addition, we believe that each successive expansion of the frontier will unlock new categories of work that, in turn, will generate the majority of incremental industry demand. We expect the industry to continue increasing investment in compute, research talent, and engineering resources to advance the frontier of AI. Within this framework, research labs with proprietary training methods, strong data quality, and differentiated research talent are well-positioned to outpace what scale alone would predict.

text:
A Near-Term Opportunity to Transform Cognitive Work
Frontier intelligence is transforming cognitive work—the application of knowledge, reasoning, and judgment to produce economic value. We believe it will make humans far more capable and expand the world’s overall capacity for that work, including accelerating scientific discovery and helping businesses grow. Knowledge workers are the leading edge of this opportunity. As the frontier advances, more capable models can unlock entirely new use cases while also efficiently serving a wide range of cognitive work at scale across the capability-cost-speed curve. We believe the work that knowledge workers perform represented more than $40 trillion in economic value globally in 2025,11 and with the potential for frontier intelligence to make them meaningfully more productive, our near-term opportunity is to expand this value and accelerate economic growth. While it is still early to forecast the full impact of frontier intelligence across the economy, IDC estimates that investment in AI solutions and services will yield a cumulative global economic impact of $22.5 trillion by 2031.12 We believe the impact could be even greater.
History suggests that transformative technologies expand the markets they enter. For example, information technology spend grew from approximately $1.2 trillion in 2006 to $4.3 trillion in 2025, a CAGR of approximately 7%, as cloud computing spend grew from zero to $1.9 trillion over the same period and expanded information technology budgets.13 We have seen other technologies, including the personal computer, the internet, and the smartphone, grow their markets as well. The companies that built these technologies grew at a far faster rate than the economy as a whole. Global GDP grew from approximately $34 trillion in 2000 to more than $118 trillion in 2025 according to the World Bank, more than tripling. Over that same period, the 10 largest publicly traded technology companies by market capitalization as of September 30, 2026 grew their aggregate revenue from $68 billion to more than $2.5 trillion, an increase of approximately 38 times, or approximately 11 times the rate of global GDP growth.

Frontier Intelligence May Reshape Entire Sectors and Accelerate Novel Discoveries
We believe frontier intelligence represents a larger opportunity than any prior technology cycle, and Claude is already demonstrating this potential. Claude can now execute complex projects autonomously over hours and days, coordinating thousands of agents in parallel to carry out sophisticated planning, long-form research, and self-correcting analysis. Claude also turns open-ended tasks into finished, high-quality deliverables—work that was beyond the reach of frontier models only a short time ago. These capabilities position Claude to transform the largest sectors of the global economy, including software development, business and professional services, cybersecurity, financial services, and healthcare and life sciences, driving meaningful gains in productivity and output for the organizations that deploy it.
