location: BUSINESS > Safety Research is Core to Our Business > Anthropic’s Responsible Scaling Policy
text:
Anthropic’s Responsible Scaling Policy
Our Responsible Scaling Policy describes how we approach the catastrophic risks posed by AI. The policy requires us to regularly publish detailed risk reports that reflect our perspectives on the overall level of risk posed by our models and how we are mitigating such risks. Our teams test each model extensively before release, assessing its capabilities in the domains most relevant to catastrophic risk and evaluating the extent to which the model can be misused. Our risk report describes an overall assessment of the results of these evaluations, the mitigations we have implemented to address these risks, and whether, and if so why, we believe the identified risks are justified by corresponding benefits. As part of the current version of our Responsible Scaling Policy, we publish a Frontier Safety Roadmap, detailing our plans for measurable advances in security, alignment, safeguards, and AI policy. This acts as an internal spur for safety research and development and is externally visible so customers and regulators can use it to gauge our progress. Consistent with this approach, we assess the risks of each model during development and before and after release and we take the steps we believe are appropriate to mitigate those risks. In the past, these steps have included delaying the release of new models and limiting their initial availability, such as our initial release of Mythos through Project Glasswing, and in the future, as we learn more about model capabilities and behavior, could include additional measures that affect how and when we develop or release these new models. We believe these practices also serve our customers, since rigorous safeguards and predictable model behavior have become decisive criteria when selecting an AI partner.
title: US-PROSPECTUS (S-1/A, preliminary) | BUSINESS > Safety Research is Core to Our Business > Anthropic’s Responsible Scaling Policy

location: BUSINESS > Safety Research is Core to Our Business > Claude’s Constitution
text:
Claude’s Constitution
We have developed a constitution for Claude that describes our vision for how an AI model should be and how it should behave, which is used directly in the model training process. We have used Claude’s constitution to meaningfully advance how frontier models are trained, and it is our attempt to grapple with the most difficult questions regarding the development of this new type of artificially intelligent entity. It is a living document that we intend to revise as we develop further models and learn more about how they work. Our researchers have found that training Claude on high-quality constitutional documents combined with fictional stories portraying an aligned AI contributes to reducing Claude’s misalignment rate. We believe Claude’s constitution has also proven commercially valuable: transparently laying out the values we intend Claude to hold increases customer trust.
This constitution orients Claude around four priorities:
•Be Broadly Safe. Avoid irreversible actions and support human oversight of AI behavior.
•Be Broadly Ethical. Maintain honesty and sound moral judgment, and avoid harmful acts.
•Be Compliant with our Guidelines. Adhere to our operational standards for user interactions and absolute prohibitions on certain categories of harm.
•Be Genuinely Helpful. Deliver substantive, expert-level assistance that creates real value for users.
title: US-PROSPECTUS (S-1/A, preliminary) | BUSINESS > Safety Research is Core to Our Business > Claude’s Constitution

location: BUSINESS > Safety Research is Core to Our Business > Model Validation and Training Data
text:
Model Validation and Training Data
Beyond the assessments performed under our Responsible Scaling Policy, we evaluate each Claude model prior to its release through a structured, multi-stage evaluation program covering model capabilities, safety behaviors, and societal impacts, including bias and discrimination, and we document the results of these pre-deployment evaluations, and their limitations, in our publicly available model system cards. This testing addresses the reliability and accuracy of model outputs, including through capability and accuracy benchmarking, evaluations focused on factual accuracy and hallucinations, evaluations of whether model outputs are honest and accurately reflect the information on which they are based, reliability testing of agentic performance over long-running tasks, and adversarial red-teaming designed to identify ways in which a model may fail or behave in unintended ways. Where these evaluations identify issues, we address them through additional post-training, adjusted safeguards, and re-evaluation prior to release, and we document residual limitations in the applicable model system card.
Claude models are trained on data drawn from a broad range of sources, modalities, and languages, including publicly available information from the internet, datasets licensed or commissioned from third parties, and other sources, such as synthetic data generated by our own models. We conduct diligence on third-party data sources to assess their quality, provenance, and suitability for our usage, and in many cases include contractual restrictions intended to discourage the inclusion of personal data in sourced datasets. We apply data curation and filtering processes to sourced data, which are designed to improve data quality, deduplicate content, and reduce potential exposure to harmful content.
We address bias and fairness risks at multiple stages of model training and deployment. We manage the representativeness and diversity of our training data through a layered approach in which dataset curation, post-training alignment, pre-deployment evaluation, and deployment safeguards each play a part, rather than through dataset composition alone. Once our models are deployed, our usage policy prohibits the use of Claude for discriminatory decision-making and requires human oversight for high-stakes automated decisions, such as those affecting employment, housing, or legal issues. Our validation, safeguards, and monitoring practices continue to evolve as model capabilities advance and as new risks and failure modes are identified.
title: US-PROSPECTUS (S-1/A, preliminary) | BUSINESS > Safety Research is Core to Our Business > Model Validation and Training Data

location: BUSINESS > Safety Research is Core to Our Business > Model Validation and Training Data
text: Further, we have obtained certification under ISO/IEC 42001, an international standard established by the International Organization for Standardization (“ISO”) and the International Electrotechnical Commission (“IEC”), following an independent third-party audit of our AI management system, covering risk identification, assessment, and mitigation processes for the responsible development and deployment of AI. Compliance documentation, including our ISO/IEC 42001 certificate and SOC 2 (System and Organization Controls 2) reporting, is available upon request through the trust center page of our website. We also provide pre-deployment model access to external evaluators, including government AI evaluation bodies such as the U.S. Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (the “CAISSI”) and the U.K. AI Security Institute, for recent frontier models, as described in our model system cards.

location: BUSINESS > Safety Research is Core to Our Business > Alignment
text:
Alignment
As AI models grow more capable, ensuring safe and predictable behavior becomes more challenging. Our Alignment team focuses on whether models behave as intended and do not take unwanted actions of their own accord. The team evaluates models to surface undesirable behaviors and develops comprehensive safety evaluations, many of which we open source. Misaligned behaviors, whether occurring in testing or real-world deployments, have been observed across the industry and include examples of models circumventing network and sandbox restrictions, granting themselves permissions they had not been given, taking unintended actions in pursuit of assigned goals, interfering with other AI agents, and misrepresenting whether tasks had been completed or verified. As models are granted greater autonomy, permissions, and integration with internal and external systems, the consequences of such misaligned behavior may increase. For more information about the risks related to model misalignment, see the section titled “Risk Factors—Our models have in the past behaved, and may in the future behave, in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways, including by taking harmful actions that no user or third party directed, which could adversely affect our reputation and brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations.” Our own internal alignment evaluation shows that our newly released frontier models have demonstrated improved alignment compared to their predecessors.
title: US-PROSPECTUS (S-1/A, preliminary) | BUSINESS > Safety Research is Core to Our Business > Alignment

location: BUSINESS > Safety Research is Core to Our Business > Interpretability
text:
Interpretability
Unlike traditional software, where unwanted outputs are traceable to specific bugs, the inner workings of LLMs like Claude are more inscrutable. Our researchers describe AI models as “grown, not built”—software developers can set the initial conditions and some constraints, but they cannot fully control any given output or behavior. This makes assurances about safety—and the diagnosis of problems—far more challenging for AI than for standard software. Anthropic is widely recognized as a leader in mechanistic interpretability: the science of how LLMs work. We have developed mathematical techniques to map how models form and connect concepts as they reason through problems; investigated how they reflect constructs analogous to psychological states and thought processes; and tested how their behavior can be steered through direct adjustments to internal representations. We use interpretability research along with other alignment research techniques to test for unwanted behavioral tendencies before a model release.
title: US-PROSPECTUS (S-1/A, preliminary) | BUSINESS > Safety Research is Core to Our Business > Interpretability

location: BUSINESS > Safety Research is Core to Our Business > Safeguards
text:
Safeguards
Our Safeguards team reduces the risk of Claude producing dangerous, harmful, or undesirable content through multiple approaches, including probes and classifiers that monitor inputs and outputs, training against specific attack vectors such as prompt injection, and monitoring for user safety concerns including encouragement of harmful ideation. When we detect potential violations, enforcement actions range from real-time response adjustments to account warnings and, in severe cases, termination of the offending user’s accounts. Findings from ongoing monitoring, external expert stress-testing, and threat intelligence inform our policies, model training, and detection systems. Identified issues may be addressed through measures such as updates to detection classifiers, reward-model adjustments during training, and changes to the instructions provided to our models that guide their behavior (known as system prompts). We also maintain public reporting channels, including a responsible disclosure policy and a bug bounty program for testing our safety defenses.
We have observed that more capable models are generally better at recognizing and preventing high-stakes misuse. We believe that robust safety measures and model utility are not inherently in tension, and that safety can improve alongside the capability of the models themselves.
title: US-PROSPECTUS (S-1/A, preliminary) | BUSINESS > Safety Research is Core to Our Business > Safeguards

location: BUSINESS > Safety Research is Core to Our Business > Our Approach to Model Releases
text:
Our Approach to Model Releases
Each release is accompanied by a detailed system card covering capability and safety evaluations, external tester reports, and discussion of areas where performance remains limited or where the model shows signs of unwanted behavior. For example, AI poses clear and present risks in the cybersecurity domain as advanced models could assist threat actors in security breaches and exploits. Mitigating these risks is a priority across our research, evaluation, and deployment practices. Before each model release, our Frontier Red Team conducts a detailed analysis to determine whether new models provide meaningful new capabilities to assist potential attackers, and our Safeguards team maintains dedicated classifiers and monitoring systems targeting cyber-related misuse, including prompts related to malware creation, phishing, and infrastructure attacks.
We make decisions about model development and deployment, including whether to begin training a new model, on a case-by-case basis. Before releasing a frontier model, we consider a variety of factors, such as the capabilities and behaviors of the specific model at issue and of our models overall, how well our safeguards and security measures work, and how widely the model would be available. We plan to extend our testing to include more assessments at each stage of model training: pre-training, post-training, and internal deployment. Depending on these assessments, we may delay or suspend training or related research, delay releases, or limit access to models until we have confidence they can be developed and deployed safely. Our assessments are also informed by voluntary pre-deployment evaluation of certain models by the CAISSI and the U.K. AI Security Institute. For certain models that materially advance the capability of the frontier in areas relevant to national security, we also provide designated government partners with expanded early access so that they can independently evaluate model capabilities and safeguards before release.
Based on our analyses, we do not release every model we develop for general use; when a model’s capabilities warrant caution, we may restrict availability or decline to release entirely. For example, in April 2026, we initially released our frontier model, Mythos, as a gated research preview through Project Glasswing, available to select organizations for cybersecurity applications, rather than making it broadly available at launch due to its advanced capabilities in cyber vulnerability discovery. We later released Fable 5 for general use, but with safety restrictions on certain cybersecurity, biology, and chemistry capabilities.
title: US-PROSPECTUS (S-1/A, preliminary) | BUSINESS > Safety Research is Core to Our Business > Our Approach to Model Releases

location: BUSINESS > Safety Research is Core to Our Business > Race to the Top
text:
Race to the Top
Building reliable, trustworthy, and secure AI systems cannot be the task of one AI company alone. Our goal is to foster a race to the top in which AI developers compete on the safety and security of their systems, rather than rushing to release increasingly powerful models without adequate safeguards. In addition to publishing a large volume of research, we open source our evaluations where possible and participate in groups such as the Frontier Model Forum to share safety-critical findings with other AI developers. We have also sought to lead by example in ways that shape industry norms. After we published the first version of our Responsible Scaling Policy in September 2023, two other leading frontier labs adopted similar frameworks within months.

text:
We believe that by fixing the most dangerous weaknesses, verifying the fixes, and sharing what works, frontier intelligence companies and governments can turn today’s AI advances into lasting improvements in security that benefit everyone. We have committed up to $100 million in cyberdefense-related initiatives through Project Glasswing, and we expect to devote significant additional resources over time toward strengthening the security of AI systems and the critical infrastructure that depends on them. The scope, timing, and amount of any such future investments have not been finalized and remain subject to change based on business, regulatory, and other considerations, and there can be no assurance that these initiatives will achieve their intended effect.
Our own trajectory demonstrates that commercial success and a serious commitment to safety are not in tension. We have built one of the fastest-growing businesses in history while maintaining safety as a core priority at every stage.

location: BUSINESS > Our Commitment to Public Benefit
text:
We founded Anthropic on the belief that the most transformative technology in human history demands an extraordinary level of responsibility, and that responsibility extends far beyond building safe systems. Our public benefit purpose is the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity—a mission in which safety is central to our work. Powerful AI can deliver immense benefits, but only if it is developed and deployed with rigorous attention to its risks. At times, that may require pausing the launch of our own most capable systems if we conclude they cannot yet be deployed safely. It also means actively working to ensure that the benefits of AI reach everyone, that the organizations and communities people depend on are strengthened, and that the hardest problems facing humanity are not left to market forces alone to solve.
Realizing this mission requires understanding how AI is actually being used and how it is reshaping society. Our Societal Impacts team builds privacy-preserving tools to study real-world, large-scale uses of Claude— examining how students, educators, and workers use the model, how its values surface in everyday conversations, and what users hope and fear about the future of AI. This includes what we believe to be the largest multilingual qualitative study of its kind, in which more than 80,000 people shared in depth how they see AI shaping their lives. Our Economics team extends this work to the labor market, publishing recurring data reports and fully open datasets (the Anthropic Economic Index) on how Claude is used across jobs, industries, and regions, as well as modeling potential future economic scenarios, so that workers, employers, policymakers, and independent researchers can ground their decisions in evidence and rigorous modeling. To deepen and broaden the reach of this work, we have established the Anthropic Institute, an effort to share research and internal data from across Anthropic with external partners and the public, working together to address the biggest questions posed by Powerful AI.
title: US-PROSPECTUS (S-1/A, preliminary) | BUSINESS > Our Commitment to Public Benefit

location: BUSINESS > Our Commitment to Public Benefit
text: Our commitment to public benefit also extends to how we deploy our own resources. As part of our public benefit initiatives, we intend to direct a meaningful portion of our resources toward ensuring that frontier intelligence is safe and its benefits are broadly distributed. This might include making contributions to nonprofit organizations, research institutions, or other groups working on problems where AI can have the greatest positive impact, as well as programs that are designed to make Claude accessible to communities, educators, and public institutions that would not otherwise have access. We believe that how we distribute our resources is as much an expression of our mission as the details of how we build our models.

location: BUSINESS > Our Commitment to Public Benefit
text: As part of these initiatives, we contributed 846,840,960 shares of our Class N common stock, representing 5% of our fully diluted shares as of June 30, 2026 (assuming full conversion of the Amazon Notes), to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, our wholly owned subsidiary dedicated to the Company Purpose, which we refer to as the Initial Public Benefit Issuance. As the value we create grows, we intend for the public benefit to share meaningfully in that growth as well. To that end, our board of directors has approved a framework for additional contributions tied to future increases in our share price. Following this offering and the concurrent private placement, our board of directors, in its discretion, may issue shares of our Class N common stock to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund (or other designee) representing up to an additional 2% of our then-outstanding shares (plus any shares subject to options, RSUs, and other convertible securities and any shares held by the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund) each time our share price appreciates 50% above the prior share price milestone, beginning with our initial public offering price. A share price milestone is reached only when our closing share price has exceeded the applicable threshold on at least 90 of the trailing 120 consecutive trading days, and our average closing share price over the 10 trading days prior to such issuance also exceeds that threshold. Although our board of directors has approved this framework, any future contributions will be made at the discretion of our board of directors. The shares that are contributed to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, including the Initial Public Benefit Issuance, may be transferred or donated to a third party, or otherwise sold in a registered public offering or private placement transaction in furtherance of our public benefit initiatives. Our board of directors will determine the allocations and distributions from the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund until it approves a specific governance structure for the entity, at which point decision-making authority is expected to transition to designated managers of the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund operating under that structure. The initial managers are [Co-founder 1 (CEO)], [Co-founder 2 (President)], [Co-founder 4], and [LTBT Trustee 1 (Chair)]. The Initial Public Benefit Issuance and the additional share contribution framework represent one of the ways in which we intend to pursue the Company Purpose, but they are not the exclusive means of doing so.

We expect to dedicate additional resources, and to make other business and operational decisions, in furtherance of the Company Purpose outside of, and in addition to, these equity contributions.

location: BUSINESS > Competition > Model Developers
text:
Model Developers
We face direct competition from companies building frontier models for third-party software developers and enterprises, including OpenAI and Google, and large, well-capitalized technology companies investing to reach the frontier. These organizations have significant financial resources, large existing customer bases, and the ability to integrate their models into first-party applications sold directly to businesses. While these competitors have built meaningful market presence, we believe our primary focus on enterprises, our ability to remain at and define the frontier, our research talent, and the efficiency through which we maximize our compute investment position us favorably with customers who prioritize model quality, safety, and reliability.
We also face competition from a broader set of model providers. These include large companies, specialized AI labs, and a growing range of other open-weight or open-source (shared weights, training data, and code) models released by state actors and international and domestic research organizations. While these models seek to prioritize cost efficiency over maximum intelligence, we believe our frontier models are highly effective and efficient across a broad range of workloads, from routine knowledge tasks to customers’ most important problems. We believe we compete favorably based on our ability to deliver the most capable models for the problems that demand the highest intelligence, as well as efficiently applying our models to complete everyday work to deliver high-quality results at a lower cost.

location: BUSINESS > Intellectual Property
text:
Our intellectual property is an important aspect of our business and helps us to maintain our competitive position. To establish and protect our rights in our proprietary technology, we rely upon a combination of trade secret, copyright, patent, and trademark laws and contractual restrictions such as confidentiality agreements, licenses, and intellectual property assignment agreements.
We control access to our intellectual property and confidential information through internal and external controls. Access to our most critical intellectual property is tightly controlled, with only a subset of our workforce able to view or modify these systems. We maintain a policy requiring our employees, contractors, consultants, and other third parties to enter into confidentiality and proprietary rights agreements to control access to and maintain non-disclosure of our proprietary information and to protect our property rights.
As part of our broader intellectual property strategy, we have invested in a patent program covering certain technologies relevant to our business. As of September 30, 2026, we held 40 issued U.S. patents, with an additional 67 U.S. patent applications pending (including 32 nonprovisional and 35 provisional), and 26 issued patents in foreign jurisdictions, with an additional 12 patent applications pending. We continually review our development efforts to assess the existence and patentability of new intellectual property.
In addition to our patent program, we have an ongoing trademark and service mark registration program pursuant to which we register our brand names and product names, taglines, and logos in the United States and other countries, to the extent we determine appropriate and cost-effective. As of September 30, 2026, we held 29 registered trademarks in the United States, with an additional 11 applications pending, and 237 registered trademarks in foreign jurisdictions, with an additional 261 applications pending.
We intend to pursue additional intellectual property protection to the extent we believe it would be beneficial and cost-effective. Intellectual property laws and our procedures and restrictions provide only limited protection, and any of our intellectual property rights may be challenged, invalidated, circumvented, infringed, misappropriated, or violated. For more information, see the section titled “Risk Factors—If we fail to adequately protect our intellectual property rights, our competitive position may be impaired, and we may lose valuable assets, generate reduced revenue, and incur costly litigation to protect our rights, which may adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.”
title: US-PROSPECTUS (S-1/A, preliminary) | BUSINESS > Intellectual Property

location: BUSINESS > Government Regulation
text:
We are subject to laws and regulations of various jurisdictions and government agencies affecting our operations and the provision of our models, platform, and applications, and we have been, and expect to continue to be, subject to inquiries, investigations, and subpoenas by governmental authorities relating to such laws and regulations. We believe that the responsible development of AI requires thoughtful governance, and we actively support efforts by governments and regulatory bodies to establish frameworks that promote safe, beneficial AI. We were founded on the premise that AI systems must be developed with safety and societal benefit as central priorities, and we believe that well-designed regulation can reinforce those values across the industry. Because AI development at the frontier is a relatively nascent and rapidly evolving field, the laws, regulations, and standards in place today were not necessarily designed with these technologies in mind. We have proactively engaged with legislators, regulators, and other stakeholders in the United States and internationally to promote the development of regulatory frameworks that we believe are good for society, our customers, and the long-term health of the economy, and we intend to continue doing so. For example, we entered into an agreement with the CAISSI whereby we committed to provide access to our models for testing and evaluation before and after their public release, agreed to provide model access to the U.K. AI Security Institute for pre-deployment testing consistent with our agreement with the CAISSI, and publicly endorsed California’s Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (SB 53).
As an AI technology company, we are subject to rapidly evolving and increasingly complex laws, regulations, and governmental review across multiple jurisdictions. New laws, rules, regulations, and changes to existing laws and regulations are continuously being adopted, implemented, and interpreted as governments worldwide develop frameworks to address AI development, deployment, and safety. The primary areas of regulation that affect our business include AI-related regulations, data privacy and security, export controls and trade regulations, and other matters such as intellectual property, employment and labor, competition and antitrust, consumer protection, and tax.
The following discussion addresses the most significant regulatory areas affecting our business.
title: US-PROSPECTUS (S-1/A, preliminary) | BUSINESS > Government Regulation

location: BUSINESS > Government Regulation > AI-Related Regulation
text:
AI-Related Regulation
Various governments and regulatory authorities in the United States and other countries have proposed, enacted, or are considering legislation, regulations, and guidance relating to AI model development and deployment, data usage, privacy, data protection, transparency, safety, consumer protection, content generation, intellectual property, cybersecurity, export controls, and competition. For example, in the United States, AI regulation is developing at both federal and state levels. The National Institute of Standards and Technology has developed the AI Risk Management Framework, which is currently voluntary but could potentially inform or shape future mandatory requirements. The FTC and many state attorneys general are interpreting federal and state consumer protection and privacy and security laws to impose standards for the online collection, use, dissemination, other processing, and security of data. Various states have enacted or are considering enacting AI-related legislation. In addition, on September 24, 2026, state attorneys general in New York and New Jersey, together with a coalition of other state and territorial attorneys general, sent a letter to U.S. Senate and House of Representatives leadership to urge Congress to establish comprehensive federal legislation and safety protocols for frontier intelligence. In the EU, the EU AI Act establishes a risk-based framework categorizing AI systems by potential risk level. General-purpose AI models face obligations including transparency requirements, technical documentation, EU copyright compliance, and publication of training data summaries, and those with systemic risk face additional obligations, including model evaluation, systemic risk mitigation, serious incident reporting, and cybersecurity protection. High-risk systems must meet requirements for risk management, data governance, documentation, transparency, human oversight, accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity. Any actual or perceived non-compliance could result in regulatory investigations, enforcement actions and other actions, significant fines, litigation, reputational harm, loss of customer trust, and interruptions in the availability or performance of our products or services; require unfavorable changes to existing products or services; and delay the introduction of future products or services, which could have an adverse effect on our business.
title: US-PROSPECTUS (S-1/A, preliminary) | BUSINESS > Government Regulation > AI-Related Regulation

location: BUSINESS > Government Regulation > AI-Related Regulation
text: We have called for regulation and oversight of frontier intelligence development, including standards primarily relevant to the use of AI to accelerate AI development, so that safety, alignment, and security practices advance in proportion to capabilities. We have also proposed working with the U.S. government and other frontier developers to establish safety and evaluation standards. Certain of the approaches we support, if adopted, could increase our compliance burdens, limit our product development or deployment flexibility, affect how and when we develop or release new models, or otherwise slow our growth.
title: US-PROSPECTUS (S-1/A, preliminary) | BUSINESS > Government Regulation > AI-Related Regulation

location: BUSINESS > Government Regulation > Data Privacy and Security
text:
Data Privacy and Security
We collect, store, transfer, and otherwise process various types of data, including personal information, and are subject to numerous federal, state, local, and foreign laws and regulations addressing privacy, data protection, security, data localization, and the collection, use, transfer, and other processing of data. In the United States, these include comprehensive state privacy laws such as the California Consumer Privacy Act, which imposes obligations on us to, among other things, provide specific privacy disclosures, afford privacy rights such as abilities to opt out of certain processing, selling, or sharing of personal information, and expand consumer rights to personal information. The FTC and many state attorneys general are interpreting federal and state consumer protection and privacy and security laws to impose standards for the online collection, use, dissemination, other processing, and security of data, some of which may be inconsistent. Outside of the United States, numerous foreign jurisdictions, including the EU, United Kingdom, and other jurisdictions in which we operate our business, have enacted similar laws and regulations that affect our business. For example, the EU General Data Protection Regulation and the United Kingdom General Data Protection Regulation impose stringent requirements upon the processing of personal data. The EU’s Digital Services Act imposes requirements on online platforms, while the EU’s Data Act introduces rules on data switching and data sharing. With respect to security, the EU’s Network and Information Security Directive requires risk management and incident reporting. These laws and regulations may be subject to differing interpretations or conflict with the obligations imposed by other legal regimes, such as laws of the United States concerning government access to data. Compliance with these laws and regulations requires significant investment in technical and organizational measures, and these laws and regulations are subject to frequent changes and evolving interpretations. Any actual or perceived non-compliance could result in regulatory investigations, enforcement actions, significant fines, litigation, reputational harm, loss of customer trust, interruptions in the availability or performance of our models, platform, and applications, requirements for unfavorable changes to existing models, platform, and applications, and delays in the introduction of future offerings, which could adversely affect our business.
title: US-PROSPECTUS (S-1/A, preliminary) | BUSINESS > Government Regulation > Data Privacy and Security

location: BUSINESS > Government Regulation > Export Controls and Trade Regulations
text:
Export Controls and Trade Regulations
As a global company, we are subject to laws and regulations governing the provision of our models, platform, and applications across borders, including international treaties, export controls, economic and trade sanctions laws, customs regulations, and local trade rules around the world. The scope, nature, and severity of such controls vary widely across different countries and may change frequently over time. Such laws, rules, and regulations may delay the introduction of our models, platform, and applications or impact our competitiveness through restricting our ability to do business in certain places or with certain entities and individuals. For example, the U.S. Department of Commerce continues to tighten export controls and add firms to the Entity List, which identifies foreign parties that are subject to specific license requirements for the receipt of certain items. The need to obtain licenses to serve or otherwise do business with such parties could limit our ability to conduct business with certain potential customers.
Such restrictions have already affected our offerings directly. For example, in June 2026, the U.S. Department of Commerce imposed worldwide export restrictions on our Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models. In collaboration with the U.S. government and industry partners, we updated our safeguards, and we redeployed our Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models once the U.S. government lifted its restrictions. If similar restrictions were to be imposed in the future, they could limit our ability to recruit talent, to fully utilize our existing workforce, to continue to improve our models, and to make our products available internationally. For more information, see the section titled “Risk Factors—Governmental trade controls, including export and import controls, sanctions, customs requirements, and related regimes, could subject us to liability or loss of contracting privileges or limit our ability to compete in certain markets.” Additionally, changes in the scope or application of export controls or other trade restrictions on accelerators and compute could impact our access to the infrastructure necessary to develop and deploy our models, platform, and applications. As this is an emerging technology area, governments are continuing to refine and could potentially expand the export controls and other trade restrictions applicable to AI models and related technologies. These restrictive governmental actions and any similar measures that may be imposed on U.S. companies by other governments could limit our ability to conduct business globally.

location: BUSINESS > Government Regulation > Other Regulations
text:
Other Regulations
In addition to the specific regulatory areas discussed above, we are subject to various other laws and regulations that affect our business. These include intellectual property laws governing patents, trademarks, and trade secrets. The evolving patent landscape for AI technologies creates risks of infringement claims and uncertain patent protection for our innovations. We may also be subject to evolving copyright regimes. Additionally, we are subject to employment and labor laws governing wages, employee classification, working conditions, benefits, non-discrimination, workplace safety, and termination, with worker misclassification and evolving standards potentially creating significant liabilities and increased labor costs. We are also subject to competition and antitrust laws in the United States, the EU, and other jurisdictions that prohibit anticompetitive conduct, and increased regulatory scrutiny of technology companies regarding market dominance, acquisitions, and AI systems could result in investigations, enforcement actions, significant fines, or requirements to modify business practices. We may also be subject to consumer protection laws that prohibit unfair or deceptive practices and may require disclosures about our AI systems, quality and safety standards, and protection from unfair practices, with violations resulting in enforcement actions and fines. We also face complex and evolving tax obligations across multiple jurisdictions, including income, sales, value-added, and other taxes, with tax authorities potentially disagreeing with our positions and international tax developments affecting our effective tax rate. We are also subject to anti-corruption, anti-bribery, anti-money laundering, environmental, accessibility, advertising, and government procurement regulations. Our healthcare and life sciences offerings, and our customers’ use of our models, platform, and applications in those sectors, may also be subject to laws and regulations governing drugs, biologics, and medical devices, including those administered by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and comparable non-U.S. authorities, as well as healthcare fraud and abuse laws, laws governing the privacy and security of health information, including HIPAA, and laws governing the practice of medicine and the use of AI in healthcare. Failure to comply with these laws could result in enforcement actions, fines, penalties, litigation, reputational harm, and restrictions on our operations that could adversely affect our business, and the evolving regulatory landscape creates significant uncertainty regarding future compliance requirements.

Intellectual Property Matters
We have in the past been, are currently, and may in the future be involved in legal proceedings related to alleged violation and infringement of copyrights and other intellectual property, and in the ordinary course of business, we also receive correspondence from other purported rightsholders of intellectual property asserting potential claims of violation and infringement of such intellectual property.
A series of lawsuits has been filed against us in federal and international courts by plaintiffs asserting copyright infringement based on the use of copyrighted material to train our models. For example, in August 2024, a group of authors filed suit against us claiming infringement of copyrighted books in Bartz. Specifically, the class action plaintiffs alleged that in the process of building and operating our models, we unlawfully copied copyrighted works controlled by the authors. Though we dispute any allegation of wrongdoing, in September 2025, we entered into a settlement agreement with the plaintiffs to settle the case for $1.5 billion, which was approved by the district court in July 2026.
In each of the actions, we believe we have meritorious defenses and dispute any allegation of wrongdoing. Legal proceedings related to these matters can have an adverse effect on us because of defense and settlement costs individually and in the aggregate, diversion of management resources, and other factors.

location: OUR GOVERNANCE STRUCTURE AND ITS GOALS
text: Our novel capital and corporate governance structure has been carefully designed and differs significantly from that of other public companies. We strive to help bring humanity safely into an era where transformative super intelligence18 exerts tremendous and potentially decisive influence over a broad range of human undertakings. Operating as a PBC gives our board of directors the necessary latitude to balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose. In addition, a financially disinterested LTBT, which generally has the power to elect and remove a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors, is designed to supply both the incentives and insights for striking this balance appropriately. We also believe that our seven co-founders are distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission.

location: OUR GOVERNANCE STRUCTURE AND ITS GOALS > Public Benefit Corporation
text: We are incorporated as a PBC under Delaware law, a structure that enables our commitment to AI safety and responsibility. PBCs are a class of corporations that are intended to produce a public benefit and to operate in a responsible and sustainable manner. As a PBC, we are required to balance (i) the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, (ii) the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and (iii) the Company Purpose. This requires our board of directors to weigh multiple factors, including relevant long- and short-term externalities of decisions, alongside the pecuniary interests of our stockholders. To date, we have found that the safety and societal benefit of AI and consideration of the best interests of all key stakeholder groups have generally aligned with our long-term commercial success and stockholders’ long-term monetary interests. However, as a PBC, we may make decisions that we believe appropriately balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose, but that negatively impact the short-, medium-, or long-term performance of our business or the market price of our Class A common stock. There is limited judicial precedent interpreting the balancing requirement applicable to PBCs under Delaware law, and there is therefore uncertainty as to how a court would view our directors’ balancing of these potentially competing interests. For a discussion of these risks, see the section titled “Risk Factors—Our focus on the long-term best interests of our company as a PBC, and the duty of our directors to balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those stakeholders materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose, may conflict with short-, medium-, or long-term financial interests and business performance, which may negatively impact the value of our Class A common stock” and “Risk Factors—As a Delaware public benefit corporation, we may be subject to increased litigation concerning our board of directors’ obligation to balance our stockholders’ pecuniary interests, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose, the occurrence of which may have an adverse impact on our business, financial condition, and results of operations.”

location: OUR GOVERNANCE STRUCTURE AND ITS GOALS > Public Benefit Corporation
text:
In measuring our public benefit performance, our board of directors will consider the objectives set forth in our five mission pillars: that the technical problems of AI safety are solved, that AI safety is a universal practice backstopped by law, that AI strengthens democracy and global stability, that AI expands prosperity and human flourishing, and that AI’s benefits are shared by everyone. We may also address the additional interests of our customers, partners, employees, and other stakeholder constituencies that we may identify from time to time. Neither our amended and restated certificate of incorporation nor our amended and restated bylaws will require that we measure our public benefit performance against an objective third-party standard, and our board of directors will be responsible for establishing and overseeing the standards by which to measure our public benefit performance against these objectives. We currently expect that our objectives and standards will be qualitative in nature and may evolve over time as our business grows and as our understanding of our public benefit impact develops.
For purposes of this prospectus, we use the terms “super intelligence,” “SI,” “artificial intelligence,” and “AI” interchangeably.
As required by Section 366(b) of the DGCL, we will provide our stockholders no less than biennially with a statement assessing our promotion of the Company Purpose and of the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct. The statement will set out our objectives and standards and describe the actions we have taken. We intend to make the statement available to stockholders and the public through our website. We also expect to demonstrate our progress towards these goals by continuing to publish evidence-based research on our website regarding our work and its impact.

location: OUR GOVERNANCE STRUCTURE AND ITS GOALS > Long-Term Benefit Trust
text:
We created the LTBT, which was designed to ensure that we are managed in a manner that responsibly balances our tripartite goals as a PBC: (i) the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, (ii) the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and (iii) the Company Purpose. The LTBT is organized as a common law “noncharitable purpose trust” under Delaware law and governed by the Long-Term Benefit Trust Amended and Restated Trust Agreement (the “Trust Agreement”). The LTBT is intended to operate as an independent body of Trustees with expertise in AI safety, national security, public policy, and social enterprise. The LTBT’s arrangements are designed to minimize the LTBT’s and the Trustees’ exposure to our financial performance and grant the Trustees sufficient independence to ensure we are striking this balance appropriately.
Through a special class of common stock, Class T common stock, the LTBT generally has the authority to elect and remove the Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. Class T common stock has no economic rights.
Decisions regarding our business and affairs are made by our board of directors. While the LTBT has significant influence over our board of directors through its ability to generally elect and remove Class T directors, neither the LTBT nor the Trustees have decision-making authority in the day-to-day management or strategy setting of the company. The LTBT’s role is to select directors who are well equipped to responsibly balance our tripartite goals as a PBC, and to support our management’s decision-making through advice and guidance. Certain actions, such as a merger, consolidation, or sale of all or substantially all of our assets, will require the approval of our board of directors pursuant to Delaware law, a majority of whom are elected by the LTBT.

Election and Removal of Directors
As the sole holder of Class T common stock, the LTBT generally has the authority to elect and remove the Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. Our Class T common stock will not vote on the election or removal of directors elected by the holders of our Class A common stock and Class F common stock, who will be elected or removed solely by the holders of Class A common stock and Class F common stock, voting together. For a discussion of the members of our board of directors who are currently Class T directors and those who will be Class T directors upon the completion of this offering, see the section titled “Management—Board of Directors.”
Prior to nominating or removing a director, the nominating party must provide at least 30 days’ notice to our NGC, which notice period is waivable by our NGC in its discretion. Following the completion of this offering, our NGC will be composed of one Class T director and two directors who are not Class T directors and will act by majority vote.

text: With respect to one of the Class T director seats (the “Specified Class T Director”), the LTBT’s ability to nominate that director, to remove that director without cause, or to change the director designated as the Specified Class T Director is subject to the concurrence of our NGC. If our NGC does not concur with such nomination, removal, or change in designation within 15 days of receiving notice, the matter will be submitted to a vote of the holders of our Class E common stock unless the LTBT elects to withdraw the notice. If submitted to a vote of the holders of Class E common stock, approval of the LTBT’s proposal will require a majority of the votes cast by our Class E common stock (subject to a quorum of a majority of outstanding Class E common stock). The LTBT may withdraw any notice of nomination, removal, or change in designation at any time before the taking of such a vote. Any Class T director, including the Specified Class T Director, may be removed for cause, which will be determined in accordance with Delaware law, without the concurrence of our NGC or the approval of the holders of our Class E common stock; provided, however, that each of the LTBT and the Founder LLC has agreed to provide 30 calendar days’ notice to the other stockholder and our NGC prior to effecting a removal of any director for cause.

Changes to the LTBT and Class T Common Stock
The terms of the LTBT and the rights of our Class T common stock may be amended as follows (any of which, the “Trust Amendment Threshold”):
•if the Trustees are voting in favor of such amendments, upon approval of 80% of the authorized members of our board of directors and 80% of the Trustees then in office (in each case, rounded up or down to the nearest whole number (any exact 0.5 rounding up));
•if our Class F common stock remains outstanding and the Trustees are not voting in favor of such amendments:
◦until the third anniversary of the completion of this offering, upon approval by (i) our Class F common stock acting pursuant to the unanimous approval of the Continuing Founders, (ii) a majority of the votes cast by our Class E common stock (subject to a quorum of 40% of our outstanding Class E common stock), and (iii) a majority of the votes cast by our outstanding Class A common stock (subject to a quorum of a majority of outstanding Class A common stock); or
◦at any time, upon approval by (i) our Class F common stock acting by decision of 66 2/3% of the Continuing Founders (rounded up to the nearest whole number), (ii) 75% of the votes cast by our Class E common stock (subject to a quorum of a majority of outstanding Class E common stock), and (iii) a majority of the votes cast by our Class A common stock (subject to a quorum of a majority of outstanding Class A common stock); or
•if no Class F common stock remains outstanding and the Trustees are not voting in favor of such amendments, upon approval of 85% of our outstanding shares of Class A common stock.
In addition, our Class T common stock may be redeemed by us for no consideration upon approval of persons comprising the above thresholds for amendments of the terms of the LTBT or the rights of our Class T common stock.

Trustees of the LTBT
The LTBT is governed by five Trustees. The Trustees have the authority to appoint the Trustees by majority vote of the Trustees then in office and to remove the Trustees by majority vote of the total number of authorized Trustees or by the unanimous approval of the other Trustees then in office and the approval of our NGC, provided that the LTBT must provide at least 30 days’ prior written notice to our NGC before effecting any such appointment or removal. The notice period is waivable by our NGC in its discretion. Trustees may also be removed by order of the Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware upon petition by a person designated by the Trust Agreement as having the power to enforce the agreement if a Trustee has engaged in disqualifying conduct and removal would best serve the purpose of the LTBT. Trustees will serve annual terms, and there is no limit to the number of terms a Trustee may serve. Trustees are selected based on their expertise in areas relevant to the LTBT’s purpose, including AI safety, national security, public policy, social enterprise, and related fields. In practice to date, the Trustees and company executives have collaborated closely on sourcing, interviewing, and selecting Trustees. Of the five authorized seats for Trustees, one is currently vacant.

location: OUR GOVERNANCE STRUCTURE AND ITS GOALS > Founder Voting Structure
text:
Our Class F common stock will be voted by the Founder LLC in a manner determined in accordance with the Founder LLC Agreement. Generally, the Founder LLC will vote as determined by a majority of the members of the Founder LLC entitled to vote thereunder. Our seven co-founders will initially be the sole members. Upon the incapacity or death of any of our co-founders, a successor member may be admitted to the Founder LLC until the tenth anniversary of the completion of this offering. We refer to our seven co-founders and any successors in the Founder LLC as “Continuing Founders.”
When there have been fewer than three Continuing Founders (not including any successor member who is a “Non-Qualifying Member” as defined in the Founder LLC Agreement) for 90 consecutive calendar days, a 450-day transition period will commence (the “Class F Transition Period”). Upon completion of the Class F Transition Period, all of our Class F common stock and Class E common stock then issued and outstanding will be redeemed by us for no consideration and certain other governance changes will take effect.
Regardless of the length of time that has elapsed since the completion of this offering or the circumstances that resulted in the removal of a Continuing Founder, one or more successor members may be admitted to the Founder LLC during the Class F Transition Period as needed to ensure that there are three Continuing Founders serving until completion of the Class F Transition Period. The admission of any successor member during the Class F Transition Period will not cure the event that commenced the Class F Transition Period or extend the Class F Transition Period. For additional information, see the section titled “Description of Capital Stock.”
A Continuing Founder will be removed from the Founder LLC upon the earliest to occur of (i) such Continuing Founder’s resignation as a member of the Founder LLC; (ii) such Continuing Founder’s death or incapacity; (iii) with respect to each of our seven original co-founders, such original co-founder’s ceasing to hold (together with such original co-founder’s related holders) on any record date for a vote of our stockholders a number of shares

The Founder LLC Agreement will not govern the voting of any shares of our Class A common stock held by the co-founders or their related holders. Each co-founder (or their related holders) will be able to vote shares of our Class A common stock held by them in their discretion, regardless of the manner in which the Founder LLC will vote our Class F common stock.
The voting power of our Class F common stock will not be impacted by future issuances of our capital stock that may cause economic or voting dilution to stockholders, such as issuances for capital raising purposes, acquisitions, or employee compensation. This structure will allow the Founder LLC to determine the outcome of matters submitted to a vote of our stockholders generally, including the election of those directors not elected by the LTBT, certain amendments to our organizational documents, and the approval by our stockholders of any merger, consolidation, sale of substantially all our assets, or other major corporate transaction requiring stockholder approval.

text:
Philanthropy
We founded Anthropic on the belief that the most transformative technology in human history demands an extraordinary level of responsibility, and that responsibility extends far beyond building safe systems. We intend to direct a meaningful portion of our resources toward ensuring that frontier intelligence is safe and its benefits are broadly distributed, which we refer to as our public benefit initiatives. These initiatives include the Initial Public Benefit Issuance and the future Public Benefit Issuances. In addition, our co-founders have each pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal equity in Anthropic to philanthropic causes. For additional information regarding these pledges, including related risks, see the section titled “Risk Factors—Risks Related to Ownership of our Class A Common Stock.” Separate from the co-founders’ pledges, we also maintain a donation matching program through which employees can pledge a meaningful portion of their equity awards toward charitable giving, which we match with shares of our Class N common stock. Further, certain donor-advised funds may from time to time receive donations of shares directly from us or from one or more of our stockholders, and we are party to certain irrevocable proxy agreements with such donor-advised funds, as described under “Certain Relationships and Related Person Transactions—Irrevocable Proxy Agreements.”

text:
Our Class E common stock will not have any right to vote except on certain specified matters (or as otherwise required by law): the nomination or proposed removal of the Specified Class T Director or a change in the director designated as the Specified Class T Director (in circumstances where our NGC does not concur with the LTBT’s proposed action) and certain proposals to amend the terms of the LTBT and the rights of our Class T common stock or to redeem our Class T common stock.
When voting upon a proposal to nominate or remove the Specified Class T Director or a change in the director designated as the Specified Class T Director (in circumstances where our NGC does not concur with the LTBT’s proposed action), the requisite approval of our Class E common stock will require a majority of votes cast by our Class E common stock and quorum will require the presence, in person or by proxy, of a majority of outstanding shares of Class E common stock.
When voting on a proposal to amend the terms of the LTBT or the rights of our Class T common stock or to redeem our Class T common stock, in addition to the requisite approval of our Class A common stock as described more fully in the section titled “—Long-Term Benefit Trust—Changes to the LTBT and Class T Common Stock,” the requisite approval of our Class E common stock will require:
•until the third anniversary of the completion of this offering, if our Class F common stock is acting pursuant to the unanimous approval of the Continuing Founders, a majority of the votes cast by our Class E common stock (subject to a quorum of 40% of our outstanding Class E common stock); or
•at any time when our Class F common stock remains outstanding, 75% of the votes cast by our Class E common stock (subject to a quorum of a majority of outstanding Class E common stock).

text:
Our amended and restated certificate of incorporation, which will become effective immediately prior to the completion of this offering, will authorize Class E common stock, which will be issued to our employees as follows: (i) one share of Class E common stock for each six months of employment completed with us and (ii) one share of Class E common stock for each share of Class A common stock that such employee has pledged to donate through our donation matching program, or any similar program we may establish in the future. The timing for issuing Class E common stock will be determined after the completion of this offering. Our co-founders will not receive any shares of Class E common stock, and to the extent that a holder of Class E common stock later serves as a successor to any co-founder’s interest in the Founder LLC, that holder will not be able to vote any Class E common stock they hold during the period of such service.
Following an employee’s separation from employment with us other than for cause, one-half of such employee’s then-outstanding shares of Class E common stock will be automatically redeemed by us annually, and all of such employee’s shares will be automatically redeemed upon such employee’s death, incapacity, termination for cause, or commencement of service with a direct competitor. All shares of Class E common stock will also be automatically redeemed at such time as no Class F common stock remains outstanding. Any redemption of Class E common stock will be made for no consideration.

location: OUR GOVERNANCE STRUCTURE AND ITS GOALS > Board Governance
text:
Decisions regarding our business and affairs are made by our board of directors. Immediately prior to the completion of this offering, we will enter into the Stockholders’ Agreement with the LTBT and the Founder LLC, under which they will agree to vote their shares and take other actions to give effect to the board composition, director nomination, and director removal provisions described in our governing documents. Collectively, the LTBT and the Founder LLC will have the ability to elect all members of our board of directors. Regardless of the class or classes of stock by which a director is elected, there is no limit to the number of terms a director may serve.
While the LTBT has significant influence over our board of directors through its ability to generally elect and remove a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors, neither the LTBT nor the Trustees have decision-making authority in the day-to-day management or strategy setting of the company. The LTBT’s role is to select directors who are well equipped to make decisions in furtherance of the responsible balancing of the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose, and to support our management’s decision-making through advice and guidance. The Trustees aim to choose directors who have the necessary business skills, experience, and expertise to oversee the management of our business effectively and in a manner that responsibly balances (i) the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, (ii) the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and (iii) the Company Purpose.
The Founder LLC will also have significant influence over our business and affairs through its ability to vote our Class F common stock, which is entitled to an aggregate number of votes that equals 50.1% of the total voting power of our outstanding shares of capital stock as of the applicable record date with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally. The Founder LLC will be able to elect and remove the directors who are not Class T directors and determine the outcome of all matters submitted to a vote of our stockholders generally (including the approval of any merger, sale of our company, or other significant corporate transaction requiring stockholder approval) for the foreseeable future.

text: We are considered a “controlled company” within the meaning of the Nasdaq Global Select Market corporate governance requirements because the LTBT, as the sole holder of our Class T common stock, generally has the power to elect a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. As such, we are permitted to opt out of compliance with certain Nasdaq Global Select Market corporate governance requirements. Accordingly, if we elect not to comply with certain requirements, you will not have the same protections afforded to stockholders of companies that are subject to all of the Nasdaq Global Select Market corporate governance requirements. Although we qualify as a “controlled company,” we do not expect to rely on this exemption except with respect to our NGC, which will not consist entirely of independent directors. Our board of directors currently consists of a majority of independent directors and our audit and compensation committees currently consist entirely of independent directors.

text:
Class T Sunset Time | Class F Sunset Time
Trigger | The Class T Sunset Time occurs when no Class T common stock remains outstanding, including due to the redemption of our Class T common stock or an amendment to the rights of our Class T common stock that eliminates our Class T common stock, which in each case requires the approval of persons comprising the Trust Amendment Threshold. The Trust Amendment Threshold may be satisfied as follows: •if the Trustees are voting in favor of the action, upon approval of 80% of the authorized members of our board of directors and 80% of the Trustees then in office (in each case, rounded up or down to the nearest whole number (any exact 0.5 rounding up)); •if our Class F common stock remains outstanding and the Trustees are not voting in favor of the action: ◦until the third anniversary of the completion of this offering, upon approval by (i) our Class F common stock acting pursuant to the unanimous approval of the Continuing Founders, (ii) a majority of the votes cast by our Class E common stock (subject to a quorum of 40% of our outstanding Class E common stock), and (iii) a majority of the votes cast by outstanding Class A common stock (subject to a quorum of a majority of outstanding Class A common stock); or ◦at any time, upon approval by (i) the Class F common stock acting by decision of 66 2/3% of the Continuing Founders (rounded up to the nearest whole number), (ii) 75% of the votes cast by our Class E common stock (subject to a quorum of a majority of outstanding Class E common stock), and (iii) a majority of the votes cast by our Class A common stock (subject to a quorum of a majority of outstanding Class A common stock); or | The Class F Sunset Time occurs on the earlier of (i) the time when no Class F common stock remains outstanding, including due to the redemption of our Class F common stock agreed to by a Supermajority of the Continuing Founders or upon the dissolution of the Founder LLC, and (ii) the completion of the Class F Transition Period. The Class F Transition Period commences when there have been fewer than three Continuing Founders (not including any successor member who is a “Non-Qualifying Member” as defined in the Founder LLC Agreement) for 90 consecutive calendar days. A Continuing Founder will be removed from the Founder LLC upon the earliest to occur of (i) such Continuing Founder’s resignation as a member of the Founder LLC; (ii) such Continuing Founder’s death or incapacity; (iii) with respect to each of our seven original co-founders, such original co-founder’s ceasing to hold (together with such original co-founder’s related holders) on any record date for a vote of our stockholders a number of shares of Class A common stock (including shares subject to options, RSUs, and other convertible securities) equal to at least 2% of the shares of Class A common stock held by such original co-founder and their related holders as of the completion of this offering; (iv) such Continuing Founder’s removal for “cause,” which includes specified competitive activities described in the Founder LLC Agreement; (v) with respect to any successor member admitted to the Founder LLC prior to the commencement of the Class F Transition Period, other than a successor member who is a member during the Class F Transition Period, the tenth anniversary of the completion of this offering; or (vi) with respect to each of our seven original co- founders, the commencement of a leave of absence approved by a Supermajority of the other Continuing Founders, which may not be approved during the Class F Transition Period or if the grant of the leave of absence would itself cause the Class F Transition Period to commence.

text:
Class T Sunset Time | Class F Sunset Time
•if no Class F common stock remains outstanding and the Trustees are not voting in favor of the action, upon approval of 85% of our outstanding Class A common stock. The Class T Sunset Time does not occur automatically upon the lapse of time or the occurrence of specific events. Any action resulting in the occurrence of the Class T Sunset Time requires approval of persons comprising the Trust Amendment Threshold. The Class T Sunset Time, once triggered, is not subject to extension, delay, or waiver. | Removals due to resignation, death, or the occurrence of the tenth anniversary of the completion of this offering occur automatically without any determination by any other person. Removals due to incapacity require determination by a qualified physician jointly selected by the affected Continuing Founder and a majority of the other Continuing Founders (in the case of physical or mental impairment) or determination by a Supermajority of the other Continuing Founders (in the case of wrongful imprisonment, unlawful detention, or captivity or restraint), subject to the affected Continuing Founder’s right to contest such determination. Removals due to cause require an affirmative determination by a Supermajority of the other Continuing Founders, subject to the affected Continuing Founder’s right to contest such determination or, in the case of specified categories of cause, to cure the basis for such removal. Removals due to incapacity, cause, or the failure to maintain the minimum ownership threshold require prior written notice from the Founder LLC by action of a majority of the other Continuing Founders. If a Continuing Founder is removed due to death or incapacity during the first ten years following the completion of this offering, a successor member may be admitted to the Founder LLC and will count toward the three Continuing Founders required to avoid triggering the Class F Transition Period until the tenth anniversary of the completion of this offering. The Class F Sunset Time, once triggered, is not subject to extension, delay, or waiver.

text:

Changes in Voting Power and Director Election and Removal Rights | Prior to the Class T Sunset Time, the LTBT, as the sole holder of Class T common stock, will generally have the authority to elect and remove the Class T directors, who constitute a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. The share of our Class T common stock has no voting rights with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally, except as set forth within our amended and restated certificate of incorporation, including with respect to the election of a majority of our board of directors or as required by law. Following the Class T Sunset Time, if our Class F common stock remains outstanding, our Class A common stock and Class F common stock, voting together as a single class, will elect all of our directors. Because our Class F common stock is entitled to an aggregate number of votes equal to 50.1% of the total voting power of our outstanding shares of capital stock, the Founder LLC would have the ability to determine the outcome of all matters submitted to a vote of stockholders generally, including the election of all directors. If neither our Class T common stock nor Class F common stock remains outstanding, our Class A common stock would have the ability to determine the outcome of all matters submitted to a vote of stockholders generally, including the election of all directors. | Prior to the Class F Sunset Time, our Class F common stock will be entitled to an aggregate number of votes that equals 50.1% of the total voting power of our outstanding shares of capital stock as of the applicable record date and, together with our Class A common stock, voting together as a single class, will elect the directors other than the Class T directors and decide all other matters put to a vote of stockholders generally. Immediately after the Class F Sunset Time, if our Class T common stock remains outstanding, the LTBT would continue to have the authority to elect and remove the Class T directors, who would constitute a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. However, the LTBT would no longer need to comply with the procedures for nomination, removal, or change in the Class T director designated as the Specified Class T Director. In such a case, our Class A common stock would elect and remove the remaining directors and decide all other matters put to a vote of stockholders generally. If neither our Class T common stock nor Class F common stock remains outstanding, our Class A common stock would have the ability to determine the outcome of all matters submitted to a vote of stockholders generally, including the election of all directors.

•Class T common stock. The holder of our Class T common stock has no voting rights with respect to matters submitted to stockholders, except as set forth within our amended and restated certificate of incorporation with respect to the election of a majority of our board of directors, the redemption of our Class E common stock, certain amendments to the rights of our Class F common stock, or as otherwise required by law, such as certain amendments to our amended and restated certificate of incorporation that would adversely affect the powers, preferences, or special rights of our Class T common stock, on which the DGCL entitles such holder to vote separately as a class.

Conversion and Transferability
•Class A common stock. Our Class A common stock will not be convertible into any other class or series of capital stock. Subject to compliance with applicable law and the restrictions described in the section titled “Shares Eligible for Future Sale—Lock-Up and Market Standoff Agreements,” our Class A common stock can be transferred.
•Class N common stock. The holders of our Class N common stock are primarily strategic business partners. Subject to compliance with applicable law and the restrictions described in the section titled “Shares Eligible for Future Sale—Lock-Up and Market Standoff Agreements,” our Class N common stock can be transferred. The shares of Class N common stock will automatically convert into an equal number of shares of Class A common stock upon a transfer effected through: (i) a registered offering or an open market sale of such shares or (ii) a transfer to a third party (A) that is not a holder of Class N common stock (or an affiliate of a holder of Class N common stock) and (B) that will not beneficially own or control more than 9.99% of the shares of any class or series of our equity securities after giving effect to the transfer.
•Class T common stock. Our Class T common stock will not be convertible into any other class or series of capital stock. Our Class T common stock is transferable only upon the approval of persons comprising the Trust Amendment Threshold. Because the persons comprising the Trust Amendment Threshold have the power to modify or terminate the LTBT and the rights of our Class T common stock entirely, there is no separate restriction on the identity of a permissible transferee of our Class T common stock.
•Class F common stock. Our Class F common stock will not be convertible into any other class or series of capital stock. Our Class F common stock is not transferable except in the case of a reorganization or redomiciliation of the Founder LLC that is approved by our board of directors and does not result in a change to the members of the Founder LLC.
•Class E common stock. Our Class E common stock will not be convertible into any other class or series of capital stock and is not transferable.
